entries.name: Farce
entries.description: Comedy built as a machine, where the plot itself is the joke and the characters are its moving parts.
entries.principle: Farce is the only comic form in which structure is the primary source of laughter rather than its delivery system. A farce sets a mechanism running in its first act, accelerates it past the point any character can control, and derives its comedy from watching the respectable be dismantled by their own arrangements. Who pays is always the person with most to lose socially; when is dictated by the machine, not by the writer's sense of timing.
entries.example: Feydeau's Une puce à l'oreille (1907) builds the mechanism from mistaken hotel identities and a double; Michael Frayn's Noises Off (1982) makes the mechanism visible by staging the same act three times, forwards, from backstage, and in collapse; Fawlty Towers runs a compressed one-room farce every episode.
entries.application: Build the machine before the characters. Ask what arrangement, once disturbed, forces every subsequent event, then cast people who cannot afford its exposure. If a scene can be cut without breaking the chain, it is not farce, it is comedy in a farce's clothing.

entries.name: Screwball
entries.description: Class inversion and verbal velocity, in which two people argue their way toward each other faster than either can think.
entries.principle: Screwball is not romantic comedy with jokes. Its engine is status reversal conducted at a speed that prevents deliberation, usually across a class line, and its dignity cost falls on the party with the higher status at the start. Remove the velocity and the inversion and the courtship arc that remains is a different genre entirely, which is why screwball stays with Comedy while romantic comedy hands off.
entries.example: His Girl Friday (1940) runs dialogue at a rate that makes the reporters' professional cynicism a form of intimacy; Bringing Up Baby (1938) strips a paleontologist of every marker of expertise; The Lady Eve (1941) inverts predator and mark twice.
entries.application: Write the argument before the attraction. Give the higher-status character something to lose in every exchange and let them lose a piece of it per scene. Cut any line that either party has time to consider.

entries.name: Picaresque
entries.description: An episodic journey by a low-born survivor through a society the reader is invited to judge instead.
entries.principle: The picaresque protects its protagonist and indicts the world. Because the picaro has no dignity to lose, the cost transfers outward to each institution encountered, and the form's episodic looseness is a feature rather than a structural weakness. Its risk is that an episodic frame with nothing to indict becomes a series of anecdotes.
entries.example: Lazarillo de Tormes (1554) established the form's blind-beggar-to-priest ladder of exploiters; Fielding's Tom Jones (1749) formalised it in English; Hašek's Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka (1921) turned the picaro's incompetence into a weapon against an army.
entries.application: Choose the institutions before the episodes. Give your picaro a survival skill rather than a virtue, and make each host reveal itself by how it treats someone it can afford to mistreat.

entries.name: Comic Epic and Mock-Heroic
entries.description: Grand form deliberately mismatched to small content, so the form itself does the mocking.
entries.principle: Mock-heroic works by holding an elevated register perfectly steady over material that cannot support it. The gap is the joke and the writer must never acknowledge it. What pays is the subject's self-importance, and the timing is architectural rather than local: the reader laughs cumulatively, at the sustained refusal to drop the register.
entries.example: Pope's The Rape of the Lock (1714) applies Homeric machinery to a stolen curl of hair; Byron's Don Juan (1819) uses ottava rima's rhyme scheme to force bathos on schedule; Fielding described Joseph Andrews (1742) as a comic epic poem in prose and meant the form seriously.
entries.application: Pick the register first and hold it without exception. Any wink at the reader collapses the gap and converts the piece into ordinary parody.

entries.name: Shaggy-Dog and Anti-Joke
entries.description: A long structure whose payoff is the deliberate refusal of the payoff the structure promised.
entries.principle: The shaggy-dog story converts the audience's own investment into the comic material. Its cost falls on the listener, who has been made complicit by continuing to listen, and its timing is unusually cruel because the length must be genuinely uncomfortable for the ending to work. It fails absolutely if the teller seems unaware of the length.
entries.example: Norm Macdonald's moth joke, told on Conan in 2009, spends several minutes on Dostoevskian misery to arrive at a one-line non-answer; Sterne's Tristram Shandy (1759) sustains the principle across nine volumes by digressing away from its own birth.
entries.application: Make the digressions individually good enough to justify themselves, so the audience cannot tell whether they are being served or strung along until the ending settles it.

entries.name: Satire
entries.description: Comedy with a target it intends to damage, and a position it can be held to.
entries.principle: Satire is the comic mode that accepts accountability. It names who pays and asks the reader to agree, which means it can be answered, refuted, and read against its own intent in a way no other comic form can. Its characteristic failure is not offence but flattery: satire that confirms an audience's existing judgement has entertained rather than attacked.
entries.example: Swift's A Modest Proposal (1729) sustains an economic register over an unspeakable proposal and refuses to break it; The Thick of It exposes the machinery of political language rather than the politics; Gogol's Revizor (1836) indicts an entire town by giving it nothing to fear but a rumour.
entries.application: State the target in one sentence before writing. If the sentence is a position your intended audience already holds, the piece is flattery and you have chosen the wrong target.

entries.name: Parody and Pastiche
entries.description: Comedy that borrows another work's form precisely enough to expose what the form conceals.
entries.principle: Parody attacks the manner; pastiche inhabits it. Both require the borrowed form to be reproduced with real competence, because an inaccurate parody indicts nothing, and this is the comic mode most dependent on the audience knowing the original. Who pays is the original's pretension rather than the original itself, which is why the best parody usually comes from people who love the source.
entries.example: Airplane! (1980) reproduces the disaster film's staging exactly and changes only the content of the dialogue; This Is Spinal Tap (1984) is close enough to rock documentary that musicians recognised themselves in it; Cold Comfort Farm (1932) parodies the rural gothic novel by out-writing it.
entries.application: Reproduce the form before altering it, and test the reproduction on someone who likes the original. If they do not recognise the manner, the parody has no purchase.

entries.name: Black Comedy
entries.description: Comedy applied to material that ordinarily forbids it, with the discomfort kept rather than dissolved.
entries.principle: Black comedy does not make its subject bearable. It uses the comic frame to hold the reader in proximity to death, atrocity or cruelty for longer than a serious treatment could, and the laugh is a symptom of that proximity rather than a relief from it. The distinction from mere tastelessness is whether the material or the audience is the target.
entries.example: Heller's Catch-22 (1961) makes military logic funny in order to make it inescapable; Dr. Strangelove (1964) plays nuclear annihilation as procedural competence; Evelyn Waugh's The Loved One (1948) turns an industry's euphemism against it.
entries.application: Decide whether your comedy is anaesthetic or accelerant before the first draft. If the laugh lets the reader off, the material has been used as an occasion rather than treated.

entries.name: Topical and Late-Night Satire
entries.description: Satire written against a deadline about events the audience learned of the same week.
entries.principle: Topicality buys shared context for free and spends the piece's shelf life to get it. The form's craft problem is that the audience arrives already holding a position, so the writing must find the angle they have not had time to reach rather than the one they arrived with. It dates faster than any other comic form and knows it.
entries.example: Spitting Image (1984) fixed caricatures that outlived the politicians; Have I Got News for You (1990) built a durable format around perishable material; The Daily Show (1996) made the video clip juxtaposition its primary rhetorical device.
entries.application: Write from the second thought, not the first. Assume every obvious observation has already been made by the audience on the way to the theatre.

entries.name: Comedy of Manners
entries.description: Comedy generated by a codified social surface and the pressure of what cannot be said beneath it.
entries.principle: The comedy of manners requires a code the audience can read and characters who are fluent in it. Its dignity cost is administered in public and in small denominations, and the wit is not decoration but the actual weapon, since the code forbids anything more direct. It fails wherever the audience cannot infer the rules from the behaviour.
entries.example: Congreve's The Way of the World (1700) makes a marriage contract the site of the wit; Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest (1895) inverts the code by having everyone obey it perfectly; Frasier transplanted the form to a radio station and a Seattle apartment.
entries.application: Establish the code in the first scene through a minor violation, so the audience learns the rules by watching them enforced rather than being told them.

entries.name: Comedy of Humours
entries.description: Characters built as single dominant traits, colliding predictably and productively.
entries.principle: The comedy of humours trades psychological depth for combinatorial reliability. Once a character is one thing, every pairing generates a scene, and the audience's pleasure comes from prediction confirmed rather than surprise. The trait must be a driver rather than a label, or the character produces catchphrases instead of behaviour.
entries.example: Jonson's Every Man in His Humour (1598) named the theory and demonstrated it; Volpone (1606) sets avarice against avarice; Molière's Le Misanthrope (1666) is the form at its most serious, since Alceste's single trait is honesty and it destroys him.
entries.application: Give each character one appetite and one thing they cannot do, then put the appetite of one in the path of the incapacity of another. Never resolve the trait.

entries.name: Comic Monologue and Character Comedy
entries.description: A sustained single voice whose comedy is the distance between what the speaker says and what the audience hears.
entries.principle: Character comedy runs on unreliable self-report. The speaker pays without knowing it, and the audience is placed in the uncomfortable position of understanding the speaker better than the speaker does. The form is nearly unique in comedy in that its laughs and its pathos come from the same mechanism, which is why the best examples turn sad without changing method.
entries.example: Alan Bennett's Talking Heads (1988) uses the technique to devastating effect within a comic register; Steve Coogan's Alan Partridge sustains a persona across three decades and several formats; the Grossmiths' The Diary of a Nobody (1892) is the form's founding text in English.
entries.application: Write what the character believes they are conveying, then check that a reader can reconstruct what is actually happening from the same words. If they cannot, the gap is too wide or too narrow.

entries.name: Children's and Family Comedy
entries.description: Comedy written to work for two audiences at once, without either being condescended to.
entries.principle: Family comedy is a dual-address problem, not a diluted adult comedy. The child's layer runs on physical logic, transgression against adult rules, and the pleasure of superior knowledge; the adult's layer runs on recognition of the adult being satirised. Material that only serves one layer is not family comedy, and jokes pitched over children's heads to keep adults awake are the form's characteristic cheat.
entries.example: Roald Dahl's writing gives children the moral authority and makes adults the grotesques; Sue Townsend's The Secret Diary of Adrian Mole Aged 13¾ (1982) is a character monologue whose two readings are simultaneous; Horrible Histories uses sketch structure to make the adult's layer historical rather than risqué.
entries.application: Draft the child's layer first and make it complete on its own. Add the adult layer as recognition rather than as innuendo, and check nothing in the second layer requires the first to be less funny.

entries.name: Sitcom (Multi-Camera)
entries.description: Comedy staged for a live audience on standing sets, where the laugh is structural input rather than decoration.
entries.principle: Multi-camera sitcom is written to a rhythm imposed by a room. The laugh break is a beat the script must accommodate, which caps line density, forces the joke to the end of the speech, and makes the audience's reaction part of the composition rather than a response to it. The standing set is the other constraint: characters must have a plausible reason to be in the same three rooms every week.
entries.example: I Love Lucy (1951) established the three-camera film technique and the set economy that followed from it; Cheers (1982) built its entire premise around a reason for the cast to be in one room; Seinfeld (1989) pushed the form's plot mechanics to convergence while keeping its rhythm.
entries.application: Write to the stress position and stop. Read every speech aloud with a two-second pause after the last word and cut anything that needs to survive the pause.

entries.name: Sitcom (Single-Camera)
entries.description: Comedy shot like film, without a room to play to, running denser script and able to break its own frame.
entries.principle: Removing the laugh break removes the beat that governed multi-camera writing, and roughly fifteen to twenty per cent more script fits the same minute. That density buys interiority, location, montage and direct address, and it costs the writer the audience's confirmation that a joke has landed. Single-camera comedy therefore has to be structurally funny, because nothing in the transmission tells the viewer when to laugh.
entries.example: The Larry Sanders Show (1992) used the absence of a laugh track to make discomfort sustainable; Arrested Development (2003) built density into narration and running gags; Fleabag (2016) made the frame-break a character's defence mechanism and then, in its second series, had another character notice it.
entries.application: Do not simply delete the laugh breaks from a multi-camera script. Rebuild the scenes to earn the density: use the recovered seconds for behaviour and reaction rather than for more lines.

entries.name: Sketch
entries.description: A single premise established, escalated, and abandoned before it can be resolved.
entries.principle: Sketch is the purest test of premise and exit. It has no arc, no continuity obligation and no time to earn sympathy, so the premise must be legible within twenty seconds and the escalation must be logical rather than merely louder. The exit is the form's hardest craft problem, since a premise fully escalated has nowhere to go and most sketches die at the end rather than in the middle.
entries.example: Monty Python's Flying Circus (1969) solved the exit problem partly by refusing it, cutting away or collapsing the frame; Saturday Night Live (1975) made the recurring sketch a commercial format with its own decay curve; I Think You Should Leave (2019) escalates by having one character refuse to accept the sketch has ended.
entries.application: Write the exit before the middle. If you cannot say how it ends, you have a premise rather than a sketch.

entries.name: Mockumentary
entries.description: Comedy that borrows documentary's authority so its subjects can expose themselves to camera.
entries.principle: The mockumentary's device is not the camera but the interview: it licenses characters to state their self-image directly, which the action then contradicts. This makes it the most efficient available machine for character comedy, and its cost is that everything must remain plausible as footage. The moment the form gets a shot the crew could not have taken, the contract breaks.
entries.example: This Is Spinal Tap (1984) built the form's grammar and the ensemble improvisation behind it; The Office (2001) added the look to camera as a silent editorial line; What We Do in the Shadows (2014) proved the device survives supernatural content because the interview does the work.
entries.application: Ask of every shot who is holding the camera and why the subject allowed it. Use the interview for what characters believe and the footage for what is true.

entries.name: Stand-Up
entries.description: One person, unprotected by character or plot, testing material against a room in real time.
entries.principle: Stand-up is the form in which comedy's pass-fail signal is most exposed, because there is nothing between the performer and the verdict. The persona is the only shield, and it determines who may pay: a self-deprecating persona can attack targets a confident one cannot. Material is written on stage rather than at a desk, since the room supplies information no draft can.
entries.example: Richard Pryor's Live on the Sunset Strip (1982) uses the act-out to voice objects and organs, converting confession into character work; George Carlin's later work moves the persona from observer to prosecutor; Hannah Gadsby's Nanette (2018) withholds the release the form promises in order to argue about the form itself.
entries.application: Establish the persona before the first hard joke, because the persona sets your permissions. Assume any material not tested in a room is unfinished.

entries.name: Improvisation
entries.description: Comedy composed in performance under rules designed to prevent the performers from protecting themselves.
entries.principle: Improvisation's rules exist to remove the instinct to stay safe. Accepting the offer, raising the stakes and playing status honestly all forbid the defensive move of refusing what a partner has established. Its comedy comes from watching structure emerge under conditions where it should not, which means an audience forgives weak jokes and never forgives a blocked offer.
entries.example: Keith Johnstone's Impro (1979) codified status transactions as the engine of scene work; Del Close's long-form Harold, documented in Truth in Comedy (1994), organises an hour around callbacks discovered rather than planned; Whose Line Is It Anyway? (1988) made short-form's constraint-as-premise legible to a television audience.
entries.application: Use improvisation as a drafting tool rather than only a performance form. Play a scene to find what the characters want, then write the version that knows.

entries.name: Slapstick
entries.description: Comedy in which the body is the site of the cost and physics is the antagonist.
entries.principle: Slapstick is the clearest case of the organising claim, since the dignity at risk is entirely physical and the timing is measurable in frames. Its craft is precision rather than violence, and it requires the performer to appear genuinely endangered while remaining in complete control. It is also the form most damaged by editing, because the audience must believe the space and the body are continuous.
entries.example: Keaton's The General (1926) plays every stunt in wide shot so the audience can verify it; Chaplin's Modern Times (1936) makes the machine the aggressor and the body the material; Tati's Les Vacances de Monsieur Hulot (1953) slows the form down until the comedy is spatial rather than kinetic.
entries.application: Stage it in one shot if you can, and design the space before the gag. If the audience cannot see the geometry, they cannot anticipate, and anticipation is most of the laugh.

entries.name: Light Verse
entries.description: Comedy in which metre and rhyme are the delivery mechanism and the constraint is the joke's collaborator.
entries.principle: Light verse puts the punchline where the form guarantees a stress, which is why a rhyme can carry material that would fall flat in prose. The reader is made complicit by anticipating the rhyme, so the comedy is partly their own participation. Its besetting failure is the rhyme that dictates the sense rather than serving it.
entries.example: Hilaire Belloc's Cautionary Tales for Children (1907) uses the nursery register to deliver disproportionate punishment deadpan; Ogden Nash extends lines past all reason to reach a rhyme and makes the strain the joke; Wendy Cope's Making Cocoa for Kingsley Amis (1986) uses parody forms to conduct real argument.
entries.application: Draft the punchline word first and build the line backwards to land on it. If the rhyme forces a thought you did not intend, cut the couplet rather than the thought.

entries.name: The Humorous Essay and Column
entries.description: A first-person prose voice that finds its comedy in observation and in the admission of its own position.
entries.principle: The humorous essay's authority comes from the writer paying first. It establishes a persona willing to be the payer, which then licenses observation about others, and its unit is the paragraph rather than the joke. The column form adds a deadline and a fixed length, which is why the best columnists are structurally recognisable from a hundred words in.
entries.example: Twain's travel writing established the American form's mixture of deadpan reportage and tall tale; Thurber's My Life and Hard Times (1933) treats family chaos with the syntax of memoir; David Sedaris's Me Talk Pretty One Day (2000) puts the narrator's own humiliation in front of every observation about anyone else.
entries.application: Find what you are willing to lose before deciding what you are going to observe. An essay that only observes others reads as superiority and will not be forgiven for it.

entries.name: Absurdist and Nonsense
entries.description: Comedy in which no dignity is at risk, and the organising claim does not reach.
entries.principle: This pack's organising claim is that comedy is the deliberate mismanagement of dignity, and this subgenre is the conceded exception. Nonsense verse, pure wordplay and absurdist non-sequitur put nothing at stake for anyone; their pleasure is the collapse of sense itself, and rescuing them by saying that language is the thing humiliated makes the claim unfalsifiable. The exception is carded rather than argued away.
entries.example: Edward Lear's A Book of Nonsense (1846) invents vocabulary with no referent and no target; The Goon Show (1951) sustains non-sequitur across a radio half-hour; Ionesco's La Cantatrice chauve (1950) and Beckett's En attendant Godot (1953) build the absurd into dramatic structure rather than decorating it.
entries.application: Do not import a target you do not need. If nonsense is what you are writing, the discipline is internal consistency of invention, not escalation of cost.

entries.name: Romcom and the Courtship Promise
entries.description: Hands off to romance-reference, which owns the courtship arc; Comedy keeps only what the jokes are doing to it.
entries.principle: Apply the boundary test and romantic comedy fails it. Remove every joke from When Harry Met Sally and a coherent courtship structure remains, complete with its promise of the ending; remove the class inversion and verbal velocity from His Girl Friday and nothing does. The romcom's load-bearing craft is the management of a promise the audience already holds, which is Romance's subject, not Comedy's.
entries.example: The Romance pack carries the subgenre card and the craft, and cards Nora Ephron, Richard Curtis, Amy Heckerling, Ernst Lubitsch and Preston Sturges as authors. Comedy's residual is narrow: the comic obstacle that must not resolve the romance early, and the tonal handbrake at the point the film stops being funny. Screwball is retained here as a separate card because it fails the same test in the opposite direction.
entries.application: For courtship structure, obstacle design and the promise, go to romance-reference. Come back here for how the comic register survives the third act, and for the screwball card if velocity rather than promise is your engine.

entries.name: Comic Crime and the Caper
entries.description: Hands off to mystery-crime-thriller-reference; the plot machinery is the puzzle's, not the farce's.
entries.principle: The caper looks like farce because both run on machinery, but the machinery is doing different work. A caper's plan must be fair to the reader and its reversals must be solvable, which is a mystery obligation; a farce's mechanism only has to be inescapable. Comic crime is crime plotting with a comic surface, and the plotting is the harder half.
entries.example: The MCT pack owns the subgenre and cards Donald E. Westlake and Richard Stark, Carl Hiaasen, Janet Evanovich, Elmore Leonard and Richard Osman, and carries a craft card on humour in crime fiction. Comedy's residual is the incompetence gradient: which member of the crew is allowed to be stupid, and how stupid, before the plan stops being fair.
entries.application: Build the plan in mystery-crime-thriller-reference. Use this pack for the ensemble's fixed-relations grid and for the escalation cards, which is what a caper's second act actually runs on.

entries.name: War Comedy and the Uniformed Absurd
entries.description: Hands off to war-military-reference, which owns the satiric and absurdist war novel; Catch-22 is dual-carded and the duplication is intended.
entries.principle: War comedy is the clearest case of the library's rule that cross-pack duplication is not a defect. War owns the novels, the historical record and the moral weight; Comedy owns the device, because military logic is a farce mechanism that happens to be real. Catch-22 appears in both packs under different questions: War asks what it says about war, Comedy asks how a circular rule is made to generate scenes.
entries.example: The War pack cards Heller, Vonnegut, Waugh, Hašek and Blackadder Goes Forth, and carries The Satiric and Absurdist War Novel as a subgenre. Its blueprint deferred this hand-off until a Comedy pack existed, and a reciprocal card is being shipped back to it. Comedy's residual is the last-minute turn, of which the final scene of Blackadder Goes Forth is the most-studied instance in the form.
entries.application: For the war novel's obligations to the record, go to war-military-reference. Come back for the anaesthetic-or-accelerant craft card, which is what a war comedy's ending decides.

entries.name: Horror Comedy
entries.description: Hands off to horror-reference, whose own card calls it two responses sequenced rather than blended.
entries.principle: Horror's formulation is correct and Comedy adopts it: the two responses cannot occupy the same instant, so the craft is the sequencing. What Comedy adds is the observation that both forms are built on the same variables. Both manage dignity and both are timing arts with a verdict delivered during the work, which is why the same performer's instincts often serve both and why the two forms share a failure mode in the beat held one second too long.
entries.example: The Horror pack owns Comedy Horror as a subgenre and cards Grady Hendrix and T. Kingfisher. The canonical demonstrations of the sequencing are An American Werewolf in London (1981), which alternates, Evil Dead II (1987), which accelerates until the alternation blurs, and Shaun of the Dead (2004), which plays the first act as a comedy of oblivious routine.
entries.application: Sequence rather than blend, and decide per scene which response you are buying. Use this pack's timing cards for the interval between them; horror-reference owns dread, which is the thing the interval is made of.

entries.name: Comic Fantasy and the Secondary World
entries.description: Hands off to fantasy-reference; secondary-world coherence is the load-bearing craft and the jokes depend on it.
entries.principle: Comic fantasy is the case where the hand-off is least intuitive and most necessary. The comedy is generated by a world that works, and the work of making it work is worldbuilding rather than joke-writing. A comic fantasy whose rules bend for a punchline stops being funny within a chapter, because the reader has learned the rules are negotiable and therefore that nothing is at stake.
entries.example: The Fantasy pack owns Comic Fantasy and cards Terry Pratchett, Neil Gaiman, Christopher Moore, Tom Holt and Jasper Fforde, and carries a specialist collection on worldbuilding systems. Comedy's residual is the register question: Pratchett's later Discworld novels move from parody of the genre to satire of institutions without changing world, which is a decision about target rather than about setting.
entries.application: Build the world in fantasy-reference and hold its rules. Return here for the satire card when the target stops being the genre and becomes something outside it.

entries.name: Comic Science Fiction
entries.description: Hands off to sf-reference; the extrapolation still has to work, and the joke does not exempt it.
entries.principle: Comic science fiction is subject to the same extrapolative obligation as any other science fiction, and its comedy usually comes from taking the extrapolation more seriously than a straight treatment would. The bureaucratic future, the badly designed technology and the indifferent universe are all extrapolations played out honestly. A comic premise that abandons its own logic is whimsy, which is a different and smaller thing.
entries.example: The Science Fiction pack owns the ground and cards Vonnegut, Lem, Scalzi and Connie Willis. The form's central texts are Adams's The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (1979), which is rigorous about its absurdities, Harrison's Bill, the Galactic Hero (1965), and Red Dwarf (1988), which runs sitcom's fixed-relations grid in a science-fictional container.
entries.application: Extrapolate first and find the comedy in the consequence. Use sf-reference for the extrapolation cards and this pack for the sitcom architecture, which is what most comic SF television is actually built on.

entries.name: Comic Historical Fiction
entries.description: Hands off to historical-reference; the period research burden is unchanged by the comic register.
entries.principle: A comic register buys no relief from research. If anything it raises the burden, because anachronism used deliberately is only legible as a joke when the surrounding period is solid, and the reader must be able to tell the error from the gag. The form's characteristic failure is the writer who uses comedy as permission not to know.
entries.example: The Historical pack owns the ground, carries a specialist on period research primers, and cards Mark Twain, Thackeray, Gogol, Peter Carey and George MacDonald Fraser. The form's demonstrations are Fraser's Flashman (1969), which is scrupulous about the campaigns it mocks, Twain's A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889) and Barth's The Sot-Weed Factor (1960).
entries.application: Do the research as though writing straight, then decide what to break. Historical-reference owns the primers; this pack owns the anachronism, which is a timing device before it is a historical one.

entries.name: The Comic Literary Novel and the Campus Novel
entries.description: Hands off to literary-reference; how the work means is Literary's question, and the campus novel is its comic corner.
entries.principle: The comic literary novel is not a literary novel with jokes added. Its comedy is a property of voice and of the relation between narration and event, which is exactly what the Literary pack's specialist collections on style, voice and form exist to analyse. The campus novel is the corner where the two packs press hardest, because its subject is a closed status system, which is comedy of manners material inside a literary frame.
entries.example: The Literary pack cards Austen, Dickens, Nabokov, Bellow, Kundera, Lorrie Moore, Saunders and Zadie Smith. The campus form's central texts are Amis's Lucky Jim (1954), Lodge's Changing Places (1975), Nabokov's Pnin (1957) and Russo's Straight Man (1997).
entries.application: For voice, free indirect style and the comedy of narration, go to literary-reference. Come back here for the comedy of manners and comedy of humours cards, which is what the campus novel's status system runs on.

entries.name: The Comic Western
entries.description: Hands off to western-reference, which has now shipped; this card was written against the plan and is corrected here against what actually built.
entries.principle: The comic western is almost entirely parody, which makes it unusual among the hand-offs: its comedy depends on the straight form being fixed enough to be recognised, so the owning pack has to exist first for this one to be usable. The genre's iconography is rigid, its moral structure is legible, and both properties make it exceptionally parodiable and exceptionally hard to write comically from the inside.
entries.example: western-reference shipped in August 2026 and discharges what this card was written against: its Frontier Myth and Revision specialist carries a How the Myth Is Built block on the iconography and where each piece came from, and a The Myth's Load-Bearing Claims block on the moral structure. The form's demonstrations are Blazing Saddles (1974), which parodies the genre and the industry that made it, Cat Ballou (1965), Support Your Local Sheriff! (1969) and Little Big Man (1970), which alternates rather than blends.
entries.application: Use this pack's parody and pastiche card, which requires the borrowed form be reproduced competently before it is altered, and take what you are reproducing from western-reference's two named specialist blocks. Western's own card on this boundary is The Western Parodied, renamed from The Comic Western so the two packs do not carry the same card name.

entries.name: Gag Manga and the Four-Panel Unit
entries.description: Japanese comic manga, the yonkoma and the nonsense line — owned by the manga-reference pack.
entries.principle: This material is handed off to the manga-reference pack, which owns the formal unit it runs on. The yonkoma's four panels are not a gag strip that happens to be four panels long: the count is structural, conventionally mapped onto a four-part setup-development-turn-conclusion shape with the weight on the third panel, and it is the medium's smallest self-contained narrative machine. **This pack's setup-and-punchline unit is the right frame and it stops at the panel border**, because the timing here is carried by panel size, gutter width and the position of the turn — a grammar with no prose equivalent. The nonsense line and the long-running newspaper family strip belong there for the same reason.
entries.example: A setup and its replacement in a single stroke is this pack's unit; the same joke timed by where the third panel sits and how much white surrounds it is manga's.
entries.application: When the joke's construction is the subject, work here. When its timing is being carried by the page rather than by the words, hand it to the manga-reference pack.

entries.name: Dramatic Irony Is the Comic Engine
entries.description: The reader knowing more than the character is the most reliable comic mechanism available in any medium.
entries.principle: Give the audience one fact the character lacks and the character's every ordinary action becomes comic without a joke being written.
entries.example: Malvolio's letter scene in Twelfth Night works entirely on the audience's foreknowledge; Fawlty Towers builds most episodes on Basil knowing something the guests do not, or the reverse; Curb Your Enthusiasm withholds nothing from the viewer and everything from the room.
entries.application: Before writing a comic scene, name the gap in knowledge and who holds it. If no gap exists, the scene will need jokes to survive, which is a more expensive way to buy the same laugh.

entries.name: Set the Foreknowledge Early and Cheaply
entries.description: The audience's advantage must be installed before the scene it pays for, and it should cost as little screen time as possible.
entries.principle: Plant the fact in a scene that is doing other work, so the audience receives it without registering that they have been handed the mechanism.
entries.example: Some Like It Hot establishes the massacre witness in an action sequence, so the disguise scenes inherit their tension free; Arrested Development plants its running gags inside exposition; Clue plants every alibi in dialogue that reads as characterisation.
entries.application: If installing the foreknowledge takes its own scene, the payoff must be large enough to justify two scenes. Otherwise fold the plant into something already earning its place.

entries.name: The Unaware Narrator
entries.description: A first-person voice that reports accurately and interprets wrongly, so the reader reconstructs the truth from the same words.
entries.principle: Let the narrator be reliable about events and unreliable about their meaning, so the reader never has to distrust the facts to distrust the man.
entries.example: The Diary of a Nobody sustains this for a whole book without the narrator ever lying; Sue Townsend's Adrian Mole reports his family's collapse in the vocabulary of adolescent grievance; Alan Partridge's memoirs describe humiliations as triumphs in convincing detail.
entries.application: Write the passage as the narrator believes it, then have someone reconstruct the actual events from it. If they cannot, the gap is too wide and the reader will read a liar rather than a fool.

entries.name: The Character Who Is In On It
entries.description: One character sharing the audience's knowledge changes who pays and how the scene is scored.
entries.principle: An in-on-it character converts the audience from observers into accomplices, and their reaction shot becomes the scene's scoring instrument.
entries.example: Jim's look to camera in The Office (2001) tells the viewer how to read Brent; Jeeves is in on everything and says nothing, which makes Bertie's confidence the payer; Blackadder gives the knowing role to the servant and the paying role to the master.
entries.application: Decide whether you want the audience alone with the knowledge or accompanied. Alone is colder and crueller; accompanied is warmer and licenses harder material.

entries.name: Shift the Payer Mid-Scene
entries.description: The strongest comic scenes move the cost from one party to another while it is running.
entries.principle: Start the scene with an obvious payer, then transfer the cost to the party the audience had been laughing with.
entries.example: The Producers moves the humiliation from Bialystock to the audience of Springtime for Hitler and back; Nanette transfers the cost from Gadsby to the room that has been laughing at her; the Spanish Inquisition sketch shifts it from the interrogated to the interrogators' incompetence.
entries.application: Mark the transfer point in the outline. A scene with one payer throughout is a joke extended; a scene that moves the cost is an argument.

entries.name: Locate the Beat Before Writing the Line
entries.description: Every comic unit has one moment where the reaction is supposed to arrive, and it should be identified before drafting.
entries.principle: Name the exact instant the laugh is meant to occur, then write only what is required to reach it.
entries.example: Airplane! is built as a sequence of located beats with no connective material between them; Frasier's cold opens locate a single beat and end on it; Cheers scenes are constructed backwards from the tag.
entries.application: Mark the intended beat in the margin of the draft. If you cannot mark it, the passage is atmosphere rather than comedy, which may be correct but should be a decision.

entries.name: Put the Operative Word Last
entries.description: In prose and in speech, the reaction arrives on the final stressed element, so the operative word must occupy it.
entries.principle: End the sentence, the speech or the shot on the word or image that carries the reversal, and move everything explanatory in front of it.
entries.example: Wodehouse's line in The Code of the Woosters about a man far from being gruntled places the invented word in the terminal position; Groucho's line in Animal Crackers withholds the pyjamas clause until the sentence is otherwise finished; Jack Benny's most-cited response is three words long.
entries.application: Read every comic line backwards from its last word. If the last word is not the reversal, the line is finished before it lands and needs reordering rather than rewriting.

entries.name: Comic Rhythm Is Metrical
entries.description: Comic prose has a measurable rhythm, and the wrong number of syllables before the operative word kills a working joke.
entries.principle: Count the beats before the stress; a comic line usually wants either an abrupt approach or a long one, rarely a middling one.
entries.example: Nash's over-extended lines make the strain audible and the rhyme inevitable; Belloc's Cautionary Tales use nursery metre to deliver disproportionate punishment; Thurber's sentences run long and stop hard.
entries.application: Read aloud. If a line is funny in your head and not in your mouth, the problem is almost always syllable count in the approach, not word choice at the stress.

entries.name: The Edit Is Punctuation
entries.description: On screen the cut performs the function the full stop performs on the page, and cutting late is the commonest visual comic error.
entries.principle: Cut on the beat, not after it; a shot held past the reaction converts a laugh into an explanation.
entries.example: Airplane! cuts out of most gags before the audience has finished processing them; Toast of London cuts hard on absurd inserts; the Naked Gun films are edited to a rhythm closer to sketch than to feature.
entries.application: Watch the assembly with the sound down and mark where you would cut on rhythm alone. Where that mark is earlier than the current cut, it is almost always right.

entries.name: Know Whether You Are Writing a Page Laugh or a Room Laugh
entries.description: The two are different products, and material optimised for one is frequently inert in the other.
entries.principle: A room laugh needs a shape the ear can anticipate; a page laugh can be quiet, slow and dependent on rereading, and the two rarely survive transplant unedited.
entries.example: Wodehouse is almost entirely page: the pleasure is syntactic and needs the eye. Pryor is almost entirely room: the pleasure is embodied and needs the voice. Bennett's Talking Heads is one of the few bodies of work that reads and performs equally.
entries.application: Decide which you are writing before the first draft, and stop apologising for the one you did not choose. A quiet page joke is not a failed room joke.

entries.name: Cost Must Match What the Work Will Say About the Payer
entries.description: A work may impose a humiliation only as large as the interest it is prepared to take in the person humiliated.
entries.principle: The more a joke costs a character, the more the work owes that character in attention, interiority or eventual seriousness.
entries.example: Peep Show humiliates both leads continuously and pays for it with total access to their thoughts; The Office (2001) earns Brent's final-episode dignity by having spent two series watching him closely; a sketch that humiliates a walk-on owes nothing because it takes nothing.
entries.application: Total the humiliations you have given a character, then check what the work knows about them. If the ledger is one-sided, either reduce the cost or increase the interest.

entries.name: The Cruelty Budget
entries.description: A work has a finite quantity of cruelty an audience will absorb before it stops finding the work funny and starts finding it unpleasant.
entries.principle: Spend cruelty early and sparingly; every subsequent cruelty costs more than the last and the budget does not refill.
entries.example: Nighty Night spends its budget deliberately and accepts the audience it loses; Curb Your Enthusiasm resets by making Larry the eventual payer of nearly every arc; Little Britain's later series are widely argued to have spent past the point of return, which is a contested case and is carded as one.
entries.application: Track the cruelties in order. Where three arrive in succession without the payer being changed, the budget is being spent faster than the work can earn it back.

entries.name: Earn the Hard Joke
entries.description: Material about grief, illness or atrocity requires the work to demonstrate competence at that material before it makes a joke about it.
entries.principle: Show the audience you understand the seriousness before you use it, or the joke reads as ignorance rather than as nerve.
entries.example: After Life earns its jokes about bereavement by being accurate about bereavement first; Tig Notaro's 2012 Largo set opens by stating the diagnosis plainly and lets the room decide; The Death of Stalin is precise about the terror before it is funny about the committee.
entries.application: Put the demonstration before the joke, not after. An apology or a serious coda following a hard joke does not earn it retroactively; it only signals that you knew.

entries.name: The Joke That Costs More Than the Scene Can Pay
entries.description: A laugh large enough to break the scene's frame is a debt, not a win.
entries.principle: Cut the joke that is funnier than the scene it sits in, because the audience will not return to the story at the level the story requires.
entries.example: This is the standard argument for the deleted material in many comedies; Frasier's writers were explicit about cutting laughs that broke Niles's credibility; sketch shows survive this problem by having no scene to return to, which is one reason sketch tolerates bigger swings.
entries.application: If a joke gets a laugh and then the next page has to work harder than it did before, the joke cost more than it paid. Keep it for something else.

entries.name: Proportion Is Cumulative
entries.description: Individual jokes can each be proportionate while the whole work is not.
entries.principle: Audit the total bill across the work, not the individual transactions, because an audience experiences the sum.
entries.example: A series can humiliate one character mildly in every episode and arrive at cruelty by the season's end without any single episode being cruel; Steptoe and Son is the canonical study, since the cumulative entrapment is the point and the show knows it.
entries.application: Read the whole thing in one sitting before locking. Per-scene proportionality is checked in revision; cumulative proportionality can only be checked at length.

entries.name: Comedy That Also Advances Plot
entries.description: A comic scene should change the situation, not merely decorate it.
entries.principle: Make the comic event the cause of the next plot event, so the scene cannot be cut without breaking the chain.
entries.example: Farce is the pure case, since every laugh is also a plot move; Fargo's comic incompetence is the engine of the escalation; Seinfeld's convergent plotting makes each strand's comedy the other strands' cause.
entries.application: For each comic scene, state what is different afterwards. If the answer is only that the audience laughed, the scene is a candidate for cutting in the first pass.

entries.name: The Scene Must Survive a Dead Beat
entries.description: Assume the biggest laugh in the scene does not land, and check whether the scene still works.
entries.principle: Build every comic scene so that it does its structural job even if the audience is silent throughout.
entries.example: The Thick of It scenes function as political process whether or not the invective lands; Fleabag's scenes carry emotional information independent of the jokes; a sketch cannot do this, which is precisely why sketch is high-variance.
entries.application: Read the scene with every joke deleted. If nothing is left, the scene will not survive a bad room, a bad reader or a translation.

entries.name: Comic Exposition
entries.description: Comedy is the cheapest available vehicle for information the audience must hold but does not want.
entries.principle: Attach necessary exposition to a joke, so the audience accepts the information in exchange for the laugh.
entries.example: The Hitchhiker's Guide entries deliver worldbuilding as digression and are the most-quoted parts of the book; Blackadder's insults carry historical setup; Clue's alibi round is exposition performed as farce.
entries.application: Find the sentences the audience must retain and attach each to a beat. Exposition delivered without payment is the material readers skim.

entries.name: Why Gag-Only Scenes Are Cut First
entries.description: In every edit and every revision, the scenes that exist only to be funny are removed before the scenes that are funny and do something else.
entries.principle: A scene with a second function survives the cut; a scene with one function is negotiable from the moment it is written.
entries.example: Deleted-scene reels are almost entirely gag-only material, frequently very funny; the Ealing comedies are unusually resistant to cutting because the gags are plot; sketch films assembled from gag-only scenes tend to collapse in the second act for this reason.
entries.application: If you love a gag-only scene, give it a second job before the read-through. It is the cheapest insurance available.

entries.name: The Load-Bearing Gag
entries.description: Some jokes carry structural weight, and identifying them changes what may be revised.
entries.principle: Identify the two or three jokes the work cannot function without, and revise everything else around them rather than through them.
entries.example: Catch-22's title rule is a load-bearing gag; the parrot's death in the Dead Parrot sketch is not a joke that can be replaced; Groundhog Day's premise is a comic device holding the entire structure.
entries.application: List them explicitly before revision. A load-bearing gag revised for freshness usually takes the structure with it.

entries.name: The Three Audience Postures
entries.description: A comic passage asks the audience to judge, to wince, or to recognise itself, and confusing them is the commonest tonal fault.
entries.principle: Choose one posture per passage and signal it, because an audience asked to judge and wince at once will do neither.
entries.example: The Thick of It asks for judgement; Peep Show asks for recognition; The Office (2001) asks for wincing and switches to recognition in its final episode. Each is legible from the first minute.
entries.application: Name the posture for each scene in the outline. Where two are marked, the scene usually needs splitting.

entries.name: Cringe Is a Distinct Contract
entries.description: Cringe comedy asks the audience to absorb the humiliation on the character's behalf, which is a different transaction from laughing at them.
entries.principle: In cringe, the audience is the payer by transfer, so the character must not know they are being humiliated or the transfer fails.
entries.example: The Office (2001) is the form's definitive statement; Curb Your Enthusiasm inverts it by making Larry aware and unbothered, which converts cringe into judgement; Peep Show achieves it through interior monologue rather than through camera.
entries.application: If the character registers the humiliation, the audience is released and the scene becomes ordinary embarrassment. Keep the character oblivious for as long as the scene needs the transfer.

entries.name: Satire Demands Judgement
entries.description: Satire is the one comic posture that requires the audience to arrive at a verdict, which is why it can be answered.
entries.principle: If your audience can enjoy the piece without reaching a judgement, you have written comedy about a subject rather than satire of it.
entries.example: A Modest Proposal cannot be enjoyed without a verdict; Veep is frequently read as cynicism rather than satire because it withholds one; Till Death Us Do Part was written to demand a verdict and a documented portion of its audience returned the opposite one.
entries.application: State the verdict you intend, then test the piece on someone who disagrees with it. Satire that only lands with the converted has not been tested.

entries.name: Self-Recognition Comedy
entries.description: The laugh of recognition is the audience paying voluntarily, and it buys permissions the other postures do not.
entries.principle: Make the audience the payer by accurate observation, and they will accept material they would refuse if it were aimed at someone else.
entries.example: Sedaris's essays make the reader complicit by describing them; Motherland's accuracy about parental competitiveness is the licence for its cruelty; Nathan Barley was received as attack by the people it described and as recognition by everyone else, which is the risk.
entries.application: Observe precisely enough that the audience recognises itself before it recognises a type. Types produce judgement; specifics produce recognition.

entries.name: The Posture Switch
entries.description: Changing the audience's posture mid-work is the most powerful move available in comedy and the easiest to bungle.
entries.principle: A posture switch must be prepared by the material that precedes it, or it reads as the work losing its nerve.
entries.example: Nanette switches from recognition to indictment and spends its first half preparing the ground; Fleabag's second series switches the frame-break from defence to exposure; a sitcom's serious episode usually fails because nothing before it earned the change.
entries.application: Work backwards from the switch and check that everything before it is doing double duty. An unprepared switch is a tonal accident, whatever the intention.

entries.name: Comedy as Anaesthetic
entries.description: Comedy used to make difficult material survivable for the audience, which is a legitimate and separable function.
entries.principle: When comedy is anaesthetic, its job is to keep the audience in the room, so the jokes should relieve pressure at intervals the material dictates.
entries.example: M*A*S*H uses comedy to keep an audience watching a field hospital for eleven seasons; Adam Kay's This Is Going to Hurt paces its jokes so the reader can continue; children's writing about grief uses the same technique deliberately.
entries.application: Place the relief where the material is hardest, not where the writing is weakest. Anaesthetic comedy is scheduled, not scattered.

entries.name: Comedy as Accelerant
entries.description: Comedy used to make difficult material less survivable, by removing the distance a serious treatment would supply.
entries.principle: When comedy is accelerant, the laugh must implicate the audience, so the relief is withdrawn at the moment it is most wanted.
entries.example: The final scene of Blackadder Goes Forth withdraws every device the series had used for four series; the last third of Nanette refuses the release the form promised; Dr. Strangelove's ending is a punchline that is also an annihilation.
entries.application: Establish the comic contract fully, then break it once. Accelerant comedy works only where the audience has been taught to expect relief.

entries.name: The Tonal Handbrake
entries.description: The moment a comedy stops being funny is a craft decision with a location, and it should be chosen rather than discovered.
entries.principle: Decide the page or minute at which the comic register is withdrawn, and remove every joke after it rather than tapering.
entries.example: Fleabag series one withdraws in its final minutes and does not resume; Harold and Maude tapers and is frequently criticised for it; Bridget Jones's Diary keeps its register throughout, which is a decision the film is often judged for.
entries.application: Mark the handbrake in the outline. Comedies that lose their register gradually read as having run out of jokes rather than having made a choice.

entries.name: The Last-Minute Turn
entries.description: A comedy that reveals in its final beat what it has actually been about, retroactively rescoring everything before it.
entries.principle: The turn must be already true of the preceding material, so the audience rereads rather than reinterprets.
entries.example: Blackadder Goes Forth's last minute makes four series of cowardice into something else without altering a line of them; The Remains of the Day performs the equivalent move outside comedy; Some Like It Hot's final line turns the whole film on a refusal to resolve.
entries.application: Write the turn first and then check that every earlier scene supports it without pointing at it. A turn that requires new information is a twist, which is a different and lesser device here.

entries.name: Comedy as Testimony
entries.description: The comic frame used to make first-person testimony bearable to deliver as well as to receive.
entries.principle: Where the material is the speaker's own, comedy gives them control of the telling, and that control is the point rather than a side effect.
entries.example: Pryor's Live on the Sunset Strip narrates his own self-immolation and keeps the room; Notaro's Largo set is testimony delivered in the only frame available to her that night; Maria Bamford's work on psychiatric hospitalisation uses character voices to hold the material at a workable distance.
entries.application: Ask whose control the comedy is protecting. Where it is the speaker's, do not smooth the discomfort out in revision, because the discomfort is the evidence that the control is real.

entries.name: Establish the Comic Frame Before You Need It
entries.description: An audience grants a work permission based on the register it establishes first, and permission cannot be requested retroactively.
entries.principle: Set the comic frame in the opening minutes or pages, because everything the work is later allowed to do is licensed by that opening.
entries.example: Dr. Strangelove opens on refuelling footage scored as romance and has declared its permissions inside two minutes; The Death of Stalin opens on a concert being rerecorded under threat; a drama that turns comic in its third act has no frame to invoke and is usually read as tonal failure.
entries.application: Ask what the hardest thing in the work is, then check the opening has already licensed it. If not, the opening is the thing to change.

entries.name: The Frame Is Elastic, Not Infinite
entries.description: A comic frame stretches to accommodate serious material, but it has a limit and the limit is set by the frame's own consistency.
entries.principle: A comedy may go as dark as its established rules allow and no darker; material outside the rules breaks the frame rather than extending it.
entries.example: M*A*S*H sustained operating-theatre death for eleven years because its frame admitted it from the first episode; Blackadder Goes Forth could end where it did because the series had always been about men who would die; a sitcom's sudden bereavement episode frequently fails because the frame never admitted mortality.
entries.application: List what your frame has already admitted. Serious material inside that list will stretch it; material outside it will tear it.

entries.name: Break the Frame Deliberately or Not at All
entries.description: Direct address, self-reference and acknowledgement of the audience are devices with rules, and inconsistent use reads as carelessness.
entries.principle: If the work breaks its frame, establish the break as a rule the work obeys, and give the break a reason inside the character rather than the script.
entries.example: Fleabag makes the frame-break a defence mechanism and then makes it a plot event when another character notices; Miller's asides in The Thick of It are absent, and the show is stronger for the consistency; a single unexplained aside in an otherwise sealed work reads as a mistake.
entries.application: Count the breaks. If they are not on a rule the audience could state, they are not a device.

entries.name: The First Minute Is a Contract
entries.description: The opening states the kind of laugh on offer, and audiences hold works to it more strictly than to any plot promise.
entries.principle: Whatever kind of comedy the opening delivers is what the audience will spend the rest of the work waiting for.
entries.example: Airplane! opens with the fin of a plane parting cloud like a shark and has promised the density it delivers; The Larry Sanders Show opens on a talk-show taping and promises the documentary-adjacent register it keeps; a broad opening followed by a subtle work loses the audience it recruited.
entries.application: Write the opening last, once you know what the work actually is. An opening written first almost always promises the wrong product.

entries.name: Frame Failure and How to Recognise It
entries.description: When an audience stops laughing and starts objecting, the frame has failed, and the cause is almost never the joke that triggered it.
entries.principle: Treat a frame failure as a fault in what preceded it, and repair the setup rather than softening the joke.
entries.example: The 2020 removals and restorations of previously mainstream comedy are largely frame failures at distance, where the frame that licensed the material no longer exists for the audience receiving it; within a single work, an unearned cruelty in act three usually indicates a missing act-one licence.
entries.application: When a joke fails in a read-through, look one scene earlier for the permission it needed. Cutting the joke removes the symptom.

entries.name: The Persona Sets the Permissions
entries.description: A performer's established persona determines which targets they may attack and how hard.
entries.principle: Build the persona before the material, because the persona is what decides whether a given joke reads as courage or as bullying.
entries.example: A self-deprecating persona can attack upward almost without limit; a confident persona attacking downward reads as cruelty from the same script; Pryor's confessional persona licensed material no other performer of his era could deliver.
entries.application: Write the persona's position relative to every target in the set. Where the persona is above the target, the joke needs more work or a different target.

entries.name: The Room Is an Instrument, Not a Verdict
entries.description: A room's response carries information about the room as well as about the material, and reading it wrongly destroys good work.
entries.principle: Distinguish material that failed from material that failed in that room, and change nothing until the same result occurs three times.
entries.example: Club audiences and theatre audiences return different verdicts on the same set; Notaro's Largo set would have read differently in any other room on any other night, which is why it exists as a recording rather than as a routine.
entries.application: Track responses per room, not per performance. Material cut after one bad night is material lost to acoustics.

entries.name: Delivery Is Revision
entries.description: In performed comedy the draft is not finished at the desk, and the stage is where the writing happens.
entries.principle: Treat every performance as a revision pass, and record it, because the changes that work are the ones made without deliberation.
entries.example: Stand-up sets are demonstrably rebuilt across dozens of performances; the Python team workshopped material through live performance before television; sketch shows with a studio audience use the taping as a final edit.
entries.application: If you write performed comedy at a desk alone, you have a first draft. Budget the room time as writing time, not as rehearsal.

entries.name: The Heckle
entries.description: An interruption is a status challenge, and the response is judged on status rather than on wit.
entries.principle: Answer a heckle by restoring the status arrangement the room needs, which is usually accomplished faster by control than by a better joke.
entries.example: The comedians most admired for handling hecklers are generally those who reassert control quickly rather than those who land the largest counter-joke; a devastating comeback that takes ninety seconds has already cost more than it recovers.
entries.application: For written comedy, the equivalent is the reader's objection. Answer it early and briefly, or the reader will hold it for the rest of the piece.

entries.name: What Transfers From Stage to Page
entries.description: Persona, act-out and status transfer to prose; timing, volume and physical presence largely do not.
entries.principle: When adapting performed comedy to the page, rebuild the timing in syntax, because the pause has no written equivalent that survives.
entries.example: Transcribed stand-up routinely reads flat because the timing lived in the delivery; Sedaris's live readings and his printed essays differ in shape for exactly this reason; Bennett's monologues are written to work both ways and are unusual in that.
entries.application: Do not transcribe. Rewrite, and put into clause order and sentence length what the voice was doing with pauses.

entries.name: Choose the Target Before the Joke
entries.description: A satirical piece with an unstated target will find one by accident, and it is rarely the one intended.
entries.principle: State the target in a single sentence before drafting, and check every joke lands on it.
entries.example: The Thick of It's target is the language of government rather than any party, which is why it survived changes of government; Spitting Image's targets were individuals and its material dated with them; a satire of an institution that becomes a satire of its junior staff has drifted.
entries.application: Write the target sentence at the top of the draft and leave it there. Any joke that does not serve it belongs in a different piece.

entries.name: Punching Direction Is a Formal Property
entries.description: The relative power of joke-teller and target is observable in the text and worth naming as craft, separately from whether it is defensible.
entries.principle: Establish the power relation between the persona and the target, because it determines how the same words will be read.
entries.example: The identical joke about a group reads differently from inside and outside it, and this is a fact about reception rather than a moral claim; the alternative comedy movement of the early 1980s defined itself explicitly by reversing the direction of the club material it replaced.
entries.application: Name the direction for each target. This pack does not tell you which direction to punch; it tells you that you have chosen one and that the audience will read it.

entries.name: The Satirist's Own Position
entries.description: Satire that exempts its author is weaker than satire that does not, and audiences detect the exemption reliably.
entries.principle: Place the satirist inside the system being satirised, or account explicitly for why they stand outside it.
entries.example: Swift's proposer is a participant in the economy he describes; Veep implicates the viewer's appetite for the process; satire written from a position of unexamined superiority is the standard failure mode of topical comedy.
entries.application: Ask where you are in the piece. If the answer is nowhere, the audience will assume you think you are above it, and will test that assumption.

entries.name: Satire That Flatters Is Not Satire
entries.description: A piece that confirms its audience's existing judgement has entertained them, which is a different transaction.
entries.principle: If the intended audience already holds the verdict the piece argues for, the piece is applause and should be rewritten toward a target they have not already condemned.
entries.example: Much late-night political comedy is argued to have this property, which is a contested claim and is carded as one; the durable satires generally attack something their own audience participates in.
entries.application: Identify the audience's existing position, then find the part of the target they are implicated in. That is where the piece is.

entries.name: Satire Read Against Its Intent
entries.description: A satire's reception is not controlled by its author, and a portion of the audience will take the indictment as endorsement.
entries.principle: Assume some readers will adopt the character you are indicting, and decide in advance whether the work can bear it.
entries.example: Till Death Us Do Part and All in the Family are the documented cases: Vidmar and Rokeach's 1974 study found prejudiced viewers read Archie Bunker as the hero. Both shows were written as indictments; neither could prevent the reading.
entries.application: There is no reliable technique for preventing it, and the pack does not pretend otherwise. Decide whether the work survives the misreading, because you cannot foreclose it.

entries.name: The Laugh That Costs the Wrong Person
entries.description: A joke's nominal target and its actual payer are frequently different people, and the difference is checkable.
entries.principle: Name who the joke is about and then name who is diminished when the room laughs; if they differ, the joke is not doing what the draft thinks it is.
entries.example: A joke about a powerful person's accent charges the accent rather than the person, and the payer becomes everyone who shares it; a joke about a doctor's incompetence that turns on the patient's condition has moved the cost; the mechanism is the same one that makes a satirical caricature outlive the politician it caricatured.
entries.application: Run the two-name test on every joke touching a group. Where the names differ, either fix the mechanism or accept the actual payer as your target and defend that instead.

entries.name: Nonsense Is a Craft, Not an Absence of One
entries.description: Comedy with nothing at stake for anyone has its own discipline, and it is internal consistency rather than escalation.
entries.principle: In nonsense, invent according to rules the reader can feel but not state, and never explain an invention.
entries.example: Lear's coinages behave like real words grammatically, which is why they read as language rather than as noise; The Goon Show sustains its logic across a half-hour by never breaking character to acknowledge the absurdity; Carroll's Jabberwocky is parsable as syntax throughout.
entries.application: Test your invented material for grammatical and internal consistency. Nonsense that is merely random is not funny for long, because there is nothing for the reader to learn.

entries.name: Where the Organising Claim Does Not Reach
entries.description: This pack's claim is that comedy is the deliberate mismanagement of dignity, and this card states the exception plainly.
entries.principle: Do not force a dignity reading onto nonsense, pure wordplay or absurdist non-sequitur; the claim has a boundary and the boundary is stated rather than argued away.
entries.example: Nothing is at stake for anyone in a Lear limerick, in most of Mitch Hedberg's one-liners, or in a Reeves and Mortimer sketch built on non-sequitur. Saying that language itself is humiliated makes the claim unfalsifiable in the way benign-violation theory is, which is a worse outcome than a conceded exception.
entries.application: When a piece has no payer, stop looking for one. Analyse it as invention and consistency, and use the timing cards, which still apply.

entries.name: The Periodic Sentence
entries.description: Suspending the sense until the end of the sentence is the prose equivalent of the setup, and subordination is how it is built.
entries.principle: Load the qualifications first and withhold the main clause, so the sentence's grammar performs the delay the joke needs.
entries.example: Wodehouse's sentences routinely defer the operative element through two or three subordinate clauses; Gibbon's irony in the Decline and Fall is built almost entirely on periodic structure; Thurber uses the technique to make domestic incidents read as catastrophes.
entries.application: Where a comic sentence lands flat, try inverting its clause order before changing a word. The failure is usually architectural.

entries.name: The Specific Noun
entries.description: Precision is funnier than exaggeration, and the specific noun does work no intensifier can.
entries.principle: Replace the general term with the exact one, because the exactness implies a world and the implication is the joke.
entries.example: Wodehouse's characters do not eat food, they eat named dishes; Sedaris's essays turn on brand names and exact sums; a sketch about an office is funnier for naming the model of photocopier.
entries.application: Search the draft for adjectives doing work a noun could do. Nearly every intensifier is a specific noun that has not been found yet.

entries.name: Register Collision
entries.description: Two vocabularies that do not belong together, held steady, generate comedy without a joke being made.
entries.principle: Apply one register consistently to material that belongs to another, and never signal that you have noticed.
entries.example: The mock-heroic is the classical case; The Thick of It applies obscenity to the register of policy; Douglas Adams applies the vocabulary of consumer guides to cosmology; a legal document about a trivial matter is funny for the same reason.
entries.application: Choose both registers explicitly, then hold the borrowed one without lapse. One slip into the natural register collapses the effect for the rest of the passage.

entries.name: The Comic Flaw
entries.description: A comic character needs one appetite and one incapacity, and neither may be resolved.
entries.principle: Give the character something they want badly and something they cannot do, and put the two in each other's way.
entries.example: Basil Fawlty wants social elevation and cannot control his temper; Alceste wants honesty and cannot dissemble; Michael Scott wants to be loved and cannot read a room. Each pairing generates scenes indefinitely.
entries.application: State both in one sentence. If you cannot, the character will need situations supplied from outside rather than generating them.

entries.name: The Grid of Fixed Relations
entries.description: An ensemble comedy is a matrix, and its capacity is the number of pairings rather than the number of characters.
entries.principle: Define what each character is to every other character, and check that every pair produces a distinct scene.
entries.example: Cheers is built as a complete grid, and every two-hander in it is different in kind; Seinfeld's four leads yield six pairings and the show uses all of them; an ensemble where two pairings produce the same scene has a redundant character.
entries.application: Draw the grid literally. Empty or duplicated cells are the fastest diagnostic available for why a comic ensemble feels thin.

entries.name: Why Sitcom Characters Cannot Learn
entries.description: Character growth spends the mechanism that generates the comedy, which is why the form resists it structurally.
entries.principle: Let the character learn within the episode and forget by the next, or accept that the series has become finite.
entries.example: Seinfeld's no-hugging rule is the explicit statement of the principle; Blackadder resets its protagonist each series rather than each episode, which is why it could end; single-camera comedy's willingness to permit growth is the main reason its series run shorter.
entries.application: Decide at the outset whether the show is renewable or finite. Growth in a renewable format is a slow structural cost, not a bonus.

entries.name: Prose to Screen
entries.description: The comedy of narration is the first thing lost in adaptation, and nothing on screen replaces it directly.
entries.principle: Where the comedy lives in the narrating voice, find a screen device that performs the same function rather than translating the lines.
entries.example: Adaptations of Wodehouse struggle because the comedy is syntactic; Bridget Jones's Diary keeps the diary as voiceover and accepts the cost; Arrested Development builds a narrator specifically to recover the device rather than to summarise.
entries.application: Identify whether the comedy is in what happens or in who is telling it. Only the first survives a straight adaptation.

entries.name: Stage to Screen
entries.description: A farce's mechanism depends on the audience seeing the whole space at once, which the camera destroys by choosing.
entries.principle: When adapting stage farce, preserve the geometry with wide staging, because the audience must be able to anticipate the collision.
entries.example: Noises Off depends on the audience holding the whole set in view and its screen version is much argued over for this reason; Keaton's staging is the model, since he plays stunts wide so the space stays verifiable; a farce shot in coverage loses the anticipation that most of the laughs were built on.
entries.application: Block for the whole space first and cut in only for reactions. Coverage is the default that kills stage comedy.

entries.name: The Laugh-Track Question
entries.description: Adding or removing an audience track changes the script's requirements, not merely its texture.
entries.principle: Do not add or remove the laugh break without rewriting to its rhythm, because the break is a structural beat rather than a sound effect.
entries.example: The American adaptation of The Office removed the documentary's silence gradually and rewrote toward warmth to fill it; multi-camera scripts stripped of their track expose the pauses as dead air; single-camera scripts fitted with one arrive too fast for it.
entries.application: If the format changes, rebuild the scenes. Fifteen to twenty per cent of the script's density is at stake in either direction.

entries.name: The Joke That Lands for the Room but Not the Page
entries.description: Material that depends on presence, timing or the shared reaction of a crowd, and its inverse, material that only works in silence.
entries.principle: Identify whether a joke's mechanism is delivery, crowd contagion or syntax, because only the last one crosses to the page unaltered.
