entries.example: An act-out is almost pure delivery and reads as stage direction; a shaggy-dog story depends on the crowd's collective commitment and shortens badly in print; a periodic sentence is pure syntax and does not work aloud at all, since the ear cannot hold the suspension.
entries.application: Sort the material by mechanism before adapting in either direction. Delivery jokes need rebuilding, crowd jokes usually need cutting, and syntax jokes need protecting from anyone who wants them read aloud.

entries.name: The Who-Pays Audit
entries.description: Run on any comic scene at second draft, and on every scene involving a group the writer does not belong to. The pack's organising claim has two variables; this checklist tests the first.
items: Whose dignity is at risk in this scene, and can you name them in one word?
Does the audience know before the payer does, and by how long?
Is the payer the person the scene is nominally about?
Would the scene still be funny if the payer were someone else, and does that tell you the cost is arbitrary?
Does the cost move during the scene, or sit on one person throughout?
Is anyone paying who is not in the room and cannot answer?
If no dignity is at risk anywhere, is this deliberately dignity-free comedy, or has the scene simply lost its engine?

entries.name: The When-It-Lands Audit
entries.description: Run line by line on any passage that reads flat despite having a joke in it. The second variable of the organising claim, and the commonest single fault in comic drafting.
items: Can you mark the exact word, cut or beat where the reaction is supposed to arrive?
Is the operative element in the final stressed position, or is it followed by explanation?
Read aloud: does the approach run too long or stop too short before the stress?
On screen, does the cut come on the beat or after it?
Has the setup delivered everything the payoff needs, and nothing else?
Is there a second joke competing with this one inside the same beat?
If the beat cannot be located, is this atmosphere rather than comedy, and is that intended?

entries.name: The Proportionality Audit
entries.description: Run at the end of a full draft, not per scene, because proportion is cumulative and per-scene checks miss it.
items: Total the humiliations each character receives across the whole work.
For each, what does the work actually know about that character, and is the interest proportionate to the cost?
Has the cruelty budget been spent early or late, and does anything in the last third exceed what the first third earned?
Is there a joke funnier than the scene containing it, and can the following scene recover?
Does any single joke cost more than the work is prepared to pay in seriousness afterwards?
Where the material is grief, illness or atrocity, has the work demonstrated competence at it before joking about it?

entries.name: The Punching Direction Audit
entries.description: Run on every joke that touches a group rather than an individual. This checklist carries the wrong-payer test and does not tell you which direction to punch; it tells you which direction you have chosen.
items: Name the joke's nominal target in one word.
Name who is actually diminished when the room laughs.
Are those two names the same? If not, the mechanism is not doing what the draft intends.
What is the power relation between the persona telling this and the target?
Does the persona's established position license this target, or is it borrowing a licence it has not earned?
Would the same words read differently from inside the group, and have you accounted for that?
If the direction is downward, is that the choice you meant to make, and can the work defend it?

entries.name: The Structural-Work Audit
entries.description: Run before the first read-through, on every comic scene in the draft. The cheapest cut list any comedy has.
items: State in one sentence what is different after this scene.
Delete every joke from the scene: does anything remain?
Is the comic event the cause of the next plot event, or merely adjacent to it?
Does any necessary exposition ride on a beat, or is it delivered unpaid?
Which two or three jokes is the work structurally unable to function without?
Which scenes exist only to be funny, and have you given each of them a second job?

entries.name: The Anaesthetic-or-Accelerant Audit
entries.description: Run once at outline stage and once at final draft on any work containing grief, illness, war, poverty or violence. The answer must be the same both times.
items: Is this comedy making the material bearable, or deliberately less bearable?
If anaesthetic: is the relief placed where the material is hardest, or where the writing is weakest?
If accelerant: has the audience been taught to expect relief, so that its withdrawal registers?
Where exactly is the tonal handbrake, in pages or minutes?
After the handbrake, are there jokes still running that should have been cut?
Is there a last-minute turn, and is it already true of everything preceding it?
Whose control is the comic frame protecting, and is that person the one telling the story?

entries.name: The Permission Audit
entries.description: Run when a joke fails in a read-through and you cannot see why. The fault is almost never in the joke that triggered the objection.
items: What is the hardest thing in this work, and has the opening already licensed it?
List what the frame has admitted so far: is this material inside that list or outside it?
If the frame breaks, is the break on a rule the audience could state?
Does the work's first minute promise the kind of comedy the rest delivers?
When something fails, look one scene earlier: what permission is missing there?
Has a posture switch occurred without preparation?

entries.name: The Dated-Material Audit
entries.description: Run on any work being analysed that predates the writer by twenty years or more, and on any material the writer suspects would not now be commissioned.
items: What did this material's original frame license that the current frame does not?
Is the change in the material, in the audience, or in the distance between them?
Can the craft be described without either endorsing or disowning the content?
Does the card state what the work did, rather than what the writer feels about it?
Is the quality tier assessing the craft, or leaking a judgement about acceptability?
Has the material been removed, edited or restored, and are those separate documented acts with dates?

entries.name: The Contested-Case Audit
entries.description: Run on every card touching a live dispute, before it is merged. A card failing any item here does not ship.
items: Is the contest named explicitly, rather than implied by tone?
Are both positions stated at their strongest, and would each side recognise its own?
Are the disputants named, and the range of the dispute given?
Is every factual claim sourced, including the ones that favour the position you find less congenial?
Has only one side been researched? If so, the card is unfinished, not balanced.
Where a legal outcome is involved, is it stated precisely, including whether a reversal was procedural?
Is a stripped or refused award distinguished from an award never won?
Delete the final sentence: is any information lost? If not, it was adjudicating and must go.

entries.name: The Repetition and Runner Audit
entries.description: Run at the end of a draft on any work with recurring jokes. Runners decay, and the decay curve is measurable.
items: How many times does each runner appear, and does each appearance change something?
Is the third appearance funnier than the second, or merely present?
Does any runner have a final appearance that pays off the earlier ones?
Has a catchphrase replaced a behaviour anywhere?
Is a callback landing on material the audience can still remember?
Which runner is one appearance past its useful life, and are you keeping it out of affection?

entries.name: The Ensemble Grid Audit
entries.description: Run at series bible stage and again after the first six episodes. The fastest diagnostic for why an ensemble feels thin.
items: Draw the grid: what is each character to every other character?
Does every pairing produce a scene that no other pairing could produce?
Are there empty cells, and is that deliberate?
Are two pairings producing the same scene, and is one character therefore redundant?
Does each character have one appetite and one incapacity, stated in a sentence?
Has anyone learned anything they should have forgotten by the next episode?

entries.name: The Cross-Media Adaptation Audit
entries.description: Run before adapting comedy in any direction, including prose to screen, stage to screen, and performance to page.
items: Sort every joke by mechanism: syntax, delivery, crowd contagion, or event.
Which of those survive the target medium unaltered, and which need rebuilding?
Does the comedy live in what happens or in who is telling it?
If the source is stage farce, is the geometry preserved, or has coverage destroyed the anticipation?
If an audience track is being added or removed, has the script been rebuilt to the new rhythm?
What is being lost, and has a device been found that performs the same function rather than the same lines?

entries.name: The Non-Anglophone Blind-Spot Audit
entries.description: Run at collection level rather than card level, whenever a body of comic work is being surveyed. A screen-forward survey over-selects for Anglophone television by construction.
items: What proportion of the examples are Anglophone, and what proportion are from the last thirty years?
Are the classical forms present as texts, or only as influences mentioned in passing?
Which comic traditions are represented only by their most-exported example?
Are non-Anglophone works dated by original-language year rather than translation year?
Is any tradition present only through a work that a Western audience found accessible?
Which forms have no representative at all, and is that a judgement or an oversight?

entries.name: The Real-Person Audit
entries.description: Run on any comic material about an identifiable living or recently dead person, including impressions, topical satire and roasts.
items: Is the subject a public figure acting in a public capacity, or a private person?
Is the material about what they did, or about what they are?
Are you analysing the published work's craft, or the person's life?
Is any factual claim about them stated as fact, and is it sourced?
Would the piece survive the subject reading it, not by being kind, but by being accurate?
Where a persona is involved, is the persona distinguished from the performer, and is the contested object the right one?

entries.name: The Complicity Audit
entries.description: Run on any piece that recruits the audience into a judgement, which is most satire and all cringe.
items: What posture is this passage asking for: judgement, wincing, or self-recognition?
Is more than one posture being requested at once?
In cringe, is the character oblivious, or has the transfer already failed?
In satire, can the audience enjoy this without reaching a verdict?
Does the intended audience already hold that verdict, and is the piece therefore flattery?
Where is the writer in the piece, and does the piece exempt them?
Can a portion of the audience take the indictment as endorsement, and does the work survive that reading?

entries.name: The Last-Sentence Audit
entries.description: Run on every card and every passage before it is merged or filed. One item, applied without exception.
items: Delete the final sentence of the passage.
Is any information lost?
If nothing is lost, the sentence was adjudicating, softening, or reassuring, and it must stay deleted.
Does the passage contain an unattributed "rightly", "of course", "problematic", or "has not aged well"?
Has a judgement been smuggled in as an adverb anywhere else?

entries.name: The Straight Man
entries.description: The character whose job is to react correctly, converting another character's absurdity into comedy by measuring it.

examples.text: Abbott's exasperation is the meter that makes Costello's confusion legible; without the measuring instrument the routine is only a man not understanding baseball.
Hacker is straight man to Sir Humphrey's syntax and simultaneously the fool to Bernard's literalism, which is how the show gets three-handers out of a two-hander structure.
Philinte's reasonableness exists so Alceste's honesty can be measured against it, and Molière makes the straight man's moderation the more disturbing position.
Darrin's exasperation is so unvarying that it stops measuring anything and becomes a second source of noise.

entries.name: The Fool Who Is Right
entries.description: The character everyone dismisses, whose incomprehension turns out to be accurate perception.

examples.text: Švejk's idiocy is never resolved into cunning, and the novel refuses to tell the reader whether he is a fool or the only sane man, which is the most sophisticated use of the trope in the form.
Chance's gardening platitudes are received as economic wisdom, which indicts the listeners rather than elevating him.
Dougal's questions are stupid and structurally correct, which is why they keep exposing the presbytery's arrangements.

entries.name: The Pompous Authority
entries.description: A figure whose claim to standing exceeds their competence, positioned so the gap must be exposed in public.

examples.text: Mainwaring's rank is real and his authority is not, and the series is careful to let him be right occasionally so the exposure keeps costing something.
Gogol makes an entire town pompous and gives it nothing to fear but a rumour, so the exposure comes from within.
Jonson stacks pomposities against each other so each is exposed by a rival rather than by the plot.
Captain Peacock's pretension is announced rather than demonstrated, so there is nothing to strip.

entries.name: The Schemer
entries.description: A character who generates plot by planning, and comedy by having the plan survive contact with nothing.

examples.text: Edmund's plans are competent and defeated by other people's stupidity, which is a different engine from plans that fail on their own terms.
Bilko's scheme is always financially rational and always exceeds the institution's tolerance, so the army rather than the plan supplies the reversal.
Ilf and Petrov let Ostap Bender succeed often enough that the reader begins to believe in him, which makes the final failure land as loss.

entries.name: The Innocent Abroad
entries.description: A protagonist whose unfamiliarity with a place or a milieu licenses the reader to have it explained and mocked at once.

examples.text: Jerome's narrator is innocent about the river and knowing about himself, which keeps the travelogue from becoming a guidebook.
The Texan's incomprehension of a Scottish village is the device, and the film's turn is that the village is running the negotiation.
Dan Ashcroft is not innocent, which is the point: the show removes the trope's protection and makes the observer complicit.

entries.name: The Long-Suffering Spouse
entries.description: A partner whose endurance is the scene's baseline, and whose eventual break is the payoff the form is saving.

examples.text: Laurence's endurance is the pressure gauge, and Leigh times the break to arrive after the audience has stopped expecting it.
Barbara's tolerance is the room's furniture, and the series gets its warmth from the moments it is briefly withdrawn.
Debra's exasperation is renewed weekly with nothing accumulating, so the endurance never converts into a break worth waiting for.

entries.name: The Sycophant
entries.description: A character whose flattery is a survival technique, and whose accuracy about the powerful is concealed inside it.

examples.text: The advisers' flattery is professional rather than personal, which makes it a description of the job rather than of their characters.
Molière makes the sycophancy so transparent that the comedy transfers entirely to the man being flattered.
Dickens gives Uriah Heep a physical vocabulary for obsequiousness, and the humility is the aggression.

entries.name: The Competent Subordinate
entries.description: The person who actually runs things, held below the person credited with running them.

examples.text: Wodehouse's innovation is that Jeeves never claims the credit, so the reader supplies the correction and the pleasure is theirs.
Every functional act in the corporation is performed by someone without the authority to perform it, which is the show's whole thesis.
Nigel's competence is the film's measure of what the institution wastes, and the comedy shades into something else when it is wasted.

entries.name: The Enthusiast Nobody Asked
entries.description: A character whose sincere passion for something minor is both the joke and the work's moral centre.

examples.text: Crook lets the enthusiasm be genuinely worth having, so the comedy never becomes contempt, and the series is the strongest available argument that the trope does not require a butt.
Tim's obsessions are treated as literacy rather than as arrested development, which is a choice the era's films mostly did not make.
Toast's investment in his own dignity as an actor is total, and the show's absurdity is measured against how seriously he takes it.

entries.name: The Social Climber
entries.description: A character whose ambition to rise is legible to everyone except themselves, so every scene is a small exposure.

examples.text: Hyacinth's aspiration is stated in every line, which makes the show relentless and its best episodes structurally airtight.
Becky Sharp is the trope written without contempt, and Thackeray withholds the punishment the form usually supplies.
Molière makes the climbing literal by having Jourdain buy lessons in being a gentleman, so the exposure happens on stage in real time.

entries.name: The Cynic in the Corner
entries.description: A character positioned outside the action whose commentary licenses the audience's own scepticism.

examples.text: Statler and Waldorf put the audience's objection inside the show, which pre-empts it and converts it into affection.
Carla's asides are the room's corrective, and the show is careful to give her scenes where the position costs her something.
The cynic's commentary agrees with the show's own position, so it confirms rather than corrects and the device does no work.

entries.name: The Man-Child
entries.description: An adult refusing adulthood, a trope that has aged more visibly than almost any other in the form.

examples.text: The refusal is treated as terminal rather than charming, and the film ends by separating the two men rather than reconciling them.
Both leads are the trope and neither is the corrective, which removes the usual structure in which someone eventually grows up.
The film's affection for the arrested state removes the cost entirely, and with nothing at risk the trope has no engine left, which is a useful demonstration of why the payer must be identifiable.

entries.name: The Wrong Room
entries.description: A character in a space they should not be in, where discovery is certain and the timing of it is the whole scene.

examples.text: Feydeau builds a hotel specifically so wrong rooms can be entered at speed, and the architecture does the plotting.
The hotel is a machine for putting people in rooms they should not be in, and Basil is always the one who must not be found.
The wrong room is a whole life, and Wilder extends the trope's clock from a scene to a picture.

entries.name: The Dinner Party That Must Not Fail
entries.description: A social occasion with a fixed duration, a captive cast and a host whose standing depends on it.

examples.text: Veber inverts the trope by making the guest the intended entertainment and the host the eventual payer.

examples.work: The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie
examples.text: Buñuel refuses to let the meal ever occur, which turns the trope inside out and exposes it as pure social apparatus.
The remake softens the host so the inversion has no one to land on.

entries.name: The Unwanted Guest
entries.description: A visitor who will not leave, whose presence exposes what the household is normally able to hide.

examples.work: The Man Who Came to Dinner
examples.text: Kaufman and Hart immobilise the guest with a broken hip so the premise cannot be escaped.
Seuss gives children the trope in its purest form: an intruder who is fun and is also a disaster, with the mess as the only proof.
Pasolini removes the comedy and keeps the structure, which is a useful demonstration that the trope is a mechanism rather than a joke.

entries.name: The Job Interview
entries.description: A scene with a built-in power gradient, a fixed script both parties know, and a strong incentive to lie.

examples.text: Brent's interview scenes invert the gradient because the audience knows what the interviewer does not.
Sharpe uses the institutional interview as an interrogation and lets the protagonist's honesty be the thing that damns him.
The gradient is removed in the first act, so every subsequent interview scene has nothing to threaten.

entries.name: The Funeral Behaving Badly
entries.description: A ceremony with an absolute decorum requirement, staged so that the requirement must be broken.

examples.text: The film stacks the breaches so each one raises the decorum cost of the next.
Waugh attacks the industry rather than the mourners, which moves the payer and makes the satire hold.
The single funeral is where the film withdraws its comic register, and the withdrawal is what makes the rest readable.

entries.name: The Wedding as Pressure Vessel
entries.description: An event with a fixed date, an assembled cast of people who avoid each other, and no possibility of postponement.

examples.text: The film uses the fixed date to force a decision the protagonist has spent the whole story avoiding.
Barry gives the vessel three suitors and a deadline and lets the pressure do the plotting.
The wedding assembles two incompatible systems of obligation, which is the film's only real engine.

entries.name: Trapped Together
entries.description: Characters who would not choose each other, confined by circumstance for a duration neither controls.

examples.text: Simon reduces the trope to two men and one apartment and gets a whole form out of it.
The confinement is literal and permanent, which lets the series treat small negotiations as high stakes.
The journey structure supplies a new confinement every twenty minutes, which is how the film avoids the form's usual second-act stall.
Three million years and a small ship is the most extreme statement of the premise available, and the show uses it mainly for status disputes.

entries.name: The Deadline Nobody Can Meet
entries.description: A clock imposed from outside, which converts ordinary incompetence into escalating panic.

examples.text: The opening night is the clock, and Frayn makes the audience watch the same deadline missed three ways.
The Olympics supplies an immovable date and the series derives every scene from proximity to it.
The bureaucratic deadline is absurd and enforced, which is what tips the comedy into dread.

entries.name: The Visit From Authority
entries.description: An inspection, review or royal visit that forces a group to pretend to be what it claims to be.

examples.text: Gogol's version needs no actual inspector, which is the most efficient possible form of the trope.
The visiting officer exposes the platoon's arrangements without ever having to criticise them.
The hotel inspector episode makes the inspection invisible, so the pretence is performed at everyone.

entries.name: The Object That Must Not Be Found
entries.description: A physical thing whose discovery would end a character, circulating through a space full of people.

examples.text: The cigarette case begins the machinery and Wilde never lets it out of the plot.
The memoir is the object, and the film's last shot is the trope's finest single payoff.
The object is a body, which is the trope at its literal limit and is why the premise cannot sustain a sequel.

entries.name: The Favour That Escalates
entries.description: A small request accepted out of politeness, which compounds until refusal is impossible and compliance is ruinous.

examples.text: Nearly every episode is this trope, and the show's innovation is that Larry's refusals escalate as fast as his agreements.
A single act of rescue compounds into total responsibility, and the film treats the politeness as the trap.
The landlady's small hospitality escalates into a criminal liability nobody can discharge, and the gang's politeness is what destroys them.

entries.name: The Reunion
entries.description: An assembly of people who knew each other when they were different, forcing comparison none of them survives.

examples.text: The weekend structure forces every comparison in sequence and the film is frank about how little anyone has moved.
The reunion is played against a second plot so the comparisons happen while something else is at stake.

examples.work: Romy and Michele's High School Reunion
examples.text: The fantasy sequence removes the comparison's cost, so the reunion stops being a pressure and becomes a setting.

entries.name: The Deadpan Report
entries.description: Extraordinary content delivered in the register of ordinary information, with the register held without exception.

examples.work: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
examples.text: Adams delivers cosmic scale in the voice of a consumer handbook and never once acknowledges the mismatch, which is the purest sustained example of register discipline in comic prose.

examples.work: The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart
examples.text: Newhart's telephone routines report catastrophe in an office voice, and the silences on the other end do the work.
Swift's economic register is maintained so precisely that the pamphlet was read straight by some contemporaries.

entries.name: The Euphemism Treadmill
entries.description: Institutional language replacing plain words with softer ones, exposing exactly what it is trying to conceal.

examples.text: Sir Humphrey's sentences are constructed so that their length is proportional to what is being hidden.
The corporation's vocabulary has replaced its capacity to state anything, and the series treats that as the plot rather than as decoration.
Orwell's essay is not comic but supplies the mechanism every euphemism joke since has used, and the examples he collects are funnier than his commentary.

entries.name: The Malapropism
entries.description: A character reaching for a register above their command and landing one word to the side of it.

examples.text: Sheridan gave the device its name and, more usefully, gave Mrs Malaprop enough dignity that the errors cost her something.
Dogberry's errors are load-bearing, since the watch's incompetence is what actually resolves the plot.
Del Boy's French is aspiration made audible, and the series never lets anyone correct him, which is what keeps it affectionate.
The literalism is charming and consequence-free, which makes it a device for teaching vocabulary rather than a comic engine.

entries.name: The Literalist
entries.description: A character who takes figurative language at face value, exposing how much ordinary speech relies on not being examined.

examples.text: The film runs the device at a rate no other comedy has matched, and its consistency is what stops it becoming a single joke.
Drebin's literalism is played entirely straight by the performer, which is the reason the same script fails in other hands.
Martin's pedantry about procedure is literalism with professional stakes, so the device generates plot rather than only lines.

entries.name: Understatement as Engine
entries.description: A response so disproportionately mild that the gap between event and reaction becomes the entire joke.

examples.work: Monty Python and the Holy Grail
examples.text: The Black Knight's assessment of his own dismemberment is the form's benchmark, and it works because the register never wavers across four amputations.
Price's narration describes murders in the vocabulary of social inconvenience and sustains it for the whole picture.
Flora responds to gothic catastrophe with practical suggestions, and Gibbons never lets her acknowledge the mismatch.

entries.name: The Insult as Craft
entries.description: Invective constructed rather than shouted, where the pleasure is the architecture and not the aggression.

examples.text: The insults are built as extended similes with a delayed operative noun, which is why they survive quotation.
Tucker's invective is baroque and precisely targeted, and the film is careful to show it failing when the target outranks him.
Parker's review copy demonstrates that the shortest form of the insult is usually the strongest, and that the target must be named.

entries.name: The Non-Sequitur
entries.description: A reply that does not follow, sustained until the absence of logic becomes its own logic.

examples.text: Milligan builds half-hours in which causation is optional and the only continuity is voice, which is the form's founding demonstration.
Ionesco makes the non-sequitur the medium rather than the joke, so the audience laughs at the collapse of exchange itself.
The show's non-sequiturs are delivered with the confidence of catchphrases, which is what stops them reading as randomness.

entries.name: The Catchphrase and Its Decay
entries.description: A repeated line that buys instant recognition and spends the character's capacity to surprise.

examples.text: The show industrialised the catchphrase and, unusually, built several sketches on the audience's anticipation of it rather than on the line.
The catchphrases outlived the sketches that produced them, which is the clearest available demonstration of the decay curve; the series is also a live contested case and is carded as one.

The show's own writers have discussed the point at which a catchphrase replaced a character, and the later seasons supply the teaching example: a line that arrives on schedule cannot also arrive as a surprise.

entries.name: The Pun and Its Defenders
entries.description: Wordplay that trades a laugh for a groan, and the small social ritual by which the groan is also the reward.

examples.text: The innuendo and the pun are doing censorship-evasion work as well as comic work, which is why the density is so high.
The names are puns in French and are re-punned rather than translated into English, which makes the series a study in what wordplay costs across languages.

examples.work: I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue
examples.text: The panel format makes the groan audible and therefore part of the score, which is the closest the form comes to acknowledging its own transaction.

entries.name: Register Slip
entries.description: A character dropping out of the vocabulary their position requires, exposing what the position is made of.

examples.text: The politburo speak in regional accents and modern idiom, which strips the historical register and leaves the committee behaviour visible.
Sharpe alternates high academic register with plain obscenity and lets the college's self-description collapse under the contrast.
The substitute-teacher and anger-translator sketches are both built on a single sustained register mismatch held past the point of comfort.

entries.name: The Interruption
entries.description: A character who cannot complete a sentence, where the incompletion is a status fact rather than a rhythm choice.

examples.text: Who may interrupt whom is the show's entire status map, and it is legible without a line of exposition.
Larry's interruptions are corrections, and the show's discomfort comes from his being right.
Bean uses interruption as farce machinery, since a completed sentence anywhere would end the deception.

entries.name: The Repeated Word
entries.description: A single word or phrase repeated past sense until repetition itself becomes the content.

examples.text: The spam sketch establishes the technique's limit case by letting the repetition drown the dialogue it interrupts.
Beckett makes repetition the structure rather than a device, and the second act's near-recurrence is the play's argument.
Robinson's characters repeat a position past the point anyone would defend it, which relocates the comedy from the line to the refusal to abandon it.

entries.name: The Pratfall
entries.description: A fall staged so the audience sees the geometry, the intention and the loss of dignity in one movement.

examples.text: Laurel and Hardy make the staircase the antagonist and let the audience see the whole flight, so every fall is anticipated before it happens.
Chaplin's falls are choreographed to end in a recovery of poise, which is what separates his physical comedy from injury.
Atkinson's falls are preceded by long preparation, so the audience is complicit in the disaster by the time it arrives.

entries.name: The Escalating Chase
entries.description: A pursuit that acquires participants, vehicles and absurdity as it runs, with each addition raising the geometry.

examples.text: Keaton builds a chase in which every gag is set up on the outward journey and paid on the return, and the whole film is legible as one continuous mechanism.
Oury adds a new mismatched pair and a new terrain at intervals, and the escalation is national as well as physical.
Wright escalates a village foot-chase into an action-film pastiche and lets the incongruity of the setting carry the joke.

entries.name: The Object That Fights Back
entries.description: An inanimate thing that behaves as an adversary, granting the scene an opponent with no motive to negotiate.

examples.text: The feeding machine is the definitive statement, and Chaplin makes the factory rather than the machine the actual antagonist.
Tati's modern house is a single object with many hostile parts, and the comedy is architectural rather than kinetic.
Tati removes the protagonist's centrality so the objects can be observed defeating everyone equally.

entries.name: The Double Take
entries.description: The delayed second look, in which a performer shows the audience the exact moment comprehension arrives.

examples.text: Laurel and Hardy's escalating destruction is punctuated by takes that give the audience permission to keep laughing at property damage.
The mirror sequence is a sustained take in which the comprehension never arrives, which inverts the device.
Abbott's takes are the punctuation of the routine, and removing them would leave a monologue.

entries.name: The Look to Camera
entries.description: A silent glance at the audience that converts them from observers into witnesses.

examples.text: Michael Caine's addresses are the device used to recruit the audience into a position they will later be asked to abandon.
Hardy's look to camera is the device's origin in screen comedy and remains its clearest use, since it asks the audience to confirm the injustice.
The looks are a music-hall convention imported wholesale, and the show is rigorous about when they are permitted.

entries.name: The Crowded Space
entries.description: More bodies than the room can hold, staged so the audience can see the arithmetic failing.

examples.text: The stateroom sequence adds people at a metronomic rate and never cheats the geometry, which is why the payoff lands.
The backstage act depends on the audience knowing the set's capacity from act one.
The physical set pieces are built on a single body being too large for the space it has entered, which is the trope reduced to one person.

entries.name: The Costume That Betrays
entries.description: A disguise that works and then begins to work against the wearer, so the deception becomes the trap.

examples.text: The disguise succeeds professionally and fails personally, and the film's comedy comes from the two consequences arriving together.
The costume becomes a life the wearer cannot exit, and Wilder refuses to resolve it in the final line.
The disguise is never at real risk until the plot requires it, so the sustained tension the trope depends on is absent for most of the running time.

entries.name: The Machine That Wins
entries.description: A system, device or process that defeats the human being conclusively, with no reversal offered.

examples.text: The bureaucratic machine wins absolutely, and the film's comedy is what makes the ending readable rather than merely bleak.
The assembly line wins on its own terms and the tramp's escape is expulsion rather than victory.
The joke is that the machine always wins and the humans have stopped expecting otherwise, which is a domesticated version of the same structure.

entries.name: The Food Disaster
entries.description: A meal as the site of catastrophe, where eating is both the pleasure and the humiliation.

examples.text: Itami treats food with total seriousness and derives the comedy from that seriousness, which is the inverse of the usual approach.
The Mr Creosote sequence is the form's limit case and is constructed as an escalation with a single, announced ending.
Ferreri removes the comic release entirely and keeps the structure, which makes the film a study in where this trope stops being funny.

entries.name: The Body in the Wrong Place
entries.description: A corpse or an unconscious person who must be moved, hidden or explained, in a space with witnesses.

examples.text: Kesselring stacks the bodies and makes the aunts' serenity the source of the comedy rather than the corpses.
Hitchcock plays the body as an inconvenience of scheduling, and the flat register is what makes it comic.
The premise is the trope with nothing else attached, which demonstrates both its power and its finite running time.

entries.name: The Class Marker
entries.description: A small detail of speech, dress or consumption that places a character exactly, and that they cannot control.

examples.text: The series makes a single class aspiration the entire engine, and Harold's cultural pretensions are precise enough to be painful rather than merely funny.
Shaw makes the marker explicit and teachable, and then makes the teaching the problem.
The markers are announced by the character herself, which is a coarser use of the trope and is instructive by comparison.

entries.name: The Small Talk That Fails
entries.description: A conversation with no content and a strict obligation to continue, where the obligation is the pressure.

examples.work: Knowing Me, Knowing You with Alan Partridge
examples.text: The chat-show format makes failed small talk professionally fatal, which raises a low-stakes trope to plot level.
The interior monologue lets the audience hear the search for a next sentence, which is the trope's mechanism made audible.
The brothers use small talk as a status contest, so the failure is competitive rather than merely awkward.

entries.name: The Queue
entries.description: Enforced waiting among strangers, in which the only available drama is procedure.

examples.text: Galton and Simpson build entire episodes from waiting, and the blood-donor material demonstrates that procedure alone can carry a half-hour.
Sorokin writes a novel almost entirely as overheard queue dialogue, which turns a Soviet fact of life into a formal experiment.
Atkinson uses queues as pure physical negotiation, since the character cannot argue his way forward.

entries.name: The Apology That Makes It Worse
entries.description: An attempt at repair that restates the offence, usually in more detail than the original.

examples.text: Michael Scott's apologies are the show's most reliable mechanism, because each one requires him to describe what he did.
The apologies are accurate and unwanted, which is a harder version of the trope than the incompetent apology.
The show's characters apologise strategically rather than sincerely, so the repair fails on inspection rather than on delivery.

entries.name: The Person Who Will Not Take the Hint
entries.description: A character immune to social signal, whose persistence forces everyone else to become explicit.

examples.text: Partridge's imperviousness converts every scene into a test of how long politeness can hold.
The film reverses the trope by making the host the one refusing to take a hint, which relocates the cost.
Coogan and Brydon's competitive impressions are each a hint the other declines to take, sustained across a whole series.

entries.name: The Public Argument
entries.description: A private dispute conducted in front of witnesses who cannot leave and are not permitted to intervene.

examples.text: Albee makes the witnesses participants and the audience the second set of witnesses, which is the trope at maximum pressure.
The argument is conducted in the vocabulary of hospitality, which is what makes it unbearable rather than merely loud.
The film escalates the trope past the point of comedy deliberately and is frequently cited as the moment black comedy stops being enjoyable, which is a contested reading.

entries.name: The Compliment That Lands Wrong
entries.description: Praise that reveals what the speaker actually believes, delivered with no awareness that it has.

examples.text: Moira's compliments are constructed from a vocabulary that flatters her rather than the recipient, and the show lets the recipients notice.
Austen builds the Box Hill scene so that a single misjudged remark undoes a whole social position, which is the trope at maximum consequence.
Compliments in the show are always transactional and always slightly too specific, which is what exposes the speaker.

entries.name: The Overheard Message
entries.description: A private communication reaching the wrong recipient, where the content is less damaging than the fact of its privacy.

examples.text: The leaked email and the open microphone are the series' recurring instruments, and both are treated as procedural rather than farcical.
Shakespeare uses deliberate overhearing twice in opposite directions, which makes the device the plot's whole mechanism.
The diary is a private document the reader is overhearing, which puts the audience permanently in the wrong-recipient position.

entries.name: The Name Nobody Remembers
entries.description: A character whose identity fails to register, making them a running measure of everyone else's attention.

examples.text: Jerry's interchangeable names are a running gag that the series eventually pays off by revealing his home life is the happiest in the cast.
The title states the premise and the Grossmiths never relieve it, so the whole book is the trope sustained.
The forgotten-employee gag is used often enough that the forgetting stops reading as characterisation and becomes a scheduling device.

entries.name: The Gift That Obligates
entries.description: A present that transfers debt rather than pleasure, which the recipient cannot refuse or discharge.

examples.text: The film is not a comedy and supplies the purest statement of the mechanism, which comic writing borrows wholesale.
The gift exchanges between the two families are class negotiations conducted in wrapping paper.
Balzac makes the obligation financial and permanent, and the comedy is entirely at the expense of those who accept.

entries.name: The Neighbour Dispute
entries.description: A conflict over something trivial between people who cannot move away from each other.

examples.text: The Kerrigans' dispute is with an airport rather than a neighbour, and the film's warmth comes from taking their attachment seriously.
The rivalry is entirely one-sided, which is a harder and better version of the trope than mutual antagonism.
Pergaud gives the dispute to children and lets the escalation follow adult logic exactly.

entries.name: The Tourist
entries.description: A visitor performing appreciation of a place they do not understand, watched by people who live there.

examples.text: Tati observes the resort's rituals with no dialogue and lets the holiday's compulsory pleasure do the indicting.
Twain writes from inside the trope and turns the mockery on his own party, which is what keeps it readable.
The film is unusually frank that the tourists are the payers and that the resort is indifferent to them.

entries.name: The Meeting That Decides Nothing
entries.description: A gathering with an agenda, minutes and no capacity to act, where procedure substitutes for outcome.

examples.text: Every episode is a meeting that fails to decide, and the series never once cheats by allowing a decision, which is the most disciplined use of the trope in the form.
The public forum episodes give the meeting an audience, which converts inertia into humiliation.
Kafka's version removes the comedy's release and keeps the structure, and the borrowing runs from him to almost every workplace comedy since.

entries.name: The Form That Cannot Be Completed
entries.description: A document whose requirements are mutually exclusive, defended by people who did not write it.

examples.text: The title rule is a form that cannot be completed, generalised into a philosophy, and the novel is the trope's founding text.
The film is not a comedy and its benefits-office scenes use exactly the comic structure, which is why they are unbearable.
The Place That Sends You Mad sequence from the original comic is staged as a bureaucratic loop with no exit, and the joke is entirely structural.

entries.name: The Policy Applied Literally
entries.description: A rule enforced exactly as written, by someone who has correctly identified that this is safer than judgement.

examples.text: Holt's literalism is presented as competence rather than obstruction, which inverts the trope's usual moral loading.
Melville inverts the trope by having the employee refuse rather than comply, and the office's inability to respond is the comedy.
The computer-says-no sketches reduce the trope to a single exchange and demonstrate how quickly the device exhausts itself.

entries.name: The Reorganisation
entries.description: A restructuring that changes every name and no function, announced as transformation.

examples.text: The merger arc uses reorganisation as an actual threat, which gives the satire stakes most workplace comedy declines.

examples.work: Then We Came to the End
examples.text: Ferris writes the layoffs in first-person plural, so the reorganisation happens to a voice rather than to individuals.
The consultants' arrival makes the reorganisation an external event, which is a weaker structure than an internal one and is instructive as a comparison.

entries.name: The Consultant
entries.description: An outsider paid to say what insiders already know, whose authority derives entirely from being external.

examples.text: The advisers are consultants in effect, and the film shows their power evaporating the moment a real institution asserts itself.
Adams's consultant strips are the most-circulated satire of the profession, and their circulation inside the organisations they satirise is the interesting fact.
Peter and Hull's book is a comic argument in the form of management theory and was widely read as the latter.

entries.name: The Memo
entries.description: A written communication whose real content is the fact of having been written, and the record it creates.

examples.text: Sir Humphrey's minutes are drafted to be defensible rather than informative, and the series treats that as the point of the document.
Parkinson's essay is a joke sustained to book length and has been cited as management science ever since, which is the joke continuing.

examples.work: Mr. Burns's memos in The Simpsons
examples.text: The plant's written communications are legally cautious and morally indifferent, which is the show's most consistent satirical register.

entries.name: Going Over Their Head
entries.description: A character bypassing the chain of command, where the offence is procedural and the punishment is social.

examples.text: Escalation to the wrong person is the series' most reliable disaster, and it is always fatal to someone junior.
Bilko's schemes routinely require bypassing a superior, and the show treats the chain of command as a resource rather than an obstacle.
The escalation to the tax inspector converts a private cruelty into an institutional one, which is how the film moves the payer.

entries.name: The Audit
entries.description: An examination of the record by someone with the authority to find, where everyone has something informal to hide.

examples.text: The audit is the entire plot mechanism, and the film's structure is a countdown to an inspection.
The college's finances are examined by an outsider and the institution's defence is entirely social rather than fiscal.
The lists are the audit, and the film derives its comedy from characters revising a record while standing next to it.

entries.name: The Loyal Servant of a Bad Institution
entries.description: A character whose competence and decency are entirely in service of something the audience can see is indefensible.

examples.text: Barrowclough's kindness inside a prison is played as futility rather than virtue, which is a harder reading than the form usually attempts.
Ishiguro writes the trope without comedy and supplies its definitive statement, which comic treatments have borrowed from since.
Baldrick's loyalty is the series' moral instrument and its final scene is what the loyalty was for.

entries.name: The Away Day
entries.description: Compulsory enjoyment organised by an employer, where attendance is voluntary in name only.

examples.text: The corporate training modules are enforced participation with a wage attached, which is the trope's most honest version.
The corporate retreat episodes let the network's language do the coercion, so nobody has to give an order.
The retreat episode states its thesis in dialogue rather than demonstrating it, which removes the audience's work and therefore the laugh.

entries.name: The Parent Who Has Not Stopped Parenting
entries.description: A parent applying childhood authority to an adult child, in front of witnesses.

examples.text: Marie's interventions are the show's engine, and the proximity of the two houses is the structural decision that makes it work.
Roth's mother is a comic construction and an indictment simultaneously, and the novel is explicit that the narrator cannot separate them.
The grandmother's refusals invert the trope by withholding the parenting the adult child expects.

entries.name: The Sibling Scorecard
entries.description: Two adults conducting a competition that was settled in childhood and has never been closed.

examples.text: The brothers' competition is conducted entirely in cultural capital, which makes every scene both a status contest and a class joke.
The Bluth siblings' scorecard is financial, romantic and parental at once, and the show tracks all three.
The competition is professional and thinly disguised as impressions, which is why the funniest scenes are also the saddest.

entries.name: The Family Holiday
entries.description: A group obliged to enjoy each other's company continuously, in a place none of them controls.

examples.text: The journey structure supplies a fresh disaster at intervals, and the father's insistence on enjoyment is the actual antagonist.
Tati observes many families at once, which converts the trope from a story into an ethnography.
The family's holidays are always financially precarious, which gives the enforced enjoyment a cost the genre usually omits.

entries.name: The Christmas Dinner
entries.description: An annual event with fixed roles, compulsory attendance and a documented history of failure.

examples.text: The Christmas specials are the series at its best because the ritual removes any need for plot.
The two families' Christmases are staged as competing systems of hospitality, and the comedy is in the translation between them.
Vinterberg uses a family dinner to deliver a revelation and keeps a comic structure underneath it, which is the clearest available case of the trope's black-comedy limit.

entries.name: The Teenager's Contempt
entries.description: An adolescent's certainty that their parents are absurd, treated as accurate and as a phase simultaneously.

examples.work: The Secret Diary of Adrian Mole Aged 13¾
examples.text: Townsend lets the contempt be wrong about everything except the things it is right about, and never adjudicates.
The contempt is aimed at parents and at a political situation at once, and the show refuses to rank them.

examples.work: Kevin and Perry in Harry Enfield's Television Programme
examples.text: The sketch reduces adolescence to a single physical posture, which is efficient and has almost no second gear.

entries.name: The Inherited House
entries.description: A property that arrives with obligations, relatives and a history the inheritor cannot dispose of.

examples.text: Chekhov called it a comedy and Stanislavski staged it as tragedy; the dispute is unresolved and the play works either way, which is itself the lesson.
The house is the landlady's authority made architectural, and the gang's error is treating it as neutral ground.
Flora inherits relatives rather than property and applies the same management approach, which is the trope's inversion.

entries.name: The In-Law
entries.description: A relative acquired by contract rather than blood, who must be tolerated without the licence blood provides.

examples.text: The film makes the assessment explicit and continuous, so every scene is a test with a stated grade.
The in-law meeting is a farce mechanism and a political argument, and the film runs both without dropping either.
The in-laws are two whole systems rather than two people, so the tolerance required is cultural rather than personal.

entries.name: The Child Who Says the Unsayable
entries.description: A child stating what the adults have agreed not to state, protected from consequence by age.

examples.text: The children's semi-improvised questions are unanswerable by design, and the parents' evasions are the actual comedy.
Goscinny writes the child's narration as entirely reasonable, so the adults' world is what looks strange.
The children's questions are aimed at the parents' compromises rather than at taboo, which is a gentler and more sustainable version of the trope.

entries.name: The Chore War
entries.description: A domestic dispute about labour that is actually about respect, conducted through objects.

examples.text: The yard's work is the relationship, and every dispute about it is a dispute about escape.
The chore disputes are about exhaustion rather than fairness, and the series is unusual in showing the labour as paid work's continuation; the show is a live contested case and is carded as one.
The household's labour is genuinely overwhelming, which means the disputes are about triage rather than about fairness.

entries.name: The Family Secret Everyone Knows
entries.description: Information the family has agreed to treat as concealed, maintained by everyone including the person it concerns.

examples.text: Letts makes the maintenance of the secret the family's only shared activity.
The show's secrets are known to the audience from episode one, which converts every concealment scene into dramatic irony.
The secret is stated aloud in act one and the comedy comes from the family continuing as though it had not been.

entries.name: The Public Failure
entries.description: A collapse with an audience, where the witnesses are the cost rather than the failure itself.

examples.text: Millman's humiliations are always performed in front of people whose opinion he has stated he does not care about.
Ignatius fails publicly and continuously and interprets every failure as vindication, which is what stops the book becoming pitiable.
The engagement-party speech is a public failure conducted through competitive politeness, which is a harder version than shouting.

entries.name: The Overreach
entries.description: A character attempting something one level above their competence, with the level clearly established first.

examples.text: The company's ambition is stated in the programme and defeated by the set, and the gap is the entire evening.
Dixon's lecture is an overreach he did not choose, which makes it a satire of the institution rather than of the man.
Jourdain buys the competence he lacks, and Molière lets the purchase be the humiliation.

entries.name: The Thing Said in the Wrong Room
entries.description: An accurate private opinion delivered where its subject can hear it.

examples.text: Austen's Box Hill remark is true, brief and socially fatal, which is the trope at its most economical.
The hot microphone is the series' standing threat, and its victims are always people who were being honest.
Risi's driver says out loud what the passenger has been thinking, and the film's whole moral position turns on it.

entries.name: The Talent Nobody Wants to See
entries.description: A performer whose sincerity exceeds their ability, staged so the audience cannot look away.

examples.text: The band's decline is measured in venue size, and the film never lets them realise it.
Guest's owners perform competence at a hobby, and the camera's neutrality is what makes it bearable.
The film's problem is that the sincerity is real and the protection around it is a conspiracy, which moves the payer to the protectors.

entries.name: Dignity in Undignified Circumstances
entries.description: A character maintaining formality while physically or socially degraded, where the maintenance is the comedy.

examples.work: Monty Python and the Holy Grail
examples.text: The Black Knight's insistence on protocol while being dismembered is the purest instance available, and it is why the sequence outlived the film.
Withnail's theatrical register never drops regardless of circumstance, and the final soliloquy is that refusal at full cost.
Adam maintains clerical composure through indignities the series refuses to make funny, and the composure is what the show is actually about.

entries.name: The Comeuppance Withheld
entries.description: A deserving character who is never punished, which converts the audience's expectation into the joke.

examples.text: Waugh sends the wrong Boot home to a knighthood and lets the deserving one keep the farm, and nobody is ever corrected.
Thackeray declines to punish Becky proportionally and the novel's subtitle does the arguing.
The film withholds the comeuppance until it arrives on the wrong person, which is the most severe use of the device in the form.

entries.name: The Self-Own
entries.description: A character defeated by their own argument, statement or precaution.

examples.text: Hacker is regularly defeated by a principle he asserted in a previous scene, and the series treats the retrieval as procedure.
Orgon's defence of Tartuffe is what supplies the evidence against him.
Beatty builds arguments that indict the speaker and the reader simultaneously, and the courtroom frame makes the self-own structural.

entries.name: Humiliation Witnessed by the Wrong Person
entries.description: A private embarrassment observed by the one person whose opinion the character was protecting.

examples.text: Baxter's arrangement is discovered by exactly the person it was hidden from, and Wilder times it to the minute.
Partridge's worst moments are witnessed by the broadcaster he is petitioning, which is the show's structural cruelty.
Svevo's narrator confesses to an analyst who is publishing the confession, which puts the wrong witness in the book's frame.

entries.name: The Apology Tour
entries.description: A sequence of repairs attempted in series, each of which creates the need for the next.

examples.text: The show's plots frequently run as chains of repair, and the convergence is that all four chains meet.
The apologies are conducted at the speed of farce inside a hospital, which supplies witnesses who cannot leave.
The film's first act is an apology tour and its second is the same route with zombies, which is a formal joke about the structure.

entries.name: The Failure That Is Also a Relief
entries.description: A collapse that frees the character from something they were too proud to abandon.

examples.text: Sturges makes the director's failure the thing that teaches him what comedy is for, which is the film arguing with itself.
Harold's failures to shock are relief rather than defeat, and the film treats each as progress.
Russo's narrator's professional collapse removes an obligation he never wanted, and the novel refuses to call it a triumph.

entries.name: The Return to the Scene
entries.description: A character revisiting the place of an earlier humiliation, where the room does the remembering.

examples.text: The house supplies the comparison the characters would not make themselves.
Fellini's town is a permanent scene of humiliation revisited annually by ritual, which makes the return structural.
The school corridor is played for dread rather than nostalgia, which is a rarer choice.

entries.name: The Person Who Does Not Know They Have Lost
entries.description: A character continuing to negotiate after the outcome has been settled by everyone else.

examples.text: Mamet's play is not a comedy and gives the trope its hardest statement, which comic writing has borrowed since.
Guests negotiate for segments already cut, and the staff's politeness is what withholds the information.
Gogol's landowners bargain over property that does not exist, and none of them registers that the transaction is impossible.

entries.name: The Lie That Requires Maintenance
entries.description: A single untruth that generates an expanding schedule of supporting untruths.

examples.text: Wilde gives both leads a maintained fiction, makes them collide, and resolves the whole play by revealing the fiction was true, which no later treatment has improved on.
Thomas builds the maintenance into a timetable, so the comedy is scheduling rather than invention.
The maintenance is professional and escalating, and the film treats the labour of the lie as the subject.

entries.name: Mistaken Identity
entries.description: A character taken for someone else, where the error is other people's and the consequences are theirs.

examples.text: Plautus establishes the mechanism the entire tradition inherits, including the resolution by recognition.
Shakespeare doubles Plautus's pair and thereby doubles the collision rate, which is a purely structural improvement.
Hitchcock plays the trope for thriller and keeps the comic rhythm, which shows how little the mechanism depends on genre.

entries.name: The Double Booking
entries.description: Two commitments in the same slot, honoured simultaneously by a character shuttling between them.

examples.text: Bean makes the shuttling physical and gives the servant a hunger that motivates the impossible schedule.
Goldoni's original establishes the mechanism inside the commedia tradition and supplies the improvised business it depends on.
Camoletti builds the double booking into an airline timetable, so a schedule change is the plot's only possible catastrophe.

entries.name: The Impersonation
entries.description: A deliberate assumption of another's identity, where the impersonator learns something the original could not.

examples.work: To Be or Not to Be
examples.text: Lubitsch makes impersonation a resistance tactic and the actors' vanity the running joke inside it.
Cantinflas is mistaken for another man and then chooses to sustain it, and the courtroom sequence is built on verbal evasion rather than plot.
The impersonation is imposed rather than chosen, which relocates the comedy from the impersonator to the people running the experiment.

entries.name: The Twin
entries.description: Identical people used as a plot device, whose value is that no deception is required for the deception to occur.

examples.text: Shakespeare adds a disguise on top of the twinning so the confusions compound rather than merely repeat.
Kästner gives the device to children and makes the reunion of parents the actual object.
The device does all the work and the characters do almost none, which is why the premise has been remade rather than developed.

entries.name: The Forged Credential
entries.description: A qualification claimed rather than held, tested by circumstances the holder cannot control.

examples.text: The credentials are literal forgeries and the film shows each being tested, which is the trope's full mechanism.
The hospital setting makes the untested competence genuinely dangerous, which raises the stakes without changing the register.
Molière's medical impostures indict a profession rather than an individual, and the final ceremony is the forgery made public.

entries.name: The Letter Sent in Error
entries.description: A written communication arriving where it was not intended, which cannot be recalled or denied.

examples.text: The forged letter is sent deliberately to the wrong reader, which is the trope weaponised.
Laclos builds the whole novel from correspondence going astray, and the comedy is entirely at the letter-writers' expense.
The reply-all is the modern form, and the series treats it as an irreversible physical event.

entries.name: The Cover Story That Becomes Real
entries.description: An invented explanation that the world begins to treat as fact, obliging the inventor to inhabit it.

examples.text: Chance invents nothing and the world supplies the cover story, which is the trope's most elegant inversion.
The fabricated war acquires participants and consequences, and the film's comedy is that nobody involved is surprised.
Boot's invented despatches shape the war they were invented to describe, and Waugh treats the reversal as ordinary journalism.

entries.name: The Eavesdropper Who Mishears
entries.description: Partial information overheard and acted on, where the listener's error is plausible and the audience holds the correction.

examples.text: Beaumarchais makes overhearing the servant's professional technique rather than an accident.
The balcony scene is an eavesdrop the listener misattributes, and Rostand makes the misattribution the whole tragedy.
Bernard acts on half-heard information at speed, and the shop's size means the correction is always available and never sought.
Beaumarchais makes overhearing the servant's professional technique rather than an accident.

entries.name: The Secret Kept From the Audience
entries.description: Information withheld from the viewer as well as the characters, which converts comedy into a reveal structure.

examples.text: The multiple endings make the withholding explicit and turn the film into an argument about the device.
The film is not a comedy and supplies the technique's cleanest demonstration, which comic capers have copied since.
Withholding from the audience removes dramatic irony, which is comedy's most reliable engine, and the film has to substitute escalation for it.

entries.name: The Con That Works Too Well
entries.description: A deception that succeeds beyond its design, creating obligations the con artist cannot meet.

examples.text: The play succeeds, which is the only possible failure, and the whole plot is engineered to make that the worst outcome.
Bender's improvisations succeed at a rate that traps him inside roles he invented to escape.
The pretence of dying attracts more gifts than Volpone can account for, and the court is what he cannot control.

entries.name: The Undercover Assignment
entries.description: A character embedded in a group they were sent to observe, who begins to prefer it there.

examples.text: The film is not a comedy and gives the trope its hardest statement: two men embedded so long that preference and cover become indistinguishable.
The officer is not undercover and the village behaves as though he were, which inverts the arrangement.

examples.work: Le Grand Blond avec une chaussure noire
examples.text: Robert is not an agent and the surveillance apparatus constructs one around him, so the deception is entirely the observers' own.

entries.name: The Man Behind the Curtain
entries.description: An authority revealed to be a person with equipment, where the revelation is deflating rather than triumphant.

examples.text: The reveal is the trope's naming instance and is played for sympathy rather than for exposure.
Chaplin strips the dictator to a man on a chair with a balloon, and the deflation is the film's central political act.
Lampedusa is not writing comedy and the mechanism is identical: the authority is a man with arrangements, and the arrangements are all there is.

entries.name: The Reveal Everyone Saw Coming
entries.description: A disclosure the audience has anticipated for some time, where the comedy is in the characters' delay.

examples.text: The audience waits an entire film for a disclosure the protagonist keeps postponing, and the postponement is what accrues the cost.
The revelation is inevitable from the first scene and the film's pleasure is watching the postponement cost more each minute.
The restaurant reveal is delayed past the point of plausibility, and the delay stops being comic once the audience can see the plot holding the character in place.

entries.name: Setup and Punchline
entries.description: The two-part unit the whole form is built from: an expectation installed, then replaced in a single stroke.

examples.text: Benny's construction is unusually visible because his persona lets the setup run long, so the audience can watch the expectation being installed.

examples.work: I'm Telling You for the Last Time
examples.text: Seinfeld's observational form is setup-punchline at very high density, with almost no persona material between units.
Hedberg strips the unit to its minimum, often two sentences, which makes the architecture impossible to miss.

entries.name: The Straight Setup
entries.description: A first line that must contain no comedy at all, because any laugh in the setup spends the payoff.

examples.text: The film's straight lines are delivered with total sincerity, which is the reason the density does not exhaust the audience.
The Four Candles sketch works because the shopkeeper plays every request as a genuine attempt to help.
Several sequences put a joke in the setup as well as the payoff, and the second joke consistently kills the first.

entries.name: The Topper
entries.description: A second punchline landing immediately on the first, which must be larger or the sequence deflates.

examples.text: The films run toppers in threes and are disciplined about the size gradient, which is why the third still lands.

examples.work: A Bit of Fry and Laurie
examples.text: The sketches often top a verbal joke with a structural one, which changes the kind of laugh as well as the size.
Groucho tops his own lines faster than the scene can absorb, and the film's pace is a consequence of that habit.

entries.name: The Tag
entries.description: A short line after the laugh has begun, riding the existing reaction rather than starting a new one.

examples.text: Benny's tags are frequently a single word or a look placed inside the laugh, and the technique is the clearest surviving demonstration that a tag is not a second joke.
The show's scenes almost always end on a tag from a character who has not spoken, which is a structural signature.
The end-of-episode joke is a formal tag appended after the scene has closed, which is the device made into a fixture.

entries.name: Misdirection
entries.description: Attention deliberately placed where the payoff will not occur, so the reversal arrives from an unwatched direction.

examples.text: The stoning sequence directs attention at blasphemy and pays off on the crowd's enthusiasm for the punishment.
The show's shortest sketches are pure misdirection, since there is no time for anything else.
Keaton misdirects with the frame itself, placing the audience's attention in the wrong plane of the shot.

entries.name: The Garden Path
entries.description: A sentence that permits only one reading until its final word forces a different one retroactively.

examples.text: Demetri Martin's one-liners are almost all garden paths, and the brevity means the reinterpretation is instant.
Goscinny's names and captions are constructed to be reread, which is the printed form of the same device.
The format rewards sentences that change direction mid-clause, so the device becomes a competitive skill.

entries.name: Pull-Back and Reveal
entries.description: A frame widened to show context that reinterprets everything the audience has just watched.

examples.text: The opening's widening from the nativity to the wrong stable is the device used as a thesis statement.
The sketch team used the reveal to relocate a scene's target, frequently from the speaker to the institution behind them.
Larson's single panel performs the pull-back in one image by placing the caption where the frame cannot show it.

entries.name: The Literalised Figure
entries.description: A metaphor or idiom made physically true, so the language rather than the character is the payer.

examples.text: Groucho's elephant line literalises a modifier's placement and then refuses to explain it.
The films stage idioms as physical events in the background of otherwise straight scenes.
Limmy's sketches frequently take a figure of speech and run it as the scene's only rule.

entries.name: The Comic Reversal
entries.description: A statement whose second half contradicts the value the first half established, in the same breath.

examples.text: Wilde's epigrams are reversals in miniature, and this is where he first sustains them at a rate the plot has to work around.
Carlin's routines reverse the moral loading of a phrase and then examine the wreckage.
Bierce builds a whole reference work from reversals, which demonstrates the device's capacity and its limits at length.

entries.name: The Switch
entries.description: The same setup re-entered with a different frame, so the audience's own memory supplies the second laugh.

examples.work: Mr. Show with Bob and David
examples.text: The show's linked sketches re-enter earlier premises from new angles, which is the switch used structurally.
Recurring characters are switches by design, since each appearance reframes the last.
The film is a switch engine: every repetition is the same setup with a changed frame, and the comedy decays and recovers deliberately.

entries.name: The Question as Setup
entries.description: An interrogative that installs the expectation, transferring part of the setup's work to the listener.

examples.text: The format makes the question the whole setup and the panel's cross-examination the escalation.
Rock uses rhetorical questions to make the audience state the premise silently before he contradicts it.
Schulz's four-panel strips frequently spend three panels on a question, which is the maximum possible setup share.

entries.name: The Double Punchline
entries.description: One setup resolved twice in different directions, where the second resolution must not invalidate the first.

examples.text: The scripts routinely resolve an exchange and then resolve it again from the servant's position.
The sketches often end twice, and the second ending recontextualises the character rather than the joke.
Several scenes resolve twice with the second resolution contradicting the first, which cancels both.

entries.name: The Punchline Withheld
entries.description: A completed setup with no payoff supplied, where the absence is the payoff.

examples.text: Lee routinely announces that a joke is coming and then declines it, which converts the audience's expectation into the material.
Beckett's structure is the withheld payoff extended to an evening, and the second act makes the withholding explicit.

examples.work: Norm Macdonald's moth joke on Conan
examples.text: The construction spends several minutes on Dostoevskian misery and terminates in a non-answer, which is the device's most-cited instance.

entries.name: The Stressed Final Word
entries.description: Placing the operative word in the sentence's terminal position, where English puts its heaviest stress.

examples.text: Wodehouse's line about a man far from being gruntled invents a word solely to occupy the stress position, and the whole sentence exists to deliver it there.
Guinness's understated deliveries all land on the final noun, which is what keeps the register flat and the joke sharp.
Quino's final panel gives the child the last word and the strip's whole argument arrives in it.

entries.name: The Rule of Three
entries.description: Two items establishing a pattern and a third breaking it, which is the smallest structure that can set and violate an expectation.

examples.text: The Spanish Inquisition sketch is a rule-of-three joke about the rule of three failing, which is the device examined from inside.
Chaplin's physical gags run in threes with the third inverted, and the boot-eating sequence is the clearest case.
Belloc's verses escalate in three stages and the punishment always arrives in the third.

entries.name: The Comic Pause
entries.description: Engineered silence, where the length is the content and shortening it removes the joke entirely.

examples.work: The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart
examples.text: The one-sided telephone routines are built almost entirely of pauses, and the unheard half is constructed by the audience.
The series lets scenes stall in real time, and the discomfort of the pause is the register.
The show's best exchanges depend on a beat held before the reply, which the studio audience learns to anticipate.

entries.name: Anticlimax and Bathos
entries.description: A descent from elevated register to trivial content, timed so the fall occurs on a single word.

examples.text: Pope's catalogue placing Bibles among cosmetics is the device's most-quoted instance and it turns on list order alone.
Byron's ottava rima forces bathos on a schedule, since the closing couplet must undercut the six lines above it.
The film builds wartime gravity and discharges it into a question about drink, repeatedly and to a rhythm.

entries.name: Comic Accumulation
entries.description: Items added at a steady rate until the quantity itself becomes the joke, independent of any single item.

examples.text: The stateroom sequence adds people metronomically and the laugh grows from arithmetic rather than from any individual arrival.

examples.work: The Twelve Days of Christmas as performed by The Two Ronnies
examples.text: The sketch weaponises an existing accumulative structure by having the list become a burden on the performer.
The Cyclops episode's catalogues are comic accumulation at literary scale, and the joke is the refusal to stop.

entries.name: The Undersized Word
entries.description: A deliberately inadequate word placed where a large one is expected, so the gap does the work.

examples.work: The Man in the White Suit
examples.text: The industrialists respond to a civilisational threat in the vocabulary of mild inconvenience.
Jerome describes catastrophes with domestic adjectives and never signals the mismatch.
Victor's mildest formulations arrive after the largest provocations, and the mismatch is the series' rhythmic signature.

entries.name: The Approach
entries.description: The syllable count between the last piece of information and the stress, which decides whether a working joke lands.

examples.text: Victoria Wood's routines are metrically exact, and her lists demonstrate that a wrong syllable count kills an otherwise sound line.
