Cope's parodies depend on the reader hearing the metre, so the approach is fixed by the form she is borrowing.

examples.work: Live at the Bolton Albert Halls
examples.text: Peter Kay's material is built on recognition, and the approach is stretched deliberately so the audience arrives at the punchline first.

entries.name: The List That Turns
entries.description: An enumeration whose final item belongs to a different category, revealed only by its position.

examples.text: Bierce's definitions frequently end on a category error placed last so it cannot be anticipated.
The insult lists are constructed so the final item is smaller and more specific than everything preceding it.
Allen's catalogues of future consumer goods turn on a final entry that reframes the whole list as satire.

entries.name: The Sentence That Outruns Itself
entries.description: A construction extended past the point of grammatical comfort, where the strain is audible and intended.

examples.text: Ogden Nash extends lines to absurd length purely to reach a rhyme, and the visible effort is the joke.

examples.work: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy
examples.text: Sterne's digressions are sentences that outrun their own subject, and the novel is the technique at book length.
Dylan Moran's sentences accumulate qualifications until the original proposition is unrecoverable, which is the persona rather than a defect.

entries.name: The Short Sentence After the Long One
entries.description: A brief clause following an extended one, where the contrast in length is the delivery mechanism.

examples.text: Thurber's paragraphs run long and stop hard, and the stop is where the reaction is placed.
Waugh reports catastrophe in short declaratives immediately after long descriptive passages, and the drop in length is where the reaction sits.
Mulaney's stories are long and his punchlines are short, and the ratio is unusually consistent across the set.

entries.name: The Broken Rhythm
entries.description: An established cadence violated once, where the violation rather than the content produces the laugh.

examples.text: Stewart Lee establishes a repetition and then alters one instance, and the alteration is frequently the only joke in the passage.
Herriman's fixed three-beat structure is broken at intervals, and the strip's readers were trained to expect the break.
Kelly's dialect rhythm is regular enough that a single plain sentence lands as an interruption.

entries.name: The Runner
entries.description: A joke returning at intervals across a work, where each return must alter the terms rather than repeat them.

examples.text: The small-and-far-away runner returns with a different pedagogical failure each time, which is what keeps it from being a catchphrase.
The background-disaster runner escalates visually while the foreground dialogue stays level, so repetition never becomes verbal.
The rug is a runner that acquires meaning rather than jokes, and by the third mention it is the plot.

entries.name: The Callback
entries.description: A single late return to earlier material, paying off a setup the audience has stopped waiting for.

examples.text: The callbacks are frequently one word recovered from an earlier season, which trains the audience to treat throwaways as deposits.
The paintball episodes call back to running material at feature length, and the show is explicit about the technique.
Pryor's set returns to the deer from the opening in a closing image, and the return converts a joke into a frame.

entries.name: The Slow Burn
entries.description: A reaction withheld across an extended beat, where the delay measures the offence more precisely than any line.

examples.text: Laurel and Hardy alternate destruction with long stationary reactions, and the burn is what converts vandalism into ceremony.
Victor's silences before responding are longer than the studio audience is comfortable with, which is the point.
The pause before a nurse decides whether to correct a superior is the series' actual comic unit.

entries.name: Escalation
entries.description: A sequence in which each event must exceed the last on a stated axis, with the axis chosen in advance.

examples.text: The violence escalates on one axis from insult to household object, and the series always stops at the point of no return rather than past it.
The escalation axis is social exposure rather than volume, and the endings arrive as arrivals rather than as shouts.
Bulgakov escalates a domestic mishap into a historical crisis by adding one impossible element at a time.

entries.name: The Mechanical Farce Plot
entries.description: A structure set running in act one, which then determines every subsequent event without further authorial choice.

examples.work: Ray Cooney's Run for Your Wife
examples.text: Cooney sets a bigamist's timetable in act one and the play executes it without a further authorial decision, which is the machine at its most naked.
Camoletti's timetable is the machine, and a change in aircraft speed is the only input required.
Feydeau's machine is a hotel with two identical rooms and a lookalike, and no further authorial choice is required after act one.

entries.name: Premise, Escalate, Out
entries.description: The sketch's three-part shape, in which the exit is the hardest part and the commonest failure.

examples.text: The Nazi officers sketch escalates on a single dawning realisation and exits by refusing to resolve it, which is one of the two available solutions.
The substitute-teacher sketches exit by escalating past the premise into a new one, which is the other solution.
The show's recurring sketches frequently end on a cutaway rather than an exit, which is a scheduling solution rather than a structural one.

entries.name: The Point of No Return
entries.description: The moment a comic escalation becomes irreversible, which must be visible to the audience as it passes.

examples.text: Monicelli marks the point at which the gang commits to a robbery none of them can execute, and everything after it is consequence.
The decision to fetch the mother rather than flee is the marked point, and the second half is its consequence.
The film is not primarily a comedy and marks its point with unusual precision, which is why comic writers study it.

entries.name: The Comic Clock
entries.description: A visible deadline that compresses the escalation, where the audience can count down alongside the characters.

examples.text: The clock is financial and stated in the premise, which removes any need to re-establish urgency.
The film's clock is the police arrival, announced early and referenced physically throughout.
The film uses historical chronology as its clock and lets the narrator acknowledge it, which is a formal joke about the device.

entries.name: Escalation by Arrival
entries.description: Raising the stakes by adding a person rather than an event, since each new arrival multiplies the concealments required.

examples.text: Every arrival forces the deception to accommodate one more observer, and Thomas paces the arrivals to a schedule.

examples.work: What We Do in the Shadows
examples.text: The flat's population grows and each addition requires the documentary crew's presence to be re-explained.
Goldoni's arrivals are the plot's only accelerator, and the servant's problem is arithmetic.

entries.name: The Reset
entries.description: Returning a situation to its starting state so the escalation can run again, which is what makes a series renewable.

examples.text: The reset is the premise, and the film's structure is a study of what escalation means when nothing accumulates.
The status-quo reset is enforced episode by episode, which is why the family can be destroyed weekly.
The reset is physical: the flat and the injuries are restored between episodes, which licenses the violence.

entries.name: The Runner That Pays Off Once
entries.description: Repetition installed early with no laugh attached, so a single late deployment can carry disproportionate weight.

examples.text: Radar's hearing the helicopters before anyone else is a runner installed for eight years, and the episode in which he does not hear them is what it was installed for.
The unseen gold beneath the field is planted repeatedly and paid once, in a shot rather than a line.
The running gag about the cellar is set up across a series and discharged in a single quiet scene.

entries.name: The Structure That Reveals Itself
entries.description: A work whose shape becomes visible to the audience partway through, converting anticipation into a second pleasure.

examples.text: The play is not a comedy and trains its audience to read a set for exits, which is the mechanism comic structure borrows.
Burnham makes the special's construction its subject, so the audience watches the structure being assembled.
The audience learns the set's failure points early and then watches the play walk into each one.

entries.name: The Act-Out
entries.description: A performer abandoning narration to become a character or an object, converting a told joke into a shown one.

examples.text: Pryor voices his own crack pipe and his own arteries, and the technique lets him deliver autobiography as dialogue without ever claiming sympathy.
Murphy's act-outs are full-body and rapidly switched, which raises the density but flattens the distinctions between characters.
Ali Wong uses brief act-outs as punctuation rather than as set pieces, which is a quieter and more sustainable use.

entries.name: The Feed
entries.description: A line written to be unfunny, whose entire function is to deliver the other performer into position.

examples.text: Wise's feeds are constructed so that any laugh on them would break the pair's status arrangement.
Sid James's lines are weighted so that no laugh can land on them, which is what leaves the whole reaction to Hancock.
The batsu games make the feed physical: one performer's job is to place the other where the punishment will land.

entries.name: Status Transactions
entries.description: Every exchange raising or lowering one party relative to the other, which Johnstone identified as the engine of scene work.

examples.text: Johnstone's book states the theory and supplies the exercises, and it remains the standard text for the technique.
The household's status is negotiated entirely through domestic routine, and Carla Lane keeps the outcome permanently undecided.
The film is not a comedy and demonstrates the mechanism at full length, with the status reversal as the entire plot.

entries.name: Crowd Work as Structure
entries.description: Audience interaction used as architecture rather than as filler, where the responses are built into the set's shape.

examples.text: Connolly's digressions are structured to return, so the crowd's interruptions become the set's connective tissue.
Moran incorporates the room's reactions into the persona's deterioration, which makes the interaction characterisation.

examples.work: Many recorded club sets released as specials
examples.text: Crowd work that is genuinely improvised frequently does not survive recording, since the audience's context is absent — a general failure the form has not solved.

entries.name: The Heckle Response
entries.description: An interruption answered so as to restore the status arrangement, which is judged on speed rather than on wit.

examples.text: Lee's responses deliberately take too long, which converts the heckle into material about heckling.
The improvised format treats interruption as an offer, which is the opposite of the stand-up convention.

examples.work: Live at the Bolton Albert Halls
examples.text: Kay's responses restore the room's warmth rather than defeating the heckler, which is a different and rarer solution.

entries.name: The Offer and the Block
entries.description: Improvisation's foundational transaction: an established fact accepted or refused, where refusal stops the scene dead.

examples.text: Johnstone names the block and demonstrates that audiences forgive weak invention and never forgive refusal.
The long-form specials retain the blocks, and the recovery from each one is visible in a way edited formats conceal.
Halpern, Close and Johnson codify acceptance as the form's only non-negotiable rule.

entries.name: Yes-And as an Escalation Engine
entries.description: Acceptance plus addition, which produces escalation automatically because each contribution must exceed the last.

examples.text: The company's long residency demonstrates the rule empirically: scenes that accept and add escalate on their own, and scenes that do not simply stop.
Guest's improvised ensembles escalate by accretion, and the editing selects the escalations that arrived.
The panel's elaborations are mutual additions nobody can retract, which is yes-and running as a competitive format.

entries.name: The Harold
entries.description: Long-form improvisation's structure, in which unconnected opening scenes are made to converge by callbacks discovered rather than planned.

examples.text: Close's form is documented here in full, including the opening, the three beats and the group games.
The show's writers came out of this tradition and the convergent episode structures are the Harold written down.
The episodes open on unrelated strands and converge on a single technical humiliation, which is the Harold's shape imported to a writers' room.

entries.name: Constraint as Premise
entries.description: Short-form improvisation's method, in which an arbitrary rule supplies the premise and the performers' compliance is the comedy.

examples.text: The games are constraints stated aloud, and the audience's pleasure is watching them obeyed under pressure.
The rule set is strict enough to be a sport, and the comedy comes almost entirely from compliance and its failure.
The format applies the principle outside improvisation and demonstrates that the constraint does most of the writing.

entries.name: The Corpse
entries.description: A performer breaking, which either destroys the scene or becomes its best moment, with almost nothing in between.

examples.text: The pair's rare breaks are visible in broadcast takes and the studio audience's response changes character when they occur.

examples.work: Peter Cook and Dudley Moore's Derek and Clive
examples.text: The recordings retain the corpsing, and the material's release depends on it being the point rather than an accident.
Broadcast breaks are retained often enough that they read as house style rather than as discovery, which is the failure mode.

entries.name: The Physical Beat Before the Line
entries.description: A movement, look or adjustment placed immediately before a spoken joke, which sets the rhythm the line will land on.

examples.text: The bar-flap fall works because of the beat before it, in which the character adjusts his cuffs.
Lloyd's physical preparation is always visible, so the audience knows the shape of the gag before it begins.
Saunders and Lumley place a physical adjustment before nearly every punchline, which is what gives the dialogue its swing.

entries.name: The Repeated Performance That Changes
entries.description: The same material delivered again with one element altered, where the audience's memory of the first supplies the second laugh.

examples.text: The series stages the same rakugo pieces performed by different tellers, which makes the variation the entire drama.
The film is not a comedy and supplies the clearest demonstration that repeating a performance with one variable changed is a complete structure.
Burnham repeats songs and segments in degraded form, and the degradation is the record of the year being described.

entries.name: The Room's Permission
entries.description: The audience's licence, granted early and revocable, which determines what a performer may attempt later in a set.

examples.text: Gadsby spends the first half earning permission and the second half spending it, and the structure is explicit about the transaction.
Notaro's Largo set opens by stating the diagnosis, and every subsequent choice is made with the room's response as information.
Bamford performs the same material to progressively larger rooms within one special, which makes permission visible as a variable.

entries.name: The Cold Open
entries.description: A self-contained comic unit before the titles, which must land without any of the episode's setup.

examples.text: The opens are self-contained garage scenes that establish nothing the episode needs, which is the form at its most disciplined.
The cold opens are built as single escalating gags with a hard out, and the show treats them as a separate writing problem.
The opens establish tone rather than premise, which buys the episode permission for its later shifts into seriousness.

entries.name: A-Plot, B-Plot, Convergence
entries.description: Parallel strands written to collide in the final act, where the collision is the episode's actual punchline.

examples.text: The Nine and a Half Minutes episode replays one span from three viewpoints and converges them on a single object, and the construction is the most rigorous instance the form has produced.
Four incompatible plans converge on one safe deposit box, and every character's strand is legible without narration.
Three separate schemes converge on a kidnapping none of the participants understands, and the film seeds each strand before it collides.

entries.name: The Laugh Break as Structural Input
entries.description: The two-second gap a live audience imposes, which caps line density and pushes the joke to the end of the speech.

examples.text: The scripts are written to the break, and reading them silently reveals gaps the room is expected to fill.
The three-camera technique fixed the break into the production method, and everything since inherits the rhythm.

examples.work: Later multi-camera sitcoms retooled for streaming
examples.text: Removing the track from scripts written to it exposes the gaps as dead air, which demonstrates that the break was structural rather than decorative.

entries.name: Script Density Without a Track
entries.description: Single-camera comedy's recovered seconds, which buy interiority and location at the cost of the audience's confirmation.

examples.text: The absence of a track lets an argument run at its real length, and the series uses the surplus for accuracy rather than for jokes.
The recovered time is spent on silence and atmosphere rather than on more lines, which is the least common use of the surplus.
The recovered seconds are spent on songs, which is a use no multi-camera format could accommodate.

entries.name: The Frame-Break
entries.description: Direct address to the audience, which must operate on a rule the audience could state or it reads as carelessness.

examples.text: The breaks begin as complicity and are later diagnosed by another character, which is the only substantial development the device has had.
The series is not a comedy and demonstrates the device's other use, which is recruiting the audience into complicity with someone they should refuse.
The address is used to recruit rather than to confess, and the film never lets another character notice.

entries.name: Cringe as Sustained Mode
entries.description: Discomfort held rather than released, where the audience absorbs the humiliation the character does not register.

examples.text: The camera stays on Brent after the moment has passed, and the holding is the entire technique.
The discomfort is real rather than performed, which raises questions the scripted form does not have to answer.
The cringe is affectionate rather than punitive, which demonstrates that the mode does not require contempt.

entries.name: The Ensemble Grid on Screen
entries.description: Fixed relations staged so that any two characters left alone produce a distinct scene.

examples.text: Six characters yield fifteen pairings and the series uses nearly all of them, which is what allowed ten years of renewal.
The grid is deliberately never repaired, so every pairing produces the same relation in a different room, which is the inverse strategy.
The grid is reset deliberately at each season break, which converts a sitcom constraint into a plot device.

entries.name: The Reaction Shot as Punctuation
entries.description: A cut to a listener rather than a speaker, which tells the audience how to read what they just heard.

examples.text: The format is reaction shots with the stimulus attached, which demonstrates how much editorial work a cutaway performs on its own.
The confessional inserts function as reaction shots displaced in time, which lets the show punctuate retroactively.
The studio cutaways are reaction shots used as scoring, and the edit decides which attempt is funny.

entries.name: Panel-Level Gag Timing
entries.description: Comics and strips controlling the beat through panel width, gutter and page turn rather than through duration.

examples.text: Watterson varies panel width to control reading speed, and the Sunday strips use the extra space as a longer pause.
Schulz's fourth panel is the punchline position and the first three are metrically identical, which is a fixed rhythm.
Herriman breaks the panel grid itself, so the timing irregularity is visible as layout.

entries.name: The Montage
entries.description: Compressed repetition used comically, where the cut rate rather than any individual image carries the joke.

examples.text: The montage sequences accelerate until the individual gags are illegible, which is the intended effect.
The training montage parodies the device by naming it, which is the only exit the form allows.
The montages compress a career into rhythm, and the film's jokes are placed on the cuts rather than in the shots.

entries.name: The Edit as Full Stop
entries.description: Cutting on the beat rather than after it, since a shot held past the reaction converts a laugh into an explanation.

examples.text: Wright's cuts land on the beat and frequently before the performer has finished, which is the show's rhythmic signature.
The news-package parodies cut on the beat of broadcast grammar rather than of dialogue, which is where the joke sits.

examples.work: Many improvised American film comedies of the period
examples.text: Scenes assembled from alternate takes routinely run past the beat, and the surplus is where the laugh dissipates.

entries.name: Anti-Comedy
entries.description: Material constructed to withhold the comic payoff entirely, where the audience's discomfort is the composition.

examples.text: Kaufman's performance withholds the persona's own competence, and the audience is never told which parts are the act.
Lee constructs passages designed to lose the room and then makes the loss the subject.

examples.work: Tim and Eric Awesome Show, Great Job!
examples.text: The show's production values are deliberately degraded so the audience cannot locate the intended reaction.

entries.name: The Deliberately Dead Beat
entries.description: A silence where a laugh is structurally due, used to change what the audience thinks the work is.

examples.text: Gadsby stops supplying the payoff partway through, and the withdrawal is announced rather than concealed.
Acaster ends several routines without a button and lets the room decide whether the piece is finished.
The series regularly withholds the release a comic setup has promised, and the withholding is where the violence sits.

entries.name: The Comic Ending Problem
entries.description: A fully escalated premise has nowhere left to go, which is why comedies more often fail at the end than in the middle.

examples.text: The final shot holds past the resolution until the characters' expressions withdraw it, which is the most-copied solution in the form.

examples.work: Le Grand Blond avec une chaussure noire
examples.text: The film resolves by having the apparatus destroy itself, which leaves the protagonist unchanged and is a rarer solution.
The film restages the first film's ending, which demonstrates that a resolved premise cannot be re-escalated.

entries.name: The Joke That Must Not Land
entries.description: Material written so the audience recognises the shape of a joke and declines to laugh, which is a controlled effect.

examples.text: The final scene's last exchange is constructed exactly like every previous joke and the audience does not laugh, which is the whole design.
Several setups are built comically and paid seriously, and the film depends on the audience noticing the switch.
The closing speech abandons the comic frame the film has spent two hours building, which is the earliest major instance of the manoeuvre.

entries.name: The Escalation That Should Have Stopped
entries.description: A sequence continued past its natural exit, where the excess is either the point or the failure and the two are hard to tell apart.

examples.text: The Mr Creosote sequence announces its ending in advance and then extends past it, and opinion on whether it works remains divided.
The series is built on extension past comfort, and it accepts the audience it loses as a cost.
Established gags are extended past their exit because the format requires the runtime, which is the failure rather than the technique.

entries.name: The Callback That Arrives Too Late
entries.description: A return to material the audience has stopped holding, which reads as a reference rather than as a payoff.

examples.text: The cutaway structure means callbacks land on material the audience was not asked to retain, so they function as citation.
The later callbacks assume an audience that has watched in order and annotated, which the series treats as a feature and its critics as a cost.
Pryor's returns work because the opening images are emotionally rather than comically loaded, which is what keeps them retrievable an hour later.

entries.name: The Runner That Outlives Its Show
entries.description: A repeated line detaching from its context and circulating alone, which strips the character it came from.

examples.text: The lines that circulated were the ones the scripts treated as filler, and the characters they came from are now read through them.
The show anticipated the detachment and built later sketches on the audience's prior knowledge of the line.
The lines that circulate are not the ones the scripts treat as jokes, which is the clearest evidence that detachment is not under the writer's control.

entries.name: The Laugh in the Wrong Place
entries.description: An audience laughing where the work did not intend it, which is information about the work rather than about the audience.

examples.text: The film is not a comedy and is received as one, and the reception is stable enough to be studied as a phenomenon.
A documented portion of the audience laughed with the bigot rather than at him, which is the best-evidenced instance in the form.
Godard's tonal instability produces laughter he did not schedule, and the film's defenders and detractors disagree about whether it is intended.

entries.name: Comedy as Accelerant, Timed
entries.description: The exact placement at which comedy stops making material bearable and starts making it worse, which is a decision with a timecode.

examples.text: The acceleration is distributed across the final act rather than concentrated, and the film keeps the comic register running underneath it.
The acceleration is the ending itself, and the song over the montage is the device stated as a joke.
The film removes its comic distance in the final act, and whether the earlier comedy earns the removal is contested from release to now.

entries.name: Knowing When the Work Has Stopped Being Funny
entries.description: The tonal handbrake as a locatable moment, chosen rather than discovered, after which no further jokes are permitted.

examples.text: The comic register is withdrawn at a locatable point and the film never resumes it, which is unusually clean for a feature.
The withdrawal tapers rather than stopping, which is frequently criticised and is instructive as the alternative.
The handbrake is the chain-gang sequence, and Sturges resumes the comic register afterwards on purpose, which is the harder manoeuvre.

entries.name: Comedy Predates the Word for It
entries.description: Ritual mockery, obscenity and inversion are attested long before any theory of the comic exists to describe them.
entries.principle: The comic impulse is documented in festival practice, graffiti and ritual licence across the ancient world before any culture produces a theory of why people laugh. A history of comedy that begins with Aristotle begins several thousand years late, and it inherits his assumption that comedy is the lesser form.
entries.example: Aristophanes' surviving plays emerge from the Dionysia's competitive framework rather than from a literary tradition; the Roman Saturnalia formalised social inversion as calendar practice; Egyptian and Mesopotamian satirical texts survive in fragments whose comic intent scholars read with varying confidence.
entries.application: Treat the theoretical account as a later arrival than the practice. When a card explains why something is funny, check whether the explanation is describing the work or the tradition of explaining works.

entries.name: Old Comedy and the Named Target
entries.description: Athenian comedy attacked living, named citizens in front of them, under a licence no later era has matched.
entries.principle: Old Comedy's defining freedom was to name and caricature identifiable public figures at a state festival. That licence produced the sharpest political satire in the tradition and the first documented claim that comedy caused real harm, which arrives from the target rather than from a critic.
entries.example: Aristophanes' Nephelai caricatures Socrates, and Plato's Apology later has Socrates cite the play as having damaged his reputation with the jury. Eleven of Aristophanes' plays survive in substantially complete form; the dates of his birth and death are both estimates.
entries.application: The Athenian settlement is the reference point for every later argument about satire and its targets. Cite it as a precedent rather than as a golden age, since the licence was bounded by a festival and by citizenship.

entries.name: New Comedy and the Plot Machine
entries.description: The shift from political attack to domestic plot, which supplied the structure nearly all later comedy runs on.
entries.principle: Menander's generation replaced the named target with the recognisable type and the invented household, and built plots from mistaken identity, concealed parentage and obstructed love. That machinery, not the satire, is what the tradition actually inherited.
entries.example: Only one complete Menander play survives, Dyskolos, recovered in the twentieth century, with the corpus still growing from papyrus finds. Plautus and Terence adapted the Greek models into Latin, and roughly twenty of Plautus's plays are readable today, with the canon resting on an ancient attribution judgement rather than on a documentary list.
entries.application: Almost every farce structure in this pack is traceable here. When building a comic plot, the question of what Menander's generation would have done with it is usually productive rather than antiquarian.

entries.name: Comedy as the Lower Form
entries.description: A hierarchy established in classical criticism and still shaping how comic work is funded, reviewed and awarded.
entries.principle: The surviving classical account treats tragedy as the serious form and comedy as its inferior, and the Poetics' lost or never-written treatment of comedy left the field without an authoritative defence. The ranking has outlived every intellectual justification offered for it.
entries.example: The pattern is visible in the modern award record: there is no Academy Award category for comedy, the Golden Globes group comedy with musicals, and the Booker and Pulitzer have rarely gone to overtly comic novels, with Percival Everett's recent recognition notable partly for that reason.
entries.application: The hierarchy is a fact about reception, not about craft. It matters to a writer mainly in that comic work is generally required to demonstrate seriousness before it is taken seriously.

entries.name: Medieval Licence and the Feast of Fools
entries.description: Sanctioned inversion inside religious institutions, in which the hierarchy licensed its own mockery for a fixed period.
entries.principle: Medieval Europe embedded comic inversion in the calendar rather than in a theatre. The licence was temporary, official and bounded, which made it both a safety valve and a genuine site of subversion, and the argument about which it mainly was remains open.
entries.example: The Feast of Fools and the boy bishop tradition are attested across medieval Europe and were repeatedly restricted by church authorities; the mystery cycles carry substantial comic material, with the Wakefield Second Shepherds' Play the most-cited English instance.
entries.application: The bounded licence is the ancestor of every format that grants comedy permission it withdraws afterwards. It is worth knowing that the arrangement is very old and that its ambiguity is original rather than modern.

entries.name: Commedia dell'Arte and the Fixed Type
entries.description: A professional improvised theatre built on stock masks and rehearsed business, which exported its types across Europe.
entries.principle: Commedia supplied a repertoire of fixed characters and transferable comic business that troupes could recombine without a script. It is the origin of the comic type as a working tool rather than a critical category, and it is also the reason improvisation and physical comedy are historically inseparable.
entries.example: The zanni, Pantalone, Il Dottore and Arlecchino circulated across Italy, France and England from the sixteenth century. Carlo Goldoni's eighteenth-century reforms wrote the improvisation out and fixed the plays as texts, which preserved the material and ended the practice.
entries.application: The stock type is still the fastest available character-building tool in comedy. Commedia's lesson is that a fixed exterior plus rehearsed business generates more scenes than a psychology does.

entries.name: The Comedy of Humours and the English Stage
entries.description: A theory of character imported from medicine, which gave English comedy a method for building people out of single traits.
entries.principle: Jonson's humours theory borrowed a physiological model to justify characters driven by one dominant appetite. The medicine was wrong and the dramaturgy was durable, and the method survives in every sitcom whose characters cannot change.
entries.example: Jonson's Every Man in His Humour and Volpone demonstrate the method; Shakespeare's comedies mostly decline it in favour of characters who can be surprised, which is the useful contrast.
entries.application: The choice between a humours character and a changeable one is a choice about renewability. Humours characters generate scenes indefinitely and cannot carry an arc.

entries.name: Restoration Comedy and the Licensed Wit
entries.description: A sudden, brief and unusually frank comic theatre, and the reaction that closed it.
entries.principle: The reopening of the English theatres in 1660 produced a comedy of sexual frankness and verbal display aimed at a narrow court audience. Its collapse under moral criticism within four decades is the clearest early case of a comic canon becoming unperformable while remaining technically admired.
entries.example: Congreve's The Way of the World marks the form's late peak; Jeremy Collier's 1698 attack on the stage's immorality is the documented turning point. The plays returned to the repertoire only in the twentieth century.
entries.application: The Restoration is the pack's oldest worked example of the dated-canon problem, and its shape is exactly the modern one: technique admired, content contested, revival argued over.

entries.category: Print, Periodical and the Comic Novel
entries.name: The Comic Novel Arrives With the Novel
entries.description: The English novel's earliest major works are comic, and the form's conventions were partly established by parody.
entries.principle: Comedy is not a later addition to the novel but present at its formation, and several founding works are parodies of other books. The form's self-consciousness about its own conventions begins as a joke.
entries.example: Cervantes' Don Quixote parodies chivalric romance and is routinely named the first modern novel; Fielding's Shamela and Joseph Andrews parody Richardson; Sterne's Tristram Shandy disassembles the novel's machinery while the novel is still being assembled.
entries.application: When a comic novel breaks form, it is using the oldest tool the form has. The device is not postmodern and predates the conventions it violates.

entries.category: Print, Periodical and the Comic Novel
entries.name: The Periodical Essay and the Comic Voice
entries.description: A regular deadline and a fixed length producing a first-person comic voice that is recognisable within a paragraph.
entries.principle: The periodical created the humorous columnist: a persona sustained across instalments, constrained by length, and required to be recognisable rather than surprising. The economics of the form shaped the voice more than any aesthetic decision did.
entries.example: The Spectator established the model in the eighteenth century; Punch industrialised it from 1841; The New Yorker's humour pieces from the 1920s produced Thurber and Perelman, whose styles are inseparable from the magazine's constraints.
entries.application: If writing to a recurring slot, the persona is the product. Readers return for a voice they can predict, which is the opposite of the requirement in most other comic forms.

entries.category: Print, Periodical and the Comic Novel
entries.name: Satire and the Law
entries.description: The long argument between comic licence and legal restraint, which has shaped what could be printed and performed in every era.
entries.principle: Comedy's history is partly a history of censorship regimes and the evasions they produced. Restriction reliably generates technique, and several of the form's most durable devices exist because a direct statement was not permitted.
entries.example: The Licensing Act of 1737 pushed English satire off the stage and into the novel; the Lord Chamberlain's power over British theatre lasted until 1968; the innuendo density of mid-century British radio comedy is a direct product of broadcasting restrictions.
entries.application: When studying a period's comedy, establish what could not be said. The technique on display is usually a solution to that constraint rather than a free choice.

entries.category: Print, Periodical and the Comic Novel
entries.name: Comic Traditions Outside Europe
entries.description: Developed comic forms with their own theory, training and canon, which an Anglophone account routinely omits.
entries.principle: Several non-European comic traditions are as formally developed as anything in the Western canon, with their own transmission systems and technical vocabulary. Their absence from general histories of comedy is a fact about those histories.
entries.example: Japanese rakugo transmits a repertoire through named lineages of tellers; manzai's boke and tsukkomi roles formalise the fool-and-straight-man pairing; Chinese xiangsheng is a two-hander crosstalk form with its own apprenticeship structure; the Nasreddin Hodja tales circulate across Turkic, Persian and Arab traditions.
entries.application: These are craft resources, not curiosities. The manzai pairing in particular is a more precise account of the straight-man relationship than the Anglophone vocabulary offers.

entries.name: Music Hall, Vaudeville and the Professional Act
entries.description: A commercial circuit that turned comedy into a repeatable, portable, timed unit of labour.
entries.principle: The variety circuits standardised the comic act: a fixed length, a portable set of material, and a persona that had to register in the first thirty seconds. Almost every convention of modern stand-up is inherited from this economic arrangement rather than from an artistic decision.
entries.example: British music hall and American vaudeville ran parallel systems from the mid-nineteenth century; the transition of their performers into radio and then film is how the screen comedy of the 1920s and 1930s acquired its personnel and its timing.
entries.application: The act is still the unit. When building a set or a character, the circuit's requirements — portable, timed, instantly legible — remain the practical constraints.

entries.name: The Double Act
entries.description: A pairing structure that recurs independently across several unconnected traditions, which suggests it solves a real problem.
entries.principle: The comic pair with asymmetric status appears in commedia, in music hall, in manzai, in xiangsheng and in vaudeville, in each case arrived at separately. The recurrence is evidence that the arrangement is a structural solution rather than a cultural habit.
entries.example: Abbott and Costello, Laurel and Hardy and Morecambe and Wise in the Anglophone line; manzai's boke and tsukkomi and xiangsheng's dougen and penggen in East Asia. In several of these traditions the roles are named and taught, which the Anglophone tradition does not do.
entries.application: Name the roles when building a pair. The traditions that formalised the vocabulary produce more reliable material than the one that left it implicit.

entries.name: Radio and the Invisible Joke
entries.description: A medium that removed the visual entirely and forced comedy to rebuild itself in sound.
entries.principle: Radio comedy had to establish character, location and reversal without an image, which produced a distinct set of techniques: the catchphrase as identification, the sound effect as visual substitute, and an unusually high dependence on voice differentiation. It also produced the first mass-simultaneous comedy audience.
entries.example: American radio built the situation comedy's shape before television existed; British radio produced Hancock's Half Hour and then The Goon Show, whose surrealism was possible precisely because nothing had to be depicted.
entries.application: Writing a scene for audio is the fastest available diagnostic of whether its comedy is in the situation or in the staging.

entries.name: Silent Film and the Universal Gag
entries.description: A period in which comedy had no dialogue, achieved global distribution, and reached a technical peak it has not since matched.
entries.principle: The absence of synchronised sound forced comedy into pure staging, geometry and timing, and the resulting work travelled across every language barrier at once. It is the only period in which comic technique was under this much pressure, and the surviving films are consequently the field's densest technical resource.
entries.example: Chaplin, Keaton and Lloyd worked within the same few years and solved the same problems differently — Chaplin through character, Keaton through space and machinery, Lloyd through jeopardy. Tati later revived the approach with sound present but dialogue withheld.
entries.application: Study the silents for staging rather than for gags. The gags are period-bound and the spatial reasoning is not.

entries.name: The Coming of Sound and the Verbal Comedians
entries.description: A technological change that ended several careers, made others possible, and moved comedy's centre from the body to the sentence.
entries.principle: Synchronised sound rewarded a different skill set within a very few years. The performers who transferred were mostly those with stage or vaudeville verbal training, and the industry's comic output moved from staged physical sequences to rapid dialogue.
entries.example: The Marx Brothers and Mae West arrived from the stage with verbal material ready; Keaton's career declined in the same period for reasons including studio contract terms as well as the medium's change, and attributing it solely to sound is a common oversimplification.
entries.application: The physical and verbal traditions did not merge; they alternated in prominence. Both remain available and most contemporary screen comedy under-uses the physical.

entries.name: The Sitcom's Invention
entries.description: A form defined by economic constraints — standing sets, a repeating cast, a fixed slot — that turned out to be an unusually productive structure.
entries.principle: The situation comedy was designed around the cost of producing weekly television, and its constraints proved to be a generative structure rather than a limitation. The requirement that nothing change is what makes the form renewable, and it is also what caps what it can say.
entries.example: American radio supplied the shape and I Love Lucy fixed the three-camera film method in 1951, which set the production economics and the rhythm for decades. The single-camera alternative arrived much later and traded the audience's confirmation for script density.
entries.application: The form's constraints are its engine. A sitcom premise that requires characters to change or to leave the set is fighting the structure rather than using it.

entries.name: Satire Booms and Their Endings
entries.description: Periodic bursts of institutionally hostile comedy, each with a recognisable arrival, peak and absorption.
entries.principle: Satirical waves recur with a similar shape: an outsider generation gains access to a mass medium, attacks institutions that had been treated as unmockable, and is then absorbed by those institutions or by the medium's commercial logic. The absorption is not a betrayal but a structural feature.
entries.example: The British satire boom of the early 1960s ran from the Beyond the Fringe revue and Private Eye into television; the American late-night and sketch tradition from the 1970s follows the same curve; the political comedy of the 2000s repeats it with a shorter cycle.
entries.application: If writing satire inside an institution, the absorption is the thing to plan for. It arrives faster than any previous wave.

entries.name: Alternative Comedy and the Break With the Club Tradition
entries.description: A deliberate generational rupture, which defined itself explicitly by what it refused rather than by what it invented.
entries.principle: British alternative comedy from the late 1970s was constituted as a rejection of the working men's club circuit's racial and sexual material. This is unusual: a comic movement whose founding statement is a refusal, which makes the material it refused historically indispensable to understanding it.
entries.example: The Comedy Store opened in 1979 and the Comic Strip and The Young Ones followed; the club tradition it defined itself against, including performers whose material is now largely unbroadcastable, is the necessary context and is carded as a contested case rather than omitted.
entries.application: A movement defined by refusal cannot be understood without the thing refused. This is the pack's clearest argument for carding material it would not endorse.

entries.name: The Stand-Up Special as a Publishing Format
entries.description: The recorded hour becoming a fixed, distributable product, which changed how material is written and how long it lasts.
entries.principle: Recording turned stand-up from a repeatable live act into a published work that can only be performed once. Material is now retired on release rather than refined over years, which raises the writing burden enormously and shortens every routine's life.
entries.example: The comedy album established the pattern from the late 1950s; the cable and later streaming special fixed the hour as the unit. Performers who once toured one act for a decade now build an hour, record it, and discard it.
entries.application: The economics changed the craft. If writing for recording, assume the material is single-use and budget the writing accordingly.

entries.name: The Global Format Trade
entries.description: Comedy formats licensed and remade across territories, which is a natural experiment in what travels.
entries.principle: The format trade demonstrates empirically which parts of a comedy are structural and which are local. Adaptations that keep the structure and replace the specifics generally succeed; those that translate the jokes generally do not.
entries.example: The Office was remade in many territories with widely differing results, and the American version's divergence from the original's cringe register is the most-studied case. Panel and game formats travel more reliably than character comedy.
entries.application: When adapting, port the structure and rewrite everything else. The evidence from the format trade is unusually clear on this point.

entries.name: Digital Distribution and the Collapse of the Gatekeeper
entries.description: Direct publishing removing the commissioner from the path between a comic and an audience, with consequences in both directions.
entries.principle: Online distribution removed the broadcaster's veto and, with it, the broadcaster's protection. Performers gained access to audiences without permission and lost the institutional buffer that had absorbed complaints, which is why the contested-material argument now lands on individuals.
entries.example: Online video, podcasting and social platforms produced comic careers with no commissioning stage from the late 2000s onward; the same period saw individual performers rather than institutions become the target of controversy.
entries.application: The gatekeeper was also a shield. A writer publishing directly is responsible for the frame as well as the material.

entries.name: Comedy's Canon Dates Faster Than Any Other
entries.description: The field's distinguishing historical fact, and the reason this pack's method differs from its neighbours'.
entries.principle: Comic material depends on a shared frame between work and audience, and frames change faster than plots, prose or images do. Comedy therefore dates faster than any adjacent form, and it dates asymmetrically: the technique remains legible while the content becomes unusable.
entries.example: Material that was mainstream broadcast comedy thirty years ago is now unbroadcastable in several territories, while the structural techniques it used remain standard. The removals and partial restorations of the early 2020s are the documented instances, and the removal and the restoration are two separate acts.
entries.application: Date every comic judgement. A card that says a work is funny is making a claim about a frame as well as about a text, and the frame should be named.

entries.name: The Superiority Account
entries.description: Laughter as a signal of triumph over another's defect, the oldest of the standing theories and the narrowest.
entries.principle: On the superiority account we laugh from a sudden sense of our own advantage over someone else's failing. It explains mockery, schadenfreude and the entire comic butt, and it is the theory that most directly supports this pack's organising claim about who pays.
entries.example: Hobbes states it in Leviathan as a sudden glory arising from a conception of eminence in ourselves compared with the infirmity of others; Plato's Philebus contains an earlier version. The account cannot explain nonsense, wordplay, or laughter at one's own misfortune, which is a substantial share of the field.
entries.application: Use it as a diagnostic rather than a definition. If a passage is funny and no one is diminished, superiority is not what is operating and the writer should know what is.

entries.name: The Relief Account
entries.description: Laughter as the discharge of accumulated tension, an account with strong intuitive appeal and weak mechanism.
entries.principle: Relief theory holds that laughter releases psychic energy that has been built up and rendered unnecessary. It fits the observed behaviour of audiences around taboo material and around suspense, and it depends on an energy model of the mind that the evidence does not support.
entries.example: Freud's Der Witz und seine Beziehung zum Unbewußten sets out the fullest version, distinguishing jokes, the comic and humour; Spencer offered an earlier physiological formulation. The account struggles with jokes that produce laughter without any prior tension.
entries.application: The tension-and-release description remains a useful working model for scene construction even where the underlying mechanism is doubted. Treat it as craft vocabulary rather than as psychology.

entries.name: The Incongruity Account
entries.description: Laughter as a response to a violated expectation, the dominant account and the one most compatible with observed structure.
entries.principle: On the incongruity account, comedy arises when a perceived pattern is broken in a way the perceiver can accommodate. It is the theory best supported by the actual architecture of jokes, since setup and punchline are precisely an expectation installed and violated.
entries.example: Kant and Schopenhauer supply the classical statements; the modern refinement is incongruity-resolution, in which the violation must be resolvable for amusement rather than confusion to follow. The account has difficulty specifying which incongruities are funny, since most are not.
entries.application: This is the theory the craft cards in this pack implicitly use. Its practical weakness is the writer's actual problem: knowing which violation will land is not derivable from the theory.

entries.name: Play Theory
entries.description: Laughter as a signal that an interaction is not serious, which locates comedy in social communication rather than in cognition.
entries.principle: Play theory treats laughter as a metacommunicative signal marking an exchange as play rather than as threat. It accounts for laughter's presence in non-human animals and in pre-linguistic infants, which the cognitive accounts do not.
entries.example: Bateson's account of the play frame is the standard reference; rough-and-tumble play in several mammal species is accompanied by vocalisations that researchers have argued are homologous to laughter. The account explains laughter better than it explains jokes.
entries.application: The play frame is another name for what this pack calls permission. A comic frame established early is the signal that the subsequent material is not an attack.

entries.name: Benign Violation
entries.description: A modern synthesis holding that amusement requires a violation that is simultaneously perceived as benign.
entries.principle: Benign violation theory proposes that humour occurs when something threatens a person's sense of how things ought to be while simultaneously seeming acceptable. It is attractive because it appears to unify the older accounts, and it is criticised because the term benign is not independently defined (robustness: unreplicated).
entries.example: McGraw and Warren's 2010 formulation is the standard citation. The seed harvest for this pack could locate no large-scale direct replication of the original experiments, which is recorded here as UNCONFIRMED rather than as a refutation.
entries.application: The unfalsifiability objection matters to a writer for a practical reason: the theory cannot tell you in advance where the benign boundary sits for a given audience, which is exactly the judgement the work requires.

entries.name: Why No Theory Predicts
entries.description: Every standing account explains laughter after the fact and none of them forecasts it, which is a fact about the field rather than a gap to be filled.
entries.principle: The available theories are descriptive rather than predictive. Each identifies a necessary-looking feature and none supplies sufficient conditions, which is why no theoretical advance has ever improved anyone's comic writing.
entries.example: Incongruity cannot say which violations amuse; superiority cannot handle nonsense; relief has no supported mechanism; benign violation cannot define benign. The pack's own organising claim is subject to the same limitation and states its exception explicitly rather than concealing it.
entries.application: Read the theories as vocabulary for describing what a passage is doing, not as instructions for making one work. The room remains the only reliable test.

entries.name: The Dignity Account and Its Limits
entries.description: This pack's organising claim stated as a psychological proposition, with the boundary it concedes.
entries.principle: The claim is that comedy is the deliberate mismanagement of dignity, performed for a reaction the work is built to elicit in real time, and that its craft is the control of who pays and when. As a psychological account it is closest to superiority theory with the cost relocated from the perceiver to the work's design.
entries.example: The claim covers slapstick, farce, satire, self-deprecation and cringe, and it covers the comedy of grief and illness by treating those as assaults on dignity that the work seizes control of. It does not reach nonsense, pure wordplay or absurdist non-sequitur, and this pack cards that exception rather than arguing it away.
entries.application: Apply it as two questions on any passage: who pays, and when does the reaction arrive. Where neither question has an answer, the passage is in the conceded exception and should be analysed as invention instead.

entries.name: Laughter Is Social Before It Is Funny
entries.description: Robust. Most laughter in ordinary life follows conversation rather than jokes, and occurs in company rather than alone.
entries.principle: Observational studies of naturally occurring laughter consistently find that the great majority of it follows unremarkable conversational utterances rather than deliberate humour, and that people laugh far more in company than alone. Laughter is primarily a social signal that happens to be recruited by comedy.
entries.example: Provine's field observations of thousands of naturally occurring laughs are the standard citation, and the finding has been reproduced in several later observational studies. The result is robust and is one of the few in the area that is.
entries.application: A comic scene is competing with a signal that mostly serves affiliation. This is why an audience laughs together, why a room's warmth precedes its laughter, and why a solitary reader's response is a different phenomenon.

entries.name: Spontaneous and Volitional Laughter Differ
entries.description: Robust. Listeners across cultures can distinguish genuine from produced laughter above chance.
entries.principle: Spontaneous and deliberately produced laughter have measurably different acoustic properties, and listeners discriminate between them at above-chance rates across widely separated cultures. The distinction appears not to be a learned cultural competence (robustness: robust; effect sizes vary).
entries.example: Cross-cultural listening studies have found the discrimination holding across several unrelated language groups. The effect sizes vary and the finding is nonetheless among the better replicated in the field.
entries.application: An audience can tell. This is the empirical basis for the practical rule that a performer cannot fake enjoyment of their own material and that a laugh track is perceptible as one.

entries.name: Laughter Is Contagious
entries.description: Robust. Hearing laughter increases the probability of laughing, independent of any comic stimulus.
entries.principle: Exposure to laughter reliably raises the listener's own likelihood of laughing, and the effect operates without any comprehension of what is being laughed at. This is a real mechanism rather than a folk belief, and it is what a live audience supplies.
entries.example: The effect underlies the laugh track's persistence in television despite decades of audience complaint about it, and it is why comedy clubs seat audiences densely rather than comfortably.
entries.application: Contagion is a resource for performed comedy and unavailable to the page. It is one of the two main reasons material tested in a room fails in print.

entries.name: Group Size Changes the Threshold
entries.description: Robust in direction, imprecise in magnitude. Larger audiences laugh more readily than smaller ones at identical material.
entries.principle: The threshold for laughing falls as audience size rises, which is a straightforward consequence of contagion combined with the reduced social cost of laughing in a crowd. The direction of the effect is well attested; the size of it is not well quantified.
entries.example: The practical knowledge is universal among performers and the formal literature is thinner than the confidence with which the claim is usually stated, which is why this card marks the magnitude as imprecise.
entries.application: Material calibrated in a large room will be over-calibrated for a small one. This is a scheduling problem as much as a writing problem.

entries.name: Anticipation Is Part of the Pleasure
entries.description: Robust. Audiences enjoy correctly predicting a punchline as well as being surprised by one.
entries.principle: Comic pleasure is not solely a function of surprise. Recognising a structure and correctly anticipating its completion produces its own reward, which is why the rule of three, the runner and the callback all work on repetition rather than on novelty.
entries.example: The effect is why a familiar catchphrase gets a laugh on arrival and why an audience will laugh before a punchline lands. It also explains the shaggy-dog story, where the anticipation is deliberately frustrated.
entries.application: Do not assume surprise is the only currency. Half the devices in this pack's specialist collection trade on the audience knowing what is coming.

entries.name: Timing Tolerances Are Narrow
entries.description: Robust as craft knowledge, under-formalised as research. Small changes in interval measurably change whether a joke lands.
entries.principle: The interval between setup and payoff has a narrow window, and shifts of a fraction of a second alter the response. Performers treat this as established; the formal literature quantifying it is thinner than the practice implies.
entries.example: The comic pause, the double take and the slow burn are all techniques built on the tolerance being narrow and locatable. Editors of screen comedy routinely report that a frame or two changes a cut's result.
entries.application: Trust the room over the page for interval. This is the one area where practitioner knowledge is substantially ahead of the research.

entries.name: The Health Claims Are Weak
entries.description: Unreplicated. The popular literature on laughter and physical health substantially exceeds the evidence.
entries.principle: Claims that laughter measurably improves immune function, longevity or pain tolerance are widely circulated and thinly supported. Study sizes are typically small, controls are often absent, and the effects reported are inconsistent across replications (robustness: unreplicated).
entries.example: The laughter-and-health literature grew rapidly from the 1980s on the back of anecdotal accounts and has not consolidated. This pack states the weakness rather than repeating the claim, because a reference work that circulates a soft finding as a hard one has no authority.
entries.application: Do not write a character's recovery as caused by laughter and present it as science. The comic frame's value to someone in distress is a matter of control, which is a different and better-supported claim.

entries.name: The Humor Styles Questionnaire
entries.description: Contested. A widely used four-factor instrument whose factor structure has not held up uniformly.
entries.principle: The instrument distinguishes affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive and self-defeating humour styles and is heavily used in personality research. Its factor structure has been questioned in several samples and its cross-cultural stability is disputed.
entries.example: The four-style model is frequently cited in popular writing as an established taxonomy of personality. The methodological criticism is available in the same literature and is much less often cited.
entries.application: The four styles are a usable vocabulary for describing a character's comic register. They are not a validated personality typology, and a card or a scene should not treat them as one.

entries.name: Sense of Humour and Attraction
entries.description: Contested. The finding is real in outline and the standard interpretation of it is disputed.
entries.principle: Studies consistently report that humour is valued in a partner, and what people mean by the phrase differs systematically enough that the finding is hard to interpret. Producing humour and appreciating it are separate traits and are valued differently.
entries.example: The commonly reported asymmetry between what different groups mean by a good sense of humour is well attested in survey data and the evolutionary explanations offered for it are contested within the same literature.
entries.application: Useful for romantic comedy, and the pack cards it as contested because the survey finding and the explanation are frequently reported as one thing.

entries.name: Humour and Coping
entries.description: Contested. Humour as a coping mechanism is supported in outline; which humour, and for whom, is not.
entries.principle: Humour is associated with better outcomes under stress in a range of studies, and the association does not distinguish reliably between styles, populations or kinds of stressor. Self-defeating humour in particular has been associated with worse outcomes in some samples.
entries.example: The clinical and occupational literatures both report the association. The mechanism proposed varies between distancing, reappraisal and social support, and no one account has consolidated.
entries.application: A character who jokes under pressure is doing something psychologically real. Whether it is helping them is a question the writer should answer deliberately rather than assume.

entries.name: Laughter in Non-Human Animals
entries.description: Contested. Play vocalisations in other species are documented; whether they are laughter depends on the definition adopted.
entries.principle: Several mammal species produce distinct vocalisations during play that resemble human laughter acoustically and functionally. Whether these constitute laughter is a definitional argument rather than an empirical one, and it is frequently reported as though it were settled.
entries.example: Rat ultrasonic vocalisations during tickling and play, and primate play panting, are the most-cited cases. The evolutionary continuity argument is strong and the equivalence claim is stronger than the data compel.
entries.application: The finding supports play theory and does not establish that animals find things funny. A pack that reported it otherwise would be repeating a press release.

entries.name: Why Laughter Recruits Comedy
entries.description: The signal exists for affiliation and comedy borrows it, which explains several otherwise puzzling features of the form.
entries.principle: If laughter is primarily an affiliative signal, comedy is a technology for triggering it deliberately. This explains why comic performance is unusually dependent on the room, why the laugh's absence is felt as rejection, and why comedy is the only form with a verdict delivered during the work.
entries.example: The observed pattern that most laughter follows ordinary conversation rather than jokes is the foundation for this reading; the professional comedian's situation, in which a signal normally exchanged between intimates is elicited from strangers on demand, is unusual and difficult by construction.
entries.application: This is why persona precedes material. A performer is asking strangers for an affiliative signal, and the persona is the relationship that makes the request answerable.

entries.name: Laughing At and Laughing With
entries.description: A distinction the audience makes reliably and the research operationalises poorly.
entries.principle: Audiences distinguish confidently between laughter directed at a target and laughter shared with them, and the distinction tracks perceived intent rather than content. The same words produce different readings depending on who is understood to be speaking.
entries.example: The most-documented instance in the comic record is the reception of Till Death Us Do Part and All in the Family, where Vidmar and Rokeach's 1974 study found that prejudiced viewers read the bigoted character as the hero rather than the target.
entries.application: Intent does not control reception. A writer can shape the reading through persona and framing and cannot foreclose it, and the pack's contested-case method exists because of this.

entries.name: Nervous Laughter
entries.description: Laughter as a response to threat or discomfort rather than to amusement, which comedy can address deliberately.
entries.principle: Laughter occurs in fear, embarrassment and grief, and is not exclusively a response to the comic. Cringe comedy and black comedy both recruit this laughter rather than the amused kind, which is why they feel different to experience.
entries.example: Audiences at funerals, at accidents and during nervous confrontations laugh reliably, and the phenomenon is well attested clinically. Cringe comedy's characteristic response is nearer to this than to the response a joke produces.
entries.application: If the intended response is a wince that resolves into a laugh, the mechanism being used is not amusement. Write for the discomfort and let the laugh be its release.

entries.name: Laughter Suppression and Its Uses
entries.description: The effort of not laughing, which several comic forms treat as their actual subject.
entries.principle: Suppressed laughter is effortful and visible, and the effort is itself a performance the audience can read. Formats built on forbidding laughter exploit a real and measurable difficulty rather than a convention.
entries.example: The Japanese batsu format makes not laughing the explicit rule and the punishment the content; corpsing on stage is the same phenomenon read as failure rather than as the point.
entries.application: A scene in which a character must not laugh gives the performer a visible internal state and gives the audience permission to laugh on their behalf.

entries.name: The First Laugh Sets the Contract
entries.description: An audience's earliest response establishes what kind of work it believes it is watching, and revising that belief is expensive.
entries.principle: The first laugh in a performance or the first comic beat in a text tells the audience what register is operating, and subsequent material is read against it. A misplaced early laugh is more damaging than a missing one because it installs the wrong contract.
entries.example: This is the practical basis for the craft rule that the opening is a contract, and for the observation that a broad opening followed by a subtle work loses the audience it recruited.
entries.application: Write the opening last, once the work's actual register is known. An opening written first almost always promises the wrong product.

entries.name: The Room Has a Memory
entries.description: An audience's response to a passage is conditioned by everything that preceded it, which makes running order a craft decision.
entries.principle: Comic responses accumulate. A room that has laughed recently laughs more easily, a room that has been made uncomfortable resists, and the interval since the last laugh alters the threshold for the next. Running order is therefore not neutral.
entries.example: The standing practice of opening a set with reliable material and placing the hardest material after the room has been warmed is a direct application, and it is one of the few pieces of practitioner knowledge that is universal across the form.
entries.application: Order the material against the room's expected state rather than against the material's own merit. The strongest joke is not always the one to open with.

entries.name: The Cost of the Laugh That Does Not Come
entries.description: Comedy's failures are public, immediate and audible, which distinguishes the form psychologically for the maker as well as the audience.
entries.principle: A comic work that fails does so in front of the people it failed with, at the moment of failure. No other form delivers its verdict this way, and the fact shapes the working lives of comic performers and writers more than any aesthetic consideration.
entries.example: The practice of testing material in rooms before recording exists because the verdict cannot be predicted from the page; the stand-up special's economics, which retire an hour on release, raise the stakes of that verdict considerably.
entries.application: Budget for failure as a normal part of the process rather than as an event. Material that has not failed anywhere has usually not been tested.

entries.name: What This Collection Does Not Claim
entries.description: An explicit statement of the collection's evidentiary limits, so a reader can tell a finding from a convention.
entries.principle: This collection carries three tiers. Robust findings are replicated and, where relevant, cross-cultural. Contested findings are live disputes in the literature and are named as such with both positions available. Unreplicated findings are stated with that status attached or omitted entirely. **This card carries no robustness tier because it is a policy statement about the collection's own evidentiary limits, not an empirical claim.**
entries.example: Laughter's predominantly social character and the discriminability of spontaneous from produced laughter are robust. The Humor Styles Questionnaire's factor structure and the attraction findings are contested. Benign violation's original experiments and the laughter-and-health literature are unreplicated.
entries.application: Check the tier before using a card as evidence. A reference work that presents a contested finding as settled is making the same error as a contested-canon card that takes a side.

entries.name: Ricky Gervais
entries.description: The writer who took the cringe register he helped establish and pointed it at bereavement.
entries.meta: English, born 1961. Came to television from radio and music in his late thirties, which is late for the form and shows in the work's preoccupation with wasted time. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Co-creating The Office and Extras with Stephen Merchant, and then writing After Life, a sitcom about a widower with no arc.
entries.signature: Gervais builds characters who are wrong about how they are perceived and then refuses to correct them within the episode. In the later work the same withholding is applied to grief: the comedy does not resolve the bereavement, and the jokes are what allow the audience to remain in the room with it.

works.title: The Office
works.note: co-created and co-written with Stephen Merchant

works.title: Extras
works.note: co-created and co-written with Stephen Merchant

entries.name: Phoebe Waller-Bridge
entries.description: The writer who made the frame-break a symptom rather than a device.
entries.meta: English, born 1985. Fleabag began as a solo stage show at the Edinburgh Fringe in 2013 and reached television three years later, and the stage original's single-performer structure survives in the address to camera. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Fleabag, and for the series-two turn in which another character notices the protagonist's asides.
entries.signature: Waller-Bridge writes a narrator who is funny in order not to be understood, and then constructs a second series whose entire subject is someone understanding her anyway. The comedy and the concealed bereavement use the same mechanism, which is why the withdrawal in the final minutes does not read as a change of register.

entries.name: Hal Ashby
entries.description: The director of the period's most durable comedy about death, and the clearest case in this pack of an award commonly misdescribed.
entries.meta: American, 1929–1988. Worked as a film editor before directing, and the editorial instinct is visible in how long his comic scenes are allowed to run.
entries.knownFor: Directing Harold and Maude, from Colin Higgins's screenplay, and a run of American features across the 1970s.
entries.signature: Ashby lets a comic premise sit without pressing it, which is why the death material in Harold and Maude neither shocks nor sentimentalises. His only Academy Award is for film editing, on In the Heat of the Night, won before he directed anything; he was nominated once for directing, for Coming Home, and did not win. The phrase Oscar-winning director is technically true of him and functionally misleading.

entries.name: Sharon Horgan
entries.description: A writer whose comedy is built from the sentences people say to each other when something has gone wrong.
entries.meta: Irish, born 1970 in Hackney, London, and raised in County Meath from the age of four. Worked for years in low-visibility comedy before Pulling, and the late arrival shows in an unusual willingness to write characters past forty. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Catastrophe, co-written with and performed opposite Rob Delaney, and a body of work in which the domestic and the catastrophic occupy the same scene.
entries.signature: Horgan writes arguments at their real length rather than at their comic length, and places the joke inside the argument rather than at the end of it. The technique means her scenes carry information about the relationship whether or not the audience laughs, which is what lets the material absorb illness and bereavement without changing method.

entries.name: Peter Nichols
entries.description: The playwright who put a severely disabled child at the centre of a comedy in 1967 and made the comedy the parents' survival mechanism.
entries.meta: English, 1927–2019. Wrote from direct experience of raising a disabled daughter, which the play states rather than conceals.
entries.knownFor: A Day in the Death of Joe Egg, in which two parents perform comic routines about their daughter's condition, to each other and to the audience.
entries.signature: Nichols gives his characters music-hall technique and lets them use it as a coping apparatus in front of the audience, so the jokes are simultaneously funny and visibly load-bearing. The device makes the audience complicit in a relief the characters need, which is the most exact demonstration of comedy-as-anaesthetic in the English repertoire.

works.title: A Day in the Death of Joe Egg

entries.category: Illness, Disability and the Comic Voice
entries.name: Adam Kay
entries.description: A former doctor whose comic diary of hospital medicine became the most-read British account of the profession.
entries.meta: British, born 1980. Practised as a junior doctor before leaving medicine, and wrote comedy professionally before the diaries. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
