entries.knownFor: Sullivan's Travels, in which a director of comedies sets out to make a serious film about suffering and is argued out of it.
entries.signature: Sturges runs dialogue at screwball velocity and inserts, without changing pace, a direct argument about the value of comedy itself. Sullivan's Travels withdraws its comic register for a chain-gang sequence and then deliberately resumes it, which is the harder manoeuvre and one almost nothing since has attempted.

works.title: The Great McGinty
works.note: Academy Award for Writing, Original Screenplay, the first in that category

entries.category: Hollywood Screwball and the Studio Comedy
entries.name: Billy Wilder
entries.description: A writer-director who moved between comedy and its opposite using the same construction, and ended the form's best-known film on a refusal.
entries.meta: Austrian-American, 1906–2002. Left Europe in the 1930s; members of his family were murdered in the Holocaust. He holds six competitive Academy Awards; the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award he received in 1988 is not competitive, and counting it produces the frequently repeated figure of seven.
entries.knownFor: Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, and for a comic method built on people maintaining an untenable arrangement.
entries.signature: Wilder writes comedies whose premises are genuinely unpleasant — impersonation under threat of murder, an apartment lent for other men's affairs — and never softens them. Some Like It Hot's final line solves the comic ending problem by refusing to resolve, which is the most-cited solution in the form.

entries.category: Hollywood Screwball and the Studio Comedy
entries.name: Groucho Marx
entries.description: The verbal comedian of the sound transition, whose delivery outran the scenes he was in.
entries.meta: American, 1890–1977. Came from vaudeville with the act already built. He holds an honorary Academy Award, granted in 1974 and accepted on behalf of the Marx Brothers; the Marx Brothers never won a competitive one.
entries.knownFor: The Marx Brothers films, and a later television career as a quiz host in the same persona.
entries.signature: Groucho tops his own lines faster than the scene can absorb them, which is why the films read as an act interrupted by a plot rather than the reverse. His central device is the literalised figure — the elephant line in Animal Crackers turns on a modifier's position and then refuses to explain itself — and he never lets the film pause to acknowledge that a joke has occurred.

entries.category: Hollywood Screwball and the Studio Comedy
entries.name: Mel Brooks
entries.description: A parodist who reproduces a genre exactly enough to be mistaken for it, and one of the very few genuine EGOT holders.
entries.meta: American, born 28 June 1926; he turned one hundred in June 2026. Wrote for television from the 1950s before directing. He holds one competitive Academy Award, for The Producers, and an honorary one granted in January 2024. He has not received the Mark Twain Prize, a misattribution in wide circulation. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: The Producers, Blazing Saddles and Young Frankenstein, and for a parody method built on technical fidelity to the source.
entries.signature: Brooks reproduces a genre's grammar with real competence before altering it, which is why Young Frankenstein reads as a Universal horror film rather than as a sketch about one. Blazing Saddles attacks the western and the industry that made it simultaneously, and its final act breaks the studio wall literally; it is also a live contested case on its racial language, defended and attacked on documented grounds.

works.title: The Producers
works.note: Academy Award for Best Story and Screenplay

entries.name: Ray Galton
entries.description: Half of the partnership that invented the British situation comedy as a character form rather than a joke vehicle.
entries.meta: English, 17 July 1930 – 5 October 2018. Met Alan Simpson in a tuberculosis sanatorium and wrote with him for four decades.
entries.knownFor: Hancock's Half Hour and Steptoe and Son, written jointly throughout.
entries.signature: The partnership's innovation was to build episodes from a character's situation rather than from a run of gags, which is why an entire half-hour could be spent waiting to give blood. Hancock's Half Hour was the first British sitcom to trust that a fully drawn character would carry the time, and the model is the direct ancestor of nearly everything in the British form since.

works.title: Hancock's Half Hour (1954 radio)
works.note: radio from 1954, television from 1956, with Alan Simpson

entries.name: Alan Simpson
entries.description: The other half of the partnership, and the case for treating a writing team as two authors rather than one credit.
entries.meta: English, 27 November 1929 – 8 February 2017. Wrote with Ray Galton from the early 1950s; the two are credited jointly on everything and worked in the same room throughout.
entries.knownFor: Steptoe and Son, a sitcom whose comedy is a status war between father and son that neither can win without losing the relationship.
entries.signature: Steptoe and Son took the sitcom's requirement that nothing change and made the entrapment the subject, so the format's structural constraint became the drama. Harold's cultural aspiration is precise enough to be painful rather than merely funny, and the series is the strongest argument in the British tradition that a sitcom can be a tragedy performed at half-hour length.

entries.name: John Cleese
entries.description: A writer and performer whose farce is the tightest in British television, and whose most-cited credit is routinely misdescribed.
entries.meta: English, born 27 October 1939. Fawlty Towers carries the on-screen credit written by John Cleese and Connie Booth; there is no created by card on the programme, and attributing it to Cleese alone or inventing a joint creator credit are both errors. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Fawlty Towers, twelve episodes across two series, and Monty Python's Flying Circus.
entries.signature: Cleese constructs each Fawlty Towers episode as a compressed one-room farce with a mechanism set in the first minutes and no exit, and the hotel exists so that people can be in rooms they should not be in. He was neither producer nor director on the series. Booth stated in 2025 that he was primarily responsible for the dialogue; his own account is of joint writing across six months per episode, and the pack records both accounts.

works.title: Monty Python and the Holy Grail

entries.name: Connie Booth
entries.description: Co-writer of all twelve episodes of the most tightly constructed British sitcom, and a case study in a credit being lost.
entries.meta: American-born, resident in Britain. Her birth year cannot be established: three mutually inconsistent values circulate across otherwise reputable sources, and this pack states none rather than choosing one. She left performing for psychotherapy in the 1990s and has given very few interviews since. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026, on two interviews she gave in 2025, the later of them a statement on the death of Prunella Scales in October 2025; nothing dated in 2026 was found. A thin confirmation, and among the first to re-run.
entries.knownFor: Fawlty Towers, co-written with John Cleese across both series, and performed by her as Polly.
entries.signature: Booth's contribution is invisible in the way a farce's construction is invisible: the episodes' timing tolerances are extremely narrow and the plots have no slack, and that work is not separable by hand into two authors. Her name is dropped from the credit more often than any other in British comedy, which makes her the pack's clearest instance of a co-writer being absorbed into a partner's reputation.

works.title: Fawlty Towers
works.note: co-written with John Cleese, all twelve episodes

entries.name: Larry David
entries.description: The writer behind two series that between them defined American comedy's move from joke to social transgression.
entries.meta: American, born 2 July 1947. Seinfeld is created by Larry David and Jerry Seinfeld; Curb Your Enthusiasm is created by Larry David, who also stars and executive-produces. He has two Emmys, both from 1993 and both for Seinfeld, and has never won an acting Emmy despite seven nominations; Curb has never won Outstanding Comedy Series. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Seinfeld's convergent plotting and Curb's outline-only improvised scripts.
entries.signature: David's method is to escalate on social cost rather than on volume, so the endings arrive quietly and the humiliation is always administered by ordinary people enforcing ordinary norms. Curb's episodes are Harold-shaped: unrelated openings converge on a single final humiliation, which is the Chicago long-form structure imported into a scripted format.

works.title: Larry David: Curb Your Enthusiasm
works.note: the one-hour special that preceded the series

entries.name: Tina Fey
entries.description: A sketch writer who moved to sitcom and built a series about the machinery of making one.
entries.meta: American, born 18 May 1970. Created 30 Rock and holds the sole creator credit; she shared the showrunning with Robert Carlock, which is a distinct function and a distinct credit. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: 30 Rock, and a body of work in which the joke density is closer to sketch than to sitcom.
entries.signature: Fey writes at sketch density inside a sitcom structure, which is why 30 Rock's episodes carry more jokes per minute than the form usually supports and why they survive rewatching. She has also stated publicly that episodes of the series satirising blackface should be withdrawn, which is a live contested case: her position and the objection that removing satire eliminates the category are both documented, and the pack states both.

works.title: 30 Rock
works.note: created; showrunning shared with Robert Carlock

entries.name: Peter Cook
entries.description: The most gifted improviser of the British satire boom, whose career is usually discussed as a decline.
entries.meta: English, 17 November 1937 – 9 January 1995. Wrote Beyond the Fringe material while still an undergraduate and founded the Establishment club in 1961.
entries.knownFor: Beyond the Fringe, the Pete and Dud sketches with Dudley Moore, and the founding of a satirical club and a magazine.
entries.signature: Cook's technique is the monologue delivered by a man with total confidence and no information, sustained until the confidence itself becomes the subject. The E. L. Wisty material and the Derek and Clive recordings are the same device at opposite ends of acceptability, and the later recordings retain the corpsing because the corpsing is the point rather than an accident.

entries.name: Dudley Moore
entries.description: The musician half of the partnership, whose straight-man function is consistently underrated.
entries.meta: English, 19 April 1935 – 27 March 2002. A trained jazz pianist and organ scholar before comedy, and a Hollywood lead afterwards.
entries.knownFor: The Pete and Dud sketches, and a later American screen career.
entries.signature: Moore's role in the partnership is the feed, and the feed is what makes Cook's monologues legible as absurd rather than merely odd. His musical training shows in the timing: the pauses between Cook's assertions and Moore's responses are metrically precise, and the sketches lose their shape when the interval is altered.

entries.name: Graham Chapman
entries.description: The Python who played authority straight, which is what allowed the surrounding absurdity to register.
entries.meta: English, 8 January 1941 – 4 October 1989. Qualified in medicine before comedy, and was among the earliest British public figures to be openly gay.
entries.knownFor: Monty Python's Flying Circus, and the lead roles in Holy Grail and Life of Brian.
entries.signature: Chapman's function in the group was to supply an unwavering straight register — the colonel, the officer, the exasperated professional — against which everything else could be measured. Both Python features depend on his lead being played entirely without irony, which is the same principle as the straight setup: any comedy in that position spends the payoff.

works.title: Monty Python and the Holy Grail

entries.name: Terry Jones
entries.description: The Python who solved the group's structural problem, and a medieval historian in a second career.
entries.meta: Welsh, 1 February 1942 – 21 January 2020. Died of complications from frontotemporal dementia, which had ended his public speech some years earlier. Published serious medieval history alongside the comedy.
entries.knownFor: Directing the Python features, and for arguing the group out of the conventional sketch ending.
entries.signature: Jones's contribution was structural: he pressed for the stream-of-consciousness format in which sketches flow into one another rather than resolving, which solved the exit problem by abolishing it. It is the single most consequential formal decision in British sketch comedy, and the reason Python's material does not date in the way its contemporaries' does.

works.title: Monty Python and the Holy Grail

entries.name: Lenny Bruce
entries.description: The comedian whose prosecutions changed what could legally be said on an American stage, and who did not live to benefit.
entries.meta: American, 13 October 1925 – 3 August 1966, of acute morphine poisoning. Lenny Bruce is an open stage name; he was born Leonard Alfred Schneider. He was granted a posthumous pardon by Governor George Pataki on 23 December 2003; the pardon did not overturn the conviction, and his appeal had abated at his death, so the conviction stands. He never won a Grammy.
entries.knownFor: Obscenity prosecutions across several American cities, and a body of work in which the material and the legal jeopardy are inseparable.
entries.signature: Bruce's method was to say the unsayable word and then examine why it could not be said, which turned the act into an argument about language rather than a delivery of jokes. The later material is substantially courtroom transcript read aloud, which is stand-up collapsing into its own legal defence and is the clearest instance in the form of a career consumed by its subject.

works.title: The Sick Humor of Lenny Bruce
I Am Not a Nut, Elect Me!
How to Talk Dirty and Influence People

entries.name: Jack Benny
entries.description: The comedian who built a persona so complete that his best-known laugh is a pause.
entries.meta: American, 14 February 1894 – 26 December 1974. Jack Benny is an open stage name; he was born Benjamin Kubelsky, in Chicago, and raised in Waukegan, Illinois. He holds two competitive Emmy Awards, from 1958 and 1959; the 1988 Television Academy Hall of Fame induction is honorary and posthumous and is not a third Emmy.
entries.knownFor: A radio and television persona defined by vanity and miserliness, sustained for four decades without variation.
entries.signature: Benny's technique is the longest setup in the form: the persona is so established that a robber's demand can be answered with a silence of several seconds and the laugh grows throughout it. His tags are frequently one word or a look placed inside an existing laugh, which is the clearest surviving demonstration that a tag rides a reaction rather than starting a new one.

works.title: To Be or Not to Be

entries.name: Bob Newhart
entries.description: A comedian who built an act out of one half of a telephone call and let the audience construct the other.
entries.meta: American, 5 September 1929 – 18 July 2024. Worked as an accountant before comedy. He created neither of the sitcoms that carried his name and won no Emmy for either; his only Emmy was a guest award in 2013 for a different series.
entries.knownFor: The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart, a comedy album built almost entirely of one-sided telephone routines.
entries.signature: Newhart's routines are constructed from engineered silences: the unheard half of the conversation is supplied by the listener, and the length of each pause is the joke's actual content. It is the most economical demonstration in the form that a comic pause carries information rather than merely spacing a line, and the technique is unperformable on the page.

works.title: The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart

entries.name: George Carlin
entries.description: A comedian who moved from observer to prosecutor across a career, and made language itself the subject.
entries.meta: American, 12 May 1937 – 22 June 2008. Began as a conventional nightclub act and rebuilt the persona entirely in the early 1970s. He won five Grammy Awards, at the 15th, 36th, 43rd, 44th and 51st ceremonies, the last posthumously. The Recording Academy's own site retroactively applies its current category name to older wins, so the ceremonies rather than the category names are what can be cited.
entries.knownFor: Class Clown and the seven-words routine, which reached the United States Supreme Court in a broadcasting case.
entries.signature: Carlin's method is to take a phrase everyone uses without examination and reverse its moral loading, then hold the reversal long enough for the audience to feel the original assumption. The later work drops the observational stance entirely for prosecution, which is a persona change rather than a change of material, and it is the clearest career-length demonstration of persona setting permissions.

entries.name: Richard Pryor
entries.description: The performer who made confession a technique rather than a disclosure, and the first recipient of the Mark Twain Prize.
entries.meta: American, 1940–2005. Abandoned an established nightclub act in the late 1960s and rebuilt from autobiography. He received the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in 1998, its first year.
entries.knownFor: Live in Concert and Live on the Sunset Strip, the second of which narrates his own self-immolation.
entries.signature: Pryor's central device is the act-out: he voices objects, organs and absent people rather than describing them, which converts autobiography into dialogue and removes the audience's option to pity him. The material is unsparing about his own conduct and never asks for sympathy, which is what earns the licence for everything else in the set.

entries.name: Joan Rivers
entries.description: A comedian who worked for five decades on material that attacked herself first, and never softened the method.
entries.meta: American, 1933–2014. Her only Grammy, awarded in 2015 and posthumously, was for a spoken-word album rather than a comedy one; her Emmy is a Daytime Emmy from 1990.
entries.knownFor: A stand-up persona built on self-deprecation about appearance and age, sustained across a career in which she continued performing into her eighties.
entries.signature: Rivers establishes herself as the payer in the opening minutes, which licenses attacks on targets a differently positioned persona could not reach. The self-deprecation is not modesty but a status transaction: having conceded her own dignity first, she can spend anyone else's. Her late material is a live contested case, defended as consistent with a lifelong method and attacked as cruelty aimed downward.

works.title: The Late Show with Joan Rivers

entries.category: Stand-Up, The British and Irish Line
entries.name: Billy Connolly
entries.description: A folk musician who became the model for British stand-up as extended digressive storytelling.
entries.meta: Scottish, born 24 November 1942. Worked as a welder in the Clyde shipyards before performing, and came to comedy through folk music rather than through clubs. Knighted in the 2017 Birthday Honours and invested that October; appointed CBE in 2003. He announced the end of his touring career in December 2018, in a Radio Times interview, five years after his Parkinson's diagnosis of 2013; this card previously dated that announcement to 2020 and tied it directly to the diagnosis, and both were wrong. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Concert performances built from very long digressions that return, and a delivery derived from working-class Glasgow speech.
entries.signature: Connolly's sets have no joke structure in the American sense: he opens a story, abandons it for another, and returns twenty minutes later, and the returns are the architecture. Audience interruptions are incorporated rather than answered, which makes the crowd part of the composition instead of a hazard, and it is the defining difference between the British storytelling line and the American joke-unit line.

works.title: Billy Connolly's World Tour of Scotland

entries.category: Stand-Up, The British and Irish Line
entries.name: Victoria Wood
entries.description: A comedian, songwriter and playwright whose timing is metrically exact and whose subject is ordinary English embarrassment.
entries.meta: English, 1953–2016. Wrote her own songs and performed them within the stand-up. She was never made a Dame, a title frequently and wrongly attached to her.
entries.knownFor: Stand-up built on precisely observed lists, and dinnerladies, a sitcom she wrote alone.
entries.signature: Wood's routines are metrically constructed: the syllable count in the approach to a punchline is fixed, and the lists escalate on a pattern the audience can feel. She is the clearest British demonstration that comic rhythm is measurable, and her material fails when performed by anyone else because the timing is written into the sentence rather than added to it.

works.title: Victoria Wood: As Seen on TV
Victoria Wood Live in Your Own Home

entries.category: Stand-Up, The British and Irish Line
entries.name: Stewart Lee
entries.description: A comedian whose method is repetition held past the audience's patience, and who deliberately loses rooms.
entries.meta: English, born 1968. Worked in the alternative circuit from the late 1980s. Contrary to a widely circulated claim, he has never won or been nominated for an Edinburgh Comedy Award from either the historic body or the separate award founded in 2023; his awards are the Hackney Empire New Act of the Year in 1990, two British Comedy Awards in 2011 and a BAFTA in 2012. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Long-form stand-up built on repetition, and a persona that comments on its own reception while performing.
entries.signature: Lee establishes a repeated phrase, alters one instance, and treats the alteration as the only joke in the passage. He also constructs passages designed to lose part of the room and then makes the loss the material, which is anti-comedy used structurally rather than as a stunt. The technique requires an audience that knows the persona, which is why the work does not travel to a general room.

works.title: How I Escaped My Certain Fate

entries.category: Stand-Up, The British and Irish Line
entries.name: Dylan Moran
entries.description: A stand-up whose sentences accumulate qualifications until the original proposition is unrecoverable.
entries.meta: Irish, born 1971. Won the main Edinburgh festival comedy award in 1996, in the years when it carried the Perrier sponsorship name. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Stand-up built on digressive, adjective-heavy sentences, and the sitcom Black Books.
entries.signature: Moran's persona is deterioration in progress, and the sentence structure performs it: each clause qualifies the last until the point is lost, which is the character rather than a defect in the writing. The technique means the laugh arrives on the accumulation rather than on a punchline, and it is the least American construction in contemporary stand-up.

entries.category: Stand-Up, The British and Irish Line
entries.name: Peter Kay
entries.description: A comedian whose material is almost entirely recognition, and who plays the largest rooms in the form.
entries.meta: English, born 1973. Works in a register drawn from Bolton family life and has sustained very large-scale arena touring. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Live arena performances and Phoenix Nights, a sitcom set in a working men's club.
entries.signature: Kay's material is built on shared recall rather than on invention: the audience arrives at the punchline before he does, and the laugh is the confirmation of a memory rather than a surprise. This is the anticipation mechanism in its purest form, and it explains both his scale and why the recordings do not travel to audiences without the shared reference.

works.title: Live at the Bolton Albert Halls

entries.name: Hannah Gadsby
entries.description: The performer who used an hour of stand-up to argue that the form's own structure was doing them harm.
entries.meta: Australian, born 1978. Worked the Australian and British circuits for a decade before the show that changed their position. Their 2017 Edinburgh Comedy Award for best show was shared with John Robins, the first shared win in the award's history. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Nanette, which withholds the release the form promises and states why.
entries.signature: Gadsby spends the first half of Nanette earning the room's permission with conventional self-deprecating material, then spends it: the argument is that a self-deprecating joke about one's own trauma freezes the story at its worst point and prevents its completion. The show is the most complete instance in the form of a posture switch prepared by everything preceding it, and the withdrawal reads as argued rather than as nerve failing.

entries.name: Tig Notaro
entries.description: A comedian whose best-known set was performed days after a cancer diagnosis and released as a recording of the room deciding.
entries.meta: American, born 1971. Has two Grammy nominations and no Grammy wins, a distinction frequently collapsed; she received an Academy Award nomination in 2026 for a documentary and did not win. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: A set performed at Largo in Los Angeles on 5 August 2012, which opened by stating the diagnosis plainly.
entries.signature: Notaro's delivery is unusually quiet and unusually slow, and the Largo set uses the room's response as information rather than as verdict: the audience's discomfort is audible on the recording and she works with it in real time. The set is the clearest available demonstration that permission is granted moment by moment and can be renegotiated inside a performance.

works.title: Live
works.note: the Largo set, released as a recording

entries.name: Maria Bamford
entries.description: A comedian who performs her own psychiatric history in the voices of everyone involved in it.
entries.meta: American, born 1970. Has spoken publicly about bipolar disorder and psychiatric hospitalisation, which the material addresses directly. She neither created nor wrote the sitcom based on her life, a credit routinely assigned to her. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Stand-up performed almost entirely in character voices, and a special performed to progressively larger rooms within a single recording.
entries.signature: Bamford uses act-outs not to depict other people but to hold her own experience at a workable distance: her mother, her doctors and her own internal voices are all performed, which places the material one remove from confession while making it more exact. The special performed to rooms of increasing size makes audience permission visible as a variable rather than a constant.

entries.name: Bo Burnham
entries.description: A performer who came up through online video and has spent a career examining what performing to a camera does to a person.
entries.meta: American, born 1990. Began posting songs online as a teenager. He won the Edinburgh festival's Panel Prize in 2010 and was a nominee for the main award, which he did not win; his Grammy, at the 64th ceremony, was for a song written for visual media rather than in a comedy category. The pre-release re-check of September 2026 found no death record and no dated activity since early 2024, when he directed a filmed stage show and then deleted his social accounts; the death-notice pages that surface for him are residue of a January 2024 hoax and report nothing. The card previously stated a bare born 1990 and no status, which reads as an assertion that he is living; that assertion is withdrawn and his status is carried as unconfirmed.
entries.knownFor: Inside, written, performed, shot and edited alone in one room over a year.
entries.signature: Burnham makes the construction of the work its subject, so the audience watches the special being assembled and degrading at the same time. Several songs end without a button, which is a deliberately dead beat rather than a failure, and the repetition of earlier material in worse condition is how the passage of time is expressed structurally rather than stated.

entries.name: James Acaster
entries.description: A comedian whose shows are built as elaborate constructions that collapse into autobiography in their final minutes.
entries.meta: English, born 1985. Was nominated for the main Edinburgh comedy award in five consecutive years without winning it, which is a record of the historic body's shortlists. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Repertoire, four hours of interlocking material released together, and a comic method built on sustained absurd premises.
entries.signature: Acaster builds an hour on a premise the audience assumes is a bit, and then reveals in the last minutes that it has been carrying something else. Several routines end without a button and let the room decide whether the piece is finished, which is the withheld payoff used as structure rather than as a single gag.

entries.name: Charles M. Schulz
entries.description: The cartoonist who made a daily four-panel strip carry melancholy for fifty years without ever resolving it.
entries.meta: American, 1922–2000. Drew and lettered every strip himself for the entire run, refusing assistants. The strip ended with his death.
entries.knownFor: Peanuts, in which children speak in the vocabulary of adult disappointment and no character ever wins.
entries.signature: Schulz's four-panel structure is metrically fixed: three panels of setup and a punchline in the fourth, which is the maximum possible setup share in the form. He also established that a comic strip could sustain unhappiness indefinitely, since a strip's characters cannot change and cannot escape, which is the same structural fact the sitcom runs on. The Emmy for the Christmas special went to the programme rather than to him.

entries.name: Bill Watterson
entries.description: A cartoonist who ended his strip at its commercial peak and declined to license it, which is the fact everything else about him is read through.
entries.meta: American, born 1958. Ran Calvin and Hobbes for ten years and stopped in 1995. He consistently refused merchandising licences for the strip, a position frequently described in stronger terms than he has stated; he works rarely and gives almost no interviews. The pre-release re-check of September 2026 found no death record and no dated activity since The Mysteries in October 2023; a 40th-anniversary feature of November 2025 could not obtain a word from him and fell back on a 2005 interview with his editor. The card previously stated a bare born 1958 and no status, which reads as an assertion that he is living; that assertion is withdrawn and his status is carried as unconfirmed.
entries.knownFor: Calvin and Hobbes, and for winning an argument with his syndicate over the layout of the Sunday strip.
entries.signature: Watterson varies panel width to control reading speed, which is the printed equivalent of the comic pause: a wide panel is a held beat and a narrow one is a fast cut. The Sunday strips use the additional space as duration rather than as area, and the fight to get that space is the clearest case in the form of a formal requirement being defended commercially.

works.title: The Calvin and Hobbes Tenth Anniversary Book

entries.name: George Herriman
entries.description: The most formally radical cartoonist in the medium's history, working inside a strip whose premise never changed.
entries.meta: American, 1880–1944. Of Louisiana Creole background; his racial classification on official records has been the subject of substantial scholarship since his death.
entries.knownFor: Krazy Kat, a strip built on a single unvarying triangle of unrequited love, thrown brick and pursuing policeman.
entries.signature: Herriman established a rigid three-beat rhythm and then broke the panel grid itself, so the timing irregularity is visible as layout rather than merely felt. The backgrounds shift between panels without explanation and the dialect is invented, which makes the strip formally experimental inside a structure that repeats daily for three decades.

entries.name: Gary Larson
entries.description: The cartoonist who compressed the pull-back-and-reveal into a single panel and a caption.
entries.meta: American, born 1950. Ran The Far Side from 1980 to 1995 and has published very little since; the most recent confirmed new work is from 2020. The pre-release re-check of September 2026 found no death record and no dated activity of any kind since the launch of the New Stuff page on his own site in June 2020 — the 2020 date this card already gave was re-checked independently and stands. The card previously stated a bare born 1950 and no status, which reads as an assertion that he is living; that assertion is withdrawn and his status is carried as unconfirmed.
entries.knownFor: The Far Side, a single-panel strip built on premises that cannot be stated before the image is seen.
entries.signature: Larson's panel performs the reveal by placing the frame where the context is missing and the caption where it arrives, so the reader assembles the joke in the wrong order deliberately. Single-panel construction removes every device that depends on duration — no runner, no escalation, no pause — leaving only the reveal, which is why the form is unforgiving and why so few practise it well.

works.title: The PreHistory of The Far Side

entries.name: Quino
entries.description: The Argentine cartoonist whose strip about a politically aware child is the most widely read comic work in the Spanish language.
entries.meta: Argentine, 1932–2020. Born Joaquín Salvador Lavado Tejón; Quino is an open pen name formed from his first name. Mafalda ran from 1964 to 1973 and he declined to revive it thereafter.
entries.knownFor: Mafalda, in which a small girl interrogates her parents and the world about politics, war and inequality.
entries.signature: Quino gives the last panel to the child, and the strip's argument always arrives in her final line, which is the stressed position applied to a four-panel form. Ending the strip at its peak and refusing to continue it is a decision he shares with Watterson, and the near-absence of Mafalda from Anglophone comedy reference is another instance of the gap this pack's non-Anglophone floor exists to close.

entries.name: Keith Johnstone
entries.description: The teacher who identified status as the engine of scene work, and wrote the field's standard text.
entries.meta: British-Canadian, 1933–2023. Worked at the Royal Court in London before emigrating to Canada, where he taught for decades and devised the Theatresports format.
entries.knownFor: Impro, which sets out status transactions, the offer and the block, and the exercises for teaching both.
entries.signature: Johnstone's contribution is the observation that every exchange raises or lowers one party relative to the other, and that a scene without status movement is dead regardless of its jokes. He also named the block and demonstrated that audiences forgive weak invention and never forgive refusal, which is the only non-negotiable rule the form has.

entries.name: Viola Spolin
entries.description: The originator of the theatre games from which American improvisation descends, working first with immigrant children.
entries.meta: American, 7 November 1906 – 22 November 1994. Trained under Neva Boyd in recreational group work in the 1920s and developed the games in a Depression-era work programme. She did not found Second City; her son Paul Sills was among its founders.
entries.knownFor: Improvisation for the Theater, which codifies the games and the vocabulary the American tradition still uses.
entries.signature: Spolin's games are structured to remove self-consciousness by giving the player a task, which is the insight the whole field rests on: an actor solving a problem is not performing and therefore cannot be embarrassed. The focus on the task rather than on the joke is what distinguishes the American training tradition from the British club one.

entries.name: Del Close
entries.description: The teacher who built long-form improvisation, and around whom more legend has accumulated than record supports.
entries.meta: American, 9 March 1934 – 4 March 1999. Taught at Second City and later at iO in Chicago, where several generations of American television comedy writers trained. He bequeathed his skull to the Goodman Theatre for use in Hamlet; the bequest was real and the delivery was not, and the skull produced was later acknowledged to have been bought from a medical supplier.
entries.knownFor: The Harold, a long-form structure in which unconnected opening scenes converge through callbacks discovered rather than planned.
entries.signature: Close's structure treats an hour of improvisation as a single composition rather than as a run of scenes, and its convergences are found in performance rather than agreed beforehand. The form is the direct ancestor of the convergent episode structure in American single-camera comedy, and Truth in Comedy is where it is documented.

works.title: Truth in Comedy
works.note: with Charna Halpern and Kim Johnson

entries.name: Christopher Guest
entries.description: A director who films improvisation and selects the escalations that arrived, in a form he did not invent but did define.
entries.meta: American-British, born 1948. Inherited a British peerage and sat in the House of Lords until hereditary peers were largely removed from it in 1999. He performed in This Is Spinal Tap but did not direct it; Rob Reiner did. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: Waiting for Guffman, Best in Show and A Mighty Wind, made from outlines rather than scripts with improvised dialogue.
entries.signature: Guest's method is yes-and captured on film: the ensembles escalate by accretion and the edit selects what worked, so the writing happens in performance and the authorship happens in the cutting room. The camera's neutrality is what keeps the affection intact — the films observe people performing competence at a hobby without inviting contempt for them.

entries.name: Barry Humphries
entries.description: The performer behind two character personas sustained for six decades, and the clearest case of a persona outgrowing its author.
entries.meta: Australian, 1934–2023. Dame Edna Everage and Sir Les Patterson are character personas presented as people, not stage names: Humphries is the author and neither title belongs to him. He was never knighted. His Tony Award, in 2000, is a Special Tony rather than a competitive one, and despite the Melbourne festival's principal prize having carried his name from 2000 to 2018, he never won it.
entries.knownFor: Dame Edna Everage, a suburban Melbourne housewife who became an international chat-show host in character.
entries.signature: Humphries built personas complete enough to conduct real interviews with real people who had to respond to them as though they were real, which is the deepest commitment to character comedy the form has produced. Late remarks on transgender people made him a live contested case in the last years of his life, and the Melbourne award was renamed in that context; the dispute and the renaming are both documented and neither is adjudicated here.

works.title: An Evening's Intercourse with Barry Humphries

entries.name: Taika Waititi
entries.description: A director whose comic register absorbs grief and atrocity without changing method.
entries.meta: New Zealander, born 1975, of Māori and Jewish descent. His Academy Award, in 2020, is for Adapted Screenplay rather than for directing. Living, confirmed at the pre-release re-check of September 2026.
entries.knownFor: What We Do in the Shadows, Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit.
entries.signature: Waititi keeps a deadpan, faintly awkward comic register running underneath material that would ordinarily require a tonal change, and lets the register itself carry the seriousness. Jojo Rabbit builds several sequences comically and pays them seriously, which depends entirely on the audience noticing the switch and is the reason the film divides opinion sharply.

works.title: What We Do in the Shadows
works.note: co-written and co-directed with Jemaine Clement

entries.name: Catherine O'Hara
entries.description: A performer who came out of Canadian sketch and spent a career building characters whose self-regard is total and unexamined.
entries.meta: Canadian, 4 March 1954 – 30 January 2026. Came up through Second City in Toronto and SCTV. She won the Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series in 2020, and a Golden Globe at the ceremony held in February 2021; a further award came posthumously in March 2026.
entries.knownFor: SCTV, the Christopher Guest improvised films, and Moira Rose in Schitt's Creek.
entries.signature: O'Hara's method is a character whose vocabulary and self-assessment are entirely unexamined and entirely consistent, delivered without any signal to the audience that she knows. Moira Rose's compliments are constructed to flatter the speaker rather than the recipient, and the performance never acknowledges it, which is why the character remains funny rather than becoming a set of catchphrases.

entries.name: Harold and Maude
entries.author: Hal Ashby
entries.awards: Two Golden Globe nominations, no wins. No Academy Award nomination.
entries.description: A young man who stages elaborate fake suicides meets a woman about to turn eighty who intends a real one. The film treats death as a subject rather…
entries.text: A young man who stages elaborate fake suicides meets a woman about to turn eighty who intends a real one. The film treats death as a subject rather than an event, and its comedy operates by making the protagonist's obsession ordinary and the world's discomfort with it the actual joke. Its tonal handbrake tapers rather than stopping, which is frequently criticised and is instructive as the alternative to a clean withdrawal. It failed commercially on release and accumulated its reputation across two decades.

entries.name: After Life
entries.author: Ricky Gervais
entries.awards: National Comedy Awards, Best Scripted Comedy, 2023, with two acting awards at the same ceremony. It won nothing in 2022, and there is no Best Comedy Programme category.
entries.description: A local newspaper journalist responds to his wife's death by deciding that rudeness is now costless. The series is structurally unusual in giving…
entries.text: A local newspaper journalist responds to his wife's death by deciding that rudeness is now costless. The series is structurally unusual in giving its protagonist no arc: the bereavement does not resolve and the character does not learn, which is the sitcom's no-growth constraint repurposed as a description of grief. The jokes are what allow the audience to stay in the room, which is comedy used as anaesthetic and openly so.

entries.name: The Loved One
entries.author: Evelyn Waugh
entries.awards: None. Waugh won no major literary prize in his lifetime, which is a verified negative rather than a documentation gap.
entries.description: A satire of the American funeral industry, in which the euphemisms of commercial mourning are collected and allowed to indict themselves. Waugh…
entries.text: A satire of the American funeral industry, in which the euphemisms of commercial mourning are collected and allowed to indict themselves. Waugh moves the payer away from the bereaved and onto the trade that serves them, which is what keeps the book from cruelty; the register never rises, so the industry's own vocabulary does all the work. It is the clearest instance in English of comedy about death that attacks an institution rather than a feeling.

entries.name: A Day in the Death of Joe Egg
entries.author: Peter Nichols
entries.awards: An Evening Standard Theatre Award in 1967. The category is not named by any source located during verification, so none is stated here.
entries.description: Two parents of a severely disabled child perform comic routines about her condition, to each other and directly to the audience. Nichols gives them…
entries.text: Two parents of a severely disabled child perform comic routines about her condition, to each other and directly to the audience. Nichols gives them music-hall technique and shows it functioning as a survival apparatus, so the jokes are simultaneously funny and visibly load-bearing. It is the most exact demonstration in the English repertoire of comedy as anaesthetic, and the audience is made complicit in a relief the characters cannot do without.

entries.name: Fleabag
entries.author: Phoebe Waller-Bridge
entries.awards: Three Primetime Emmy Awards in 2019 for the second series — Outstanding Comedy Series, Lead Actress in a Comedy Series, and Writing for a Comedy Series. None of the three is for Killing Eve, a common conflation.
entries.description: A woman narrates her life to the camera in order not to be understood by anyone in it. The first series withholds the bereavement driving the…
entries.text: A woman narrates her life to the camera in order not to be understood by anyone in it. The first series withholds the bereavement driving the behaviour until its final minutes and then withdraws the comic register entirely; the second makes the address to camera a plot event by having another character notice it. The frame-break moves from device to symptom, which is the only substantial development the technique has had.

entries.name: This Is Going to Hurt
entries.author: Adam Kay
entries.awards: Three Specsavers National Book Awards in 2018 — Popular Non-Fiction Book of the Year, Book Club Book of the Year, and New Writer of the Year. Not the British Book Awards, a common substitution.
entries.description: A diary of hospital shifts written as comedy and paced so a reader can continue through material that would otherwise be unreadable. Kay places the…
entries.text: A diary of hospital shifts written as comedy and paced so a reader can continue through material that would otherwise be unreadable. Kay places the relief where the material is hardest rather than where the writing is weakest, which is what anaesthetic comedy requires, and then removes the register once, at the end, without warning. The final entry works because nothing preceding it was adjusted to prepare the way.

entries.name: Live
entries.author: Tig Notaro
entries.awards: Grammy nomination for Best Comedy Album, 2014; it did not win. Notaro has no Grammy wins.
entries.description: Comedy album. A set performed at Largo in Los Angeles on 5 August 2012, days after a cancer diagnosis, which opens by stating the diagnosis plainly…
entries.text: Comedy album. A set performed at Largo in Los Angeles on 5 August 2012, days after a cancer diagnosis, which opens by stating the diagnosis plainly and then works with whatever the room returns. The recording captures permission being negotiated in real time: the audience's discomfort is audible and Notaro adjusts against it. It is the clearest available evidence that a room's licence is granted moment by moment rather than at the start of a set.

entries.name: Lost Voice Guy: Ability
entries.author: Lee Ridley
entries.awards: None recorded.
entries.description: Radio series. A sitcom whose protagonist communicates through a speech synthesiser, written by a performer who does the same. Removing pitch, volume…
entries.text: Radio series. A sitcom whose protagonist communicates through a speech synthesiser, written by a performer who does the same. Removing pitch, volume and vocal warmth leaves only construction, so every pause must be typed in advance and comic timing becomes a compositional decision rather than a performance one. The series is the most direct demonstration in the form of how much comic weight ordinarily sits in delivery.

entries.name: Special
entries.author: Ryan O'Connell
entries.awards: One Primetime Emmy nomination, Outstanding Short Form Comedy or Drama Series, 2019; State of the Union won. No further nomination is confirmed.
entries.description: A comedy about a gay man with cerebral palsy who tells colleagues his limp is the result of a car accident, because the lie is easier than the…
entries.text: A comedy about a gay man with cerebral palsy who tells colleagues his limp is the result of a car accident, because the lie is easier than the truth. The series makes disability a source of plot rather than of pathos, and its central joke is that concealment costs more effort than disclosure would. Written by and starring a disabled creator, which is the condition that lets it be unsentimental.

entries.name: Catch-22
entries.author: Joseph Heller
entries.awards: None. It was a National Book Award finalist and lost to The Moviegoer; Heller never received a Pulitzer or a National Book Award. A verified negative rather than a documentation gap.
entries.description: A bomber squadron is held in place by a regulation that makes any request to stop flying evidence of the sanity required to keep flying. Heller…
entries.text: A bomber squadron is held in place by a regulation that makes any request to stop flying evidence of the sanity required to keep flying. Heller writes military logic as a functioning machine and lets the comedy come from its correct operation, then arranges the chronology so the same events are approached repeatedly and become less funny each time. The title rule left the book and entered the language, which is the clearest case of a load-bearing gag outliving its work.

entries.name: Dr. Strangelove
entries.author: Stanley Kubrick
entries.awards: Four Academy Award nominations, no wins. Four BAFTA Film Awards in 1965 — Film, British Film, British Art Direction Black and White for Ken Adam, and the United Nations Award. BAFTA dates by ceremony year, so these are the 1965 awards for a 1964 film.
entries.description: A nuclear war begins because a chain of command works exactly as designed. The film opens on refuelling footage scored as a love scene, which…
entries.text: A nuclear war begins because a chain of command works exactly as designed. The film opens on refuelling footage scored as a love scene, which declares its permissions inside two minutes, and it plays annihilation as procedural competence throughout. Its ending is a punchline over a montage of detonations, which is comedy as accelerant stated as a joke and is the earliest instance most viewers encounter.

entries.name: Blackadder Goes Forth
entries.author: Richard Curtis and Ben Elton
entries.awards: BAFTA Television Award, Comedy Series, 1990, for the 1989 series, to Lloyd, Boden, Elton and Curtis. BAFTA has never used the category name Best Situation Comedy.
entries.description: The fourth series relocates a serial coward to the trenches of the First World War, and spends six episodes on the same joke density as its…
entries.text: The fourth series relocates a serial coward to the trenches of the First World War, and spends six episodes on the same joke density as its predecessors. The final scene constructs an exchange exactly like every previous joke, does not resolve it, and sends the cast over the top; the audience does not laugh, which is the design. It is the most economical instance in television of a comedy withdrawing its own register, occupying under sixty seconds with nothing before it altered.

entries.name: The Great Dictator
entries.author: Charlie Chaplin
entries.awards: Five Academy Award nominations including Best Picture and Best Actor; no wins.
entries.description: Chaplin plays both a Jewish barber and a dictator, in a film released while the United States was still neutral and before the full extent of the…
entries.text: Chaplin plays both a Jewish barber and a dictator, in a film released while the United States was still neutral and before the full extent of the persecution was known. The globe dance reduces a tyrant to a man alone with a balloon, which is deflation used as a political act. The closing speech abandons the comic frame entirely and addresses the audience directly, the earliest major instance of the manoeuvre, and Chaplin later said he could not have made the film had he known what was happening.

entries.name: The Death of Stalin
entries.author: Armando Iannucci
entries.awards: None. Nominated for the British Independent Film Award for Best Screenplay in 2017 and did not win; the award went to God's Own Country. Its release licence was revoked in Russia.
entries.description: The Soviet leadership manoeuvres over a dying man while a purge continues in the background. The politburo speak in regional accents and modern…
entries.text: The Soviet leadership manoeuvres over a dying man while a purge continues in the background. The politburo speak in regional accents and modern idiom, which strips the historical register and leaves committee behaviour visible as itself. The film accelerates in its final act by removing the comic distance it has maintained: the executions are shot straight, and the audience is left holding a register that has stopped working.

entries.name: Four Lions
entries.author: Chris Morris
entries.awards: BAFTA Film Award, Outstanding Debut By A British Writer, Director or Producer, 2011, to Chris Morris, for a 2010 film.
entries.description: Four incompetent men in Sheffield plan a suicide bombing. Morris researched the subject for three years and the comedy is entirely in the…
entries.text: Four incompetent men in Sheffield plan a suicide bombing. Morris researched the subject for three years and the comedy is entirely in the incompetence rather than in the ideology, which is what makes the film's final act survivable and what its critics identified as its evasion. The acceleration is distributed across the last third rather than concentrated, and the comic register keeps running underneath the deaths.

entries.name: Steptoe and Son
entries.author: Ray Galton and Alan Simpson
entries.awards: None located. Nothing appears in BAFTA's database and no award is named by any reference source consulted; Galton and Simpson's 1959 BAFTA for scriptwriting predates the series and does not attach to it. This is a documentation gap rather than a verified negative.
entries.description: A rag-and-bone man and his father conduct a status war from two chairs, in which the son's cultural aspiration is precise enough to be painful and…
entries.text: A rag-and-bone man and his father conduct a status war from two chairs, in which the son's cultural aspiration is precise enough to be painful and the father's sabotage is affectionate. The sitcom's requirement that nothing change becomes the subject: Harold cannot leave, and every episode is a demonstration of why. It is the strongest argument in the British tradition that a sitcom can be a tragedy performed at half-hour length.

entries.name: The Royle Family
entries.author: Caroline Aherne, Craig Cash and Henry Normal
entries.awards: BAFTA Television Award, Situation Comedy, 2000, and again in 2007. In 1999 it was a nominee only, in the category then named Comedy — Programme or Series.
entries.description: A family watches television and talks, filmed on one sofa without a laugh track, plot or exterior. Removing every sitcom convention leaves…
entries.text: A family watches television and talks, filmed on one sofa without a laugh track, plot or exterior. Removing every sitcom convention leaves observation, and the series demonstrates that ritual can substitute for structure entirely. The Christmas episodes are its strongest work for exactly that reason, and the warmth comes from the writers plainly liking people the era's other observational comedy would have used as material.

entries.name: Only Fools and Horses
entries.author: John Sullivan
entries.awards: BAFTA Television Awards — Comedy Series in 1986 and 1989, and Comedy — Programme or Series in 1997. The category was renamed between those wins, and BAFTA has never used the name Best Situation Comedy.
entries.description: Two brothers trade unsellable goods from a tower block, sustained by a conviction that next year they will be millionaires. Sullivan supplies…
entries.text: Two brothers trade unsellable goods from a tower block, sustained by a conviction that next year they will be millionaires. Sullivan supplies obstacles that are financial rather than comic, so the failures land as economics; the series is unusual in the form for letting the situation eventually change. Its most-quoted moment is a fall through a bar flap, and the fall works because of the beat before it, in which the character adjusts his cuffs.

entries.name: This Country
entries.author: Daisy May Cooper and Charlie Cooper
entries.awards: BAFTA Television Awards, Scripted Comedy and Female Performance in a Comedy, both 2018, plus a BAFTA Television Craft Award for Breakthrough Talent the same year.
entries.description: A mockumentary about two cousins in a Cotswold village with nothing to do and no prospect of anything to do. The documentary conceit means the…
entries.text: A mockumentary about two cousins in a Cotswold village with nothing to do and no prospect of anything to do. The documentary conceit means the audience watches them perform for a camera with no reason to be interested in them, which is the humiliation the form supplies for free. The boredom is real rather than comic, and the affection for the characters is what separates it from the observational comedy of the preceding decade.

entries.name: Pygmalion
entries.author: George Bernard Shaw
entries.awards: Shaw received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925, for his body of work rather than for this play.
entries.description: First performed in English in 1914; the 1913 premiere frequently cited was in German translation, in Vienna, and this pack dates by original…
entries.text: First performed in English in 1914; the 1913 premiere frequently cited was in German translation, in Vienna, and this pack dates by original language. A phonetician wagers that he can pass a flower seller off as a duchess by correcting her speech. Shaw makes the class marker explicit, teachable and purchasable, and then makes the teaching the problem: the experiment succeeds and leaves its subject fitted for no available life. The comedy is entirely in the code being stated aloud, which is the comedy of manners with the rules written on the wall.

entries.name: The Office
entries.author: Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant
entries.awards: BAFTA Television Awards, Situation Comedy, in 2002 and 2003, both to the producers, and again in 2004 for the specials. Two Golden Globe Awards in 2004 — Best Television Series, Musical or Comedy, to producer Ash Atalla, and Best Actor in a Television Series, Musical or Comedy, to Gervais. It is widely reported as the first British sitcom to win a Golden Globe, which is a press claim rather than an entry in the awarding body's record.
entries.description: A documentary crew films a paper merchant's Slough branch and its manager performs continuously for them. The camera stays on him after the moment…
entries.text: A documentary crew films a paper merchant's Slough branch and its manager performs continuously for them. The camera stays on him after the moment has passed, and the holding is the entire technique: the humiliation transfers to the audience because the character never registers it. A second, silent editorial line runs through the reaction shots of a colleague, which tells the viewer how to read him without anyone saying so.

entries.name: Peep Show
entries.author: Jesse Armstrong and Sam Bain
entries.awards: BAFTA Television Award, Situation Comedy, 2008 — its only win in that category.
entries.description: Two flatmates are filmed entirely in point of view, with their internal monologues audible. Both leads are the arrested-adult type and neither is…
entries.text: Two flatmates are filmed entirely in point of view, with their internal monologues audible. Both leads are the arrested-adult type and neither is the corrective, which removes the structure in which someone eventually grows up. The interior monologue fills the recovered seconds a single-camera format supplies with a second script running under the first, and it makes the search for a next sentence audible in a way no other comedy has matched.

entries.name: Nighty Night
entries.author: Julia Davis
entries.awards: None. Two BAFTA Television Award nominations in 2005, for Situation Comedy and for Julia Davis in Comedy Performance, neither of which won. A verified negative.
entries.description: A woman responds to her husband's cancer diagnosis by pursuing her neighbour's husband, and the series supplies no character who registers that any…
entries.text: A woman responds to her husband's cancer diagnosis by pursuing her neighbour's husband, and the series supplies no character who registers that any of it is unacceptable. Davis removes the corrective presence that cringe comedy normally provides, so the audience must hold that position alone for the duration. It spends its cruelty budget deliberately and accepts the viewers it loses, which is a legible artistic decision rather than a miscalculation.

entries.name: A Confederacy of Dunces
entries.author: John Kennedy Toole
entries.awards: Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, 1981, awarded posthumously.
entries.description: An enormous, unemployable medievalist fails continuously in New Orleans and interprets every failure as vindication. Toole gives Ignatius Reilly a…
entries.text: An enormous, unemployable medievalist fails continuously in New Orleans and interprets every failure as vindication. Toole gives Ignatius Reilly a complete and internally consistent worldview and never allows the narration to correct it, so the reader supplies the entire judgement. The technique keeps a fundamentally unpleasant protagonist readable across a long novel, which is harder than it appears. Written in the early 1960s and published eleven years after the author's death.

entries.name: Nathan for You
entries.author: Nathan Fielder
entries.awards: Writers Guild of America Award, Comedy/Variety Sketch Series, 2019. It received no Emmy nomination at any point, contrary to frequent assertion.
entries.description: A comedian offers absurd business advice to real small businesses that have not been told the premise. The discomfort is not performed, which is the…
entries.text: A comedian offers absurd business advice to real small businesses that have not been told the premise. The discomfort is not performed, which is the whole difference from scripted cringe: the audience's laughter arrives with a question attached about who consented to what. The series is a live contested case on exactly that ground, defended as a study of American commercial desperation and attacked as an unequal transaction with its participants.

entries.name: Till Death Us Do Part
entries.author: Johnny Speight
entries.awards: None recorded for the series.
entries.description: A West Ham docker delivers racist and reactionary opinions at his family, written as an indictment. It is the best-evidenced case in the whole field…
entries.text: A West Ham docker delivers racist and reactionary opinions at his family, written as an indictment. It is the best-evidenced case in the whole field of satire read against its intent: a documented portion of the audience took the character as a hero rather than a target. The writer's intention is not in dispute and the reception is not in dispute either, which makes it the pack's model contested card — the contest is between intention and effect, and neither side is arguable away.

entries.name: All in the Family
entries.author: Norman Lear
entries.awards: Primetime Emmy Awards for the series in 1971 and 1972 under the category name Outstanding Series — Comedy, and in 1973 under Outstanding Comedy Series; all three were awarded to the producers, Norman Lear among them.
entries.description: The American adaptation of Speight's premise, with a Queens loading-dock worker in the central role. Vidmar and Rokeach's 1974 study found that more…
entries.text: The American adaptation of Speight's premise, with a Queens loading-dock worker in the central role. Vidmar and Rokeach's 1974 study found that more prejudiced viewers were more likely to read Archie Bunker as the hero and to see the show as endorsing him, which is the only case in this field with empirical data on both sides. It is the reason this pack states that intent does not control reception and that no technique reliably forecloses the misreading.

entries.name: The Producers
entries.author: Mel Brooks
entries.awards: Academy Award for Best Story and Screenplay, a competitive Award of Merit, for the 1968 award year, presented at the 41st ceremony in 1969. The film was released in 1967, so three different years attach to it and are routinely collapsed into one.
entries.description: Two producers plan to profit from a guaranteed flop and stage a musical celebrating Hitler, which succeeds. The film's argument is that ridicule is…
entries.text: Two producers plan to profit from a guaranteed flop and stage a musical celebrating Hitler, which succeeds. The film's argument is that ridicule is the one response a dictator cannot survive, made by a writer who served in the Second World War. It is also a demonstration of the audit trope used as a whole plot: the entire structure is a countdown to an inspection, and the only possible failure is success.

entries.name: Blazing Saddles
entries.author: Mel Brooks
entries.awards: Three Academy Award nominations; no wins.
entries.description: A western parody in which a Black sheriff is appointed to a racist frontier town as a cynical political manoeuvre. The film reproduces the genre's…
entries.text: A western parody in which a Black sheriff is appointed to a racist frontier town as a cynical political manoeuvre. The film reproduces the genre's grammar competently before altering it, and attacks the industry that made the genre as well as the genre itself, breaking the studio wall literally in its final act. It is a live contested case on its racial language: defended as satire whose target is the racists, attacked as material that no longer reads that way to every audience, and both positions are documented.

entries.name: Withnail and I
entries.author: Bruce Robinson
entries.awards: None recorded.
entries.description: Two unemployed actors leave London for a cottage they are unequipped for. The refusal of adulthood is treated as terminal rather than charming, and…
entries.text: Two unemployed actors leave London for a cottage they are unequipped for. The refusal of adulthood is treated as terminal rather than charming, and the film ends by separating the two men rather than reconciling them. Its tonal handbrake is a single scene in a park, after which nothing is played for a laugh, and the closing soliloquy is the theatrical register maintained at full cost with no audience but a wolf enclosure.

entries.name: Old Baby
entries.author: Maria Bamford
entries.awards: None recorded.
entries.description: Stand-up special. Bamford performs the same material to progressively larger audiences within a single recording, beginning with one person on a…
entries.text: Stand-up special. Bamford performs the same material to progressively larger audiences within a single recording, beginning with one person on a bench and ending in a theatre. The escalation makes audience permission visible as a variable rather than a constant, which no other special has attempted. Her psychiatric history is performed in the voices of everyone involved in it, which holds the material at a workable distance while making it more exact than description would.

entries.name: Crazy Ex-Girlfriend
entries.author: Rachel Bloom and Aline Brosh McKenna
entries.awards: Two Primetime Emmy Awards in 2016, for Outstanding Original Music and Lyrics and Outstanding Choreography. Golden Globe for Best Actress in a Television Series, Musical or Comedy, 2016.
entries.description: A musical comedy whose protagonist's romantic obsession is diagnosed, mid-series, as borderline personality disorder, after which the songs…
entries.text: A musical comedy whose protagonist's romantic obsession is diagnosed, mid-series, as borderline personality disorder, after which the songs continue. The title is a challenge the show spends four seasons dismantling, and the musical numbers are the character's interior life rendered as pastiche rather than as decoration. It is the clearest television case of a comic format being used to make a psychiatric account survivable without softening it.

entries.name: Nanette
entries.author: Hannah Gadsby
entries.awards: Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Writing for a Variety Special, 2019, and a Peabody Award, which is board-selected and has no categories.
entries.description: Stand-up special. Gadsby spends the first half earning the room's permission with conventional self-deprecating material and the second half…
entries.text: Stand-up special. Gadsby spends the first half earning the room's permission with conventional self-deprecating material and the second half spending it, arguing that a joke about one's own trauma freezes the story at its worst point and prevents its completion. The show withholds the release the form promises and states why it is doing so, which makes the posture switch argued rather than a failure of nerve. It is the most complete instance in the form of a comedy withdrawing its own contract deliberately.

entries.name: I May Destroy You
entries.author: Michaela Coel
entries.awards: Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Writing for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie, 2021. Four BAFTA Television Awards in 2021, including Mini-Series and Leading Actress.
entries.description: A writer reconstructs a night on which she was drugged and raped, in a series that runs comic scenes at full strength alongside the reconstruction.…
entries.text: A writer reconstructs a night on which she was drugged and raped, in a series that runs comic scenes at full strength alongside the reconstruction. It is a hard boundary case for this pack rather than a comedy: the comic register is real and continuous, and the work is not organised around a reaction signal. It is carded because it demonstrates the limit of the anaesthetic-or-accelerant question — the comedy neither softens the material nor sharpens it, but establishes that the protagonist's life continued.

entries.name: Lysistrate
entries.author: Aristophanes
entries.awards: None. The Athenian dramatic festivals awarded prizes and no record survives of this play's placing.
entries.description: The women of the warring Greek states withhold sex until the men negotiate peace. Aristophanes builds the play on one impossible premise executed…
entries.text: The women of the warring Greek states withhold sex until the men negotiate peace. Aristophanes builds the play on one impossible premise executed with complete logical seriousness, which is the Old Comedy method, and the obscenity is structural rather than incidental. The production year is secure; which festival it was staged at is contested among scholars, and this pack does not resolve it.

entries.name: Batrachoi
entries.author: Aristophanes
entries.awards: First prize at the Lenaia, 405 BCE, and the play was granted the rare honour of a second production.
entries.description: Dionysus travels to the underworld to bring back a tragedian and ends up judging a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides. It is literary criticism…
entries.text: Dionysus travels to the underworld to bring back a tragedian and ends up judging a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides. It is literary criticism performed as comedy, with the two poets' verse weighed on an actual pair of scales, and it is the earliest surviving example of parody functioning as sustained critical argument. The date is secure.

entries.name: Nephelai
entries.author: Aristophanes
entries.awards: Third and last place at the City Dionysia, 423 BCE.
entries.description: A farmer enrols his son in a school of sophistry run by Socrates in order to argue his way out of debt. Plato's Apology has Socrates cite the…
entries.text: A farmer enrols his son in a school of sophistry run by Socrates in order to argue his way out of debt. Plato's Apology has Socrates cite the caricature as having damaged him with the jury, which makes this the oldest surviving case of a comedian's target claiming injury. The 423 production is securely dated, but the surviving text is a later revision from around 420 to 417 BCE which, on the majority scholarly view, was never staged — the play that came last is not the play that survives.

entries.name: Dyskolos
entries.author: Menander
entries.awards: First prize at the Lenaia, 316 BCE.
entries.description: A misanthropic farmer obstructs his daughter's suitor until he falls down a well and has to be rescued by him. It is the only complete Menander play…
entries.text: A misanthropic farmer obstructs his daughter's suitor until he falls down a well and has to be rescued by him. It is the only complete Menander play in existence, recovered from papyrus and first published in the late 1950s, and it is therefore the sole direct evidence for the New Comedy machinery the entire later tradition inherited. The competition date is a secure record.

entries.name: Menaechmi
entries.author: Plautus
entries.awards: None recorded. Roman comedy was performed at public festivals without a competitive prize structure comparable to the Athenian one.
entries.description: Twin brothers separated in childhood are mistaken for one another across a single day in Epidamnus. The plot reaches Shakespeare as The Comedy of…
entries.text: Twin brothers separated in childhood are mistaken for one another across a single day in Epidamnus. The plot reaches Shakespeare as The Comedy of Errors and the mechanism is still in use. The date given here is a conventional placeholder rather than a record: no year is securely attested for the play, and stating one with confidence is the most common error made about it.

entries.category: Commedia dell'Arte and the Italian Line
entries.name: Il servitore di due padroni
entries.author: Carlo Goldoni
entries.awards: [no award research performed — retroactive audit 2026-08-27]
entries.description: A servant takes a second employer without telling either, and spends the play preventing the two from meeting. Goldoni wrote it first as a scenario…
entries.text: A servant takes a second employer without telling either, and spends the play preventing the two from meeting. Goldoni wrote it first as a scenario for improvising actors and only later fixed it as a full text, so two versions exist and the difference between them is the difference between commedia and its replacement. The double booking is the whole mechanism, and the servant's hunger is what motivates an otherwise impossible schedule.

entries.category: Commedia dell'Arte and the Italian Line
entries.name: La locandiera
entries.author: Carlo Goldoni
entries.awards: [no award research performed — retroactive audit 2026-08-27]
entries.description: An innkeeper manages three suitors of different rank and defeats the one who claims to despise women. Goldoni gives the central role psychological…
entries.text: An innkeeper manages three suitors of different rank and defeats the one who claims to despise women. Goldoni gives the central role psychological consistency rather than a mask, which is the reform that ended improvised commedia while preserving its plots. The comedy is entirely a status contest, conducted through hospitality, and the woman running the inn wins every exchange in it.

entries.category: French Farce and the Molière Line
entries.name: Tartuffe
entries.author: Molière
entries.awards: [no award research performed — retroactive audit 2026-08-27]
entries.description: A religious impostor is installed in a household by a man who will not hear a word against him. The three-act version performed in 1664 was banned…
entries.text: A religious impostor is installed in a household by a man who will not hear a word against him. The three-act version performed in 1664 was banned and is lost; the five-act text that survives premiered in 1669 after five years of suppression, and dating the surviving play to 1664 is a common error. Molière makes the sycophancy transparent to everyone but the dupe, which transfers the whole comedy to the man being flattered.

entries.category: French Farce and the Molière Line
entries.name: Le Misanthrope
entries.author: Molière
entries.awards: [no award research performed — retroactive audit 2026-08-27]
entries.description: A man who insists on total honesty finds it incompatible with living among people, and loses everything to the principle. It is the hardest case in…
entries.text: A man who insists on total honesty finds it incompatible with living among people, and loses everything to the principle. It is the hardest case in the comedy of humours, because the single fixation driving the protagonist is a virtue rather than a vice, and Molière does not resolve it: Alceste is right and is destroyed anyway. The reasonable friend exists to measure him, which makes moderation the more disturbing position.

entries.category: French Farce and the Molière Line
entries.name: Une puce à l'oreille
entries.author: Georges Feydeau
entries.awards: [no award research performed — retroactive audit 2026-08-27]
entries.description: A wife's suspicion of her husband sends the entire cast to a hotel with two identical rooms and a porter who is his double. Feydeau designs the…
entries.text: A wife's suspicion of her husband sends the entire cast to a hotel with two identical rooms and a porter who is his double. Feydeau designs the building before the characters, so the plot is a consequence of the floor plan and no further authorial decision is required after the first act. It is the clearest surviving demonstration that farce is architecture, and the respectability of the characters is the fuel.

entries.category: French Farce and the Molière Line
entries.name: La Cantatrice chauve
entries.author: Eugène Ionesco
entries.awards: [no award research performed — retroactive audit 2026-08-27]
